The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

We start with bodies we know from everyday life: an eggshell, a tin can, a pressure vessel, the roof of a dome. All of them are thin compared with their other two dimensions, and all are curved. In chapter 5 we saw how structures are divided by shape: a surface structure has one dimension, the thickness, much smaller than the other two, and if it is flat it is called a plate (chapter 18), if it is curved, a shell (lupina). This chapter is its treatment.

In everyday language a shell is the thin hard cover of an egg or a nut. Engineers use the word for every thin curved body, because it has the same property: the cover is thin and therefore light, yet it carries a lot, because it is curved. The Slovenian word lupina has the same everyday meaning (the cover of an egg or a nut). Why curvature is so useful we show in figure 22.1 with two walls of the same steel, equally thick and under the same pressure.

First take the flat wall, a strip of thickness \(h = 2\) mm that lies on two supports, \(100\) mm apart. We draw it grey and dashed, as it is before loading. From above oil presses on it with the pressure \(p = 3\) MPa, everywhere perpendicular to the wall. A force pulling along the flat wall has no component in the direction of the pressure, so it cannot balance the pressure. The wall bends, we draw it orange, and at the middle it sags by \(w\) (the drawing magnifies the bending greatly). In bending the upper fibres shorten, the lower ones lengthen, and the middle ones stay as they are. So the stress in the cross-section at the middle of the strip is compressive at the top, tensile at the bottom and zero at mid-thickness: the material around mid-thickness does almost no work. By corollary 18.26 the moment at the middle of the strip is \(pL^2/8\), per millimetre of width

\[\frac{3\ \text{N/mm}^2 \cdot (100\ \text{mm})^2}{8} = 3750\ \text{N mm/mm} ,\]

and by (18.10) the largest stress is \(6 \cdot 3750/2^2 = 5625\) MPa. This is more than 25 times the yield stress of the steel, \(220\) MPa (definition 2.7), so the flat wall would bend permanently.

Now we roll the same wall into a tube with the mean radius \(R = 50\) mm and the thickness \(h = 2\) mm. The wall is only \(2/50 = 1/25\) of the radius thick, and the diameter of the tube is \(100\) mm, equal to the span of the flat wall. We fill the tube with oil at the pressure \(p = 3\) MPa, which presses on the wall from inside, again everywhere perpendicular to it. The tube widens equally everywhere, by \(w\), and stays round (the drawing magnifies the widening greatly). Why does it not bend? We cut the tube horizontally through the axis and keep the upper half, of unit length, as with the thick tube in chapter 11 (figure 11.56). The oil pushes it upward, in total with the force \(p \cdot 2R\), the pressure times the width of the bore. The bore is really \(2R - h = 98\) mm wide, but we neglect the difference of 2 % here, and section 22.5.2 computes it. The half is at rest, so the lower half must pull it downward on both cuts of the wall, each time with the force \(N = pR = 150\) N/mm. Since the wall runs vertically at the cut, this force pulls along the wall: a curved wall carries pressure by tension. The whole thickness pulls equally, so the stress is constant over the thickness, \(N/h = pR/h = 75\) MPa (the thin-wall formula (11.36) with the mean radius), about a third of the yield stress.

The same wall thus carries the same pressure, when curved, with a stress \(5625/75 = 75\) times smaller than when flat. From the two formulas the ratio is

\[\frac{6\,p\,(2R)^2/8}{h^2} \Big/ \frac{p\,R}{h} = \frac{3R}{h} ,\]

so the advantage of the curved wall is the larger, the thinner the wall. The chapter will show how pressure loads an arbitrary curved wall, by tension instead of bending, and where this fails.

The chapter promises three things. First, we will be able to describe any curved wall: where a point of the wall is, how far apart two points are along the wall, at which angle two lines on the wall meet, and how curved the wall is. Second, for a thin wall we will derive from chapter 11 the strains, the internal forces per unit length and the energy, with the limit up to which a thin wall is really thin, and compute the stresses in vessels and domes with numbers from the earlier chapters. Third, we will show where the simple calculation fails, at edges and junctions, and how the finite elements known from chapters 7 and 12 deal with it. What we cannot prove from the book we will state with a source and say that it is stated.

First geometry. Without it we cannot even say where a point of the shell is.

22.1 The middle surface of a shell

The wall of a boiler is a piece of iron with a length and a width, and a thickness that is much smaller. How do we determine a point of this piece? With two numbers we say where on the wall it is, and with a third how deep in the wall. What is "the wall" if it has two surfaces, an inner and an outer one? We take the surface that lies halfway between them and measure everything else from it.

Let us draw a piece of the wall as seen obliquely from above. We have the inner and the outer surface with their edges. Between them is the iron, which along the top edge and at the right end we see in section as a grey area of thickness \(h\). Between them we draw the middle surface and divide it with two families of lines, counted by the parameters \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). A surface described by two parameters we know from chapter 4 (definition 4.61), with points \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\) and normal vector \(\vek N\) ((4.33)). At a chosen point of the middle surface we draw the normal, the perpendicular to the surface with unit vector \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) (definition 2.17). A point of the shell is thus on the normal through a point of the middle surface, at the distance \(|z|\) from it, with \(z > 0\) on the side to which \(\vek n\) points, and the thickness \(h\) is the distance between the surfaces measured along the normal, so \(-h/2 \le z \le h/2\). We write this as a definition.

Definition 22.1 Shell and its middle surface (lupina in njena srednja ploskev)

Let \(\vek r\) be a description of a surface \(S\) on a set \(M\) of the parameter plane \((q_1, q_2)\) (definition 4.61), which has continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order on an open set \(U \supseteq M\), and \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) the unit normal of the surface. Let \(h > 0\) be a number with the unit of length. The map

\[\vek x(q_1, q_2, z) = \vek r(q_1, q_2) + z\,\vek n(q_1, q_2) , \qquad (q_1, q_2) \in M , \quad -\frac{h}{2} \le z \le \frac{h}{2} , \tag{22.1}\]

has a triple of numbers as input and a point of space as output. Let it be injective on this set of triples. The set of its points is a shell (lupina), \(S\) is its middle surface (srednja ploskev), \(h\) its thickness (debelina), and the points with \(z = \pm h/2\) form its faces (površini). A shell is thin if \(h\) is much smaller than every other dimension of the middle surface (radii, lengths, distances between edges).

Source: VK §11.1 (PDF p. 308) for a surface given by two parameters, and §12.1 (PDF p. 330) for the thickness and the requirement that the shell is thin in comparison with its other dimensions. The form \(\vek x = \vek r + z\,\vek n\) and the requirement of injectivity are ours: VK does not write them so.

The name middle surface is understandable: it lies halfway between the faces. The definition is not as simple as it looks, in two places, which figure 22.3 shows.

At the top left is the cross-section of a tube with the middle surface, a circle of radius \(R\). At the point \(\vek r\) of the middle surface the normal \(\vek n\) points toward the axis, and the point \(\vek x\) of the shell is on it, at \(z\) from the middle surface. First, we require the second derivative of the map \(\vek r\), because the normal \(\vek n\) must change continuously differentiably with \((q_1, q_2)\), as we will measure in section 22.2 how it turns. The requirement does not hold at a kink, for example where the tube meets a conical head: there the normal jumps from one direction to another. Such a piece we therefore divide into two shells with an edge between them, and what happens at the edge is told in section 22.7. Second, injectivity is not always satisfied. The normals of a circular tube approach each other and meet on the axis, at the distance \(R\) from the middle surface. If \(h/2\) were larger than \(R\) (top right), the normal from the point \(A\) would reach past the axis, and so would the normal from the opposite point \(B\), and the point \(X\) would be given by two different triples \((q_1, q_2, z)\). The shell would overlap itself there. So injectivity holds for \(h/2 < R\). The thick tube of chapter 11 with radii 40 mm and 60 mm has a mean radius of 50 mm and \(h = 20\) mm, so \(h/(2R) = 0{,}2\) and the tube is still a shell by the definition, but not thin: \(h/R = 0{,}4\) is not "much smaller". The thin tube of the introduction has \(h/R = 2/50 = 0{,}04\). Both are drawn in true proportion. How precisely "thin" is meant in a calculation, we fix in section 22.3 with the bound \(h/(2R)\) and with numbers. What matters here is only that we will describe the shell everywhere by its middle surface and its thickness.

What remains is to describe the middle surface alone: how it changes when we move along it. We need directions and lengths on it.

On the surface we take a net of lines, in which once the parameter \(q_2\) is constant and once \(q_1\), and look at one point. If we move along a line \(q_2 = \) const. with the parameter \(q_1\), the point \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\) moves along a curve, its velocity is the vector \(\partial\vek r/\partial q_1\) and points along the line. Such a vector is the first tangent vector \(\vek a_1\) at the point. The same along a line \(q_1 = \) const. gives the second, \(\vek a_2\). Through the chosen point they span a plane that touches the surface. The word tangent is from the Latin tangere, to touch. The vector product \(\vek a_1 \times \vek a_2\) is perpendicular to both (lemma 2.34, item 4) and is the normal vector of the surface, which we know from (4.33). Between the vectors there is an angle \(\gamma\), and here we see that the net need not be rectangular.

Definition 22.2 Tangent vectors of a surface (tangentna vektorja ploskve)

Let \(\vek r\) be a description of a surface \(S\) (definition 4.61). The vectors

\[\vek a_1 = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial q_1} , \qquad \vek a_2 = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial q_2} \tag{22.2}\]

are the tangent vectors (tangentna vektorja) of the surface at the point \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\), functions with a pair of parameters as input and a vector with the unit of length per unit of parameter as output. Their linear span is the tangent plane (tangentna ravnina). The normal vector is \(\vek N = \vek a_1 \times \vek a_2 \neq \vek 0\), so the vectors are linearly independent, and the normal \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) is perpendicular to the tangent plane. If \(\vek a_1 \cdot \vek a_2 = 0\) at every point of \(M\), the coordinate lines are perpendicular at every point (theorem 2.10) and the coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) are orthogonal on the surface.

Source: VK §11.1 (11.5) (PDF p. 309): the tangent vectors \(\vek r_{,\alpha}\) and \(\vek r_{,\beta}\) along the coordinate lines. The letters \(q_1\), \(q_2\) are ours, because in chapter 11 the coordinates are \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\).

But how do we compute from the tangent vectors the length of a curve that runs along the surface? Let us look at figure 22.5.

On the left is the parameter plane with a net in which every small square has sides of one unit of both parameters. Along it runs a curve \(\vek q(t)\), and at the chosen point it has the velocity \(\vek q'\). The velocity is the diagonal of a rectangle with sides \(q_1'\) and \(q_2'\), so by the Pythagorean theorem its length is \(\sqrt{q_1'^2 + q_2'^2}\). The description \(\vek r\) maps the parameter plane onto the surface, and the curve becomes the curve \(\vek c(t) = \vek r(\vek q(t))\) on the surface. The net is stretched and tilted in this. At the chosen point \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) point along the coordinate lines, of lengths \(|\vek a_1|\) and \(|\vek a_2|\), with the angle \(\gamma\) between them, and span a parallelogram in the tangent plane. On the right this plane is magnified. The velocity of the curve on the surface is by the chain rule \(\vek c' = q_1'\vek a_1 + q_2'\vek a_2\) (the proof is in lemma 22.5), so it is the diagonal of a parallelogram with the sides \(q_1'\vek a_1\) and \(q_2'\vek a_2\), of lengths \(q_1'|\vek a_1|\) and \(q_2'|\vek a_2|\), with the angle \(\gamma\) between them. There is no right angle any more, so the law of cosines replaces the Pythagorean theorem. In the triangle of one side, the other side and the diagonal, the angle opposite the diagonal is \(180^\circ - \gamma\), and \(\cos(180^\circ - \gamma) = -\cos\gamma\), so the diagonal has the squared length

\[|\vek c'|^2 = q_1'^2\,|\vek a_1|^2 + 2\,q_1'q_2'\,|\vek a_1||\vek a_2|\cos\gamma + q_2'^2\,|\vek a_2|^2 .\]

Only three numbers appear in it, \(|\vek a_1|^2 = \vek a_1\cdot\vek a_1\), \(|\vek a_2|^2 = \vek a_2\cdot\vek a_2\) and \(|\vek a_1||\vek a_2|\cos\gamma = \vek a_1\cdot\vek a_2\). They tell how much length in space a move in the parameter plane gives in each direction and at which angle the directions meet, and we collect them in a matrix.

Definition 22.3 First fundamental form of a surface (prva osnovna forma ploskve)

Let \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) be the tangent vectors of a surface \(S\) with description \(\vek r\) (definition 22.2). The first fundamental form (prva osnovna forma) is the function with a pair \((q_1, q_2)\) of \(M\) as input and a symmetric matrix with two rows and two columns as output

\[\mat A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{12} & a_{22} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{i}} \cdot \vek a_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{22.3}\]

If \(\mat F\) is the matrix with three rows and two columns whose columns are \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) (the matrix of derivatives of the map \(\vek r\)), then \(\mat A = \mat F^\T\mat F\). For a pair of numbers \(\vek u = (u_1, u_2)\), \(\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek u = |u_1\vek a_1 + u_2\vek a_2|^2\) is a quadratic function of both numbers, called a quadratic form.

Source: VK §11.3 (11.10), (11.11) (PDF p. 313) writes \(a_{\mathrm{ik}} = \vek r_{,\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek r_{,\mathrm{k}}\) and the "first quadratic form" \(ds^2 = a_{\mathrm{ik}}\,d\alpha_{\mathrm{i}}\,d\alpha_{\mathrm{k}}\). Instead of the arc length with differentials we use it on the velocity of a curve in lemma 22.5 (rule 47). The notation \(\mat A = \mat F^\T\mat F\) is ours.

The name is composed like this: the form is called quadratic because \(\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek u\) is quadratic in the numbers \(u_1\) and \(u_2\), namely \(\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek u = a_{11}u_1^2 + 2a_{12}u_1u_2 + a_{22}u_2^2\). For \(\vek u = \vek q'\) this is the squared length of the velocity from the figure. It is fundamental because from it we compute everything that we measure on a surface with a ruler and a protractor: lengths, angles and areas. It is first because in section 22.2 we will need a second one, which measures how the surface curves in space and which the first does not know. Before we use it, let us say what the matrix \(\mat A\) certainly has.

We describe the same surface in two ways and connect them. We draw the plane \((\tilde q_1, \tilde q_2)\) with the new parameters and the plane \((q_1, q_2)\) with the old ones. The change \(\tau\) assigns to every point of the first plane a point of the second, and the description \(\vek r\) assigns to a point of the second plane a point on the surface. Together, \(\vek r_2 = \vek r\circ\tau\) is another description of the same surface. A curve in the first plane goes under \(\tau\) to a curve in the second and under \(\vek r\) to the curve \(\vek c\) on the surface, which is the same whatever the description. A small step \(\mathrm{d}\tilde{\vek q}\) in the first plane is mapped by \(\tau\) to the step \(\mat J\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\vek q}\) in the second, and this by \(\vek r\) to the step \(\mat F\mat J\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\vek q}\) on the surface. On the surface we also draw the parallelogram of the tangent vectors, with area \(|\vek N|\).

Lemma 22.4 Determinant of the first form and change of description (determinanta prve forme in zamenjava opisa)

Let \(\vek r\) be a description of a surface \(S\) and \(\mat A\) its first fundamental form (definition 22.3).

  1. \(\det\mat A = a_{11}a_{22} - a_{12}^2 = |\vek N|^2 > 0\).
  2. Let \(\vek r_2 = \vek r\circ\tau\) be another description of the same surface, as in corollary 4.64, and \(\mat J\) the matrix of derivatives of the map \(\tau\) with two rows and columns. Then the first form of the description \(\vek r_2\) at the point \((\tilde q_1, \tilde q_2)\) is
    \[\mat A_2 = \mat J^\T\,\mat A\big(\tau(\tilde q_1, \tilde q_2)\big)\,\mat J . \tag{22.4}\]
Proof

We must show that the determinant equals the square of the normal vector and that under a change of description the matrix transforms with the matrix of derivatives of the change.

  1. By lemma 2.34, item 5, \(|\vek a_1\times\vek a_2|^2 = |\vek a_1|^2|\vek a_2|^2 - (\vek a_1\cdot\vek a_2)^2\), and the right side is \(a_{11}a_{22} - a_{12}^2\). In the figure this is the square of the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors: the area is \(|\vek a_1||\vek a_2|\sin\gamma\), and its square is \(|\vek a_1|^2|\vek a_2|^2(1 - \cos^2\gamma)\), the same right side.
  2. Since \(\vek N \neq \vek 0\) by definition 4.61, \(|\vek N|^2 > 0\).
  3. The matrix of derivatives of the composite map \(\vek r\circ\tau\) is by corollary 4.44 the product of the matrices of derivatives: \(\mat F_2 = \mat F\,\mat J\), where \(\mat F\) is evaluated at the point \(\tau(\tilde q_1, \tilde q_2)\).
  4. Since the step on the surface is \(\mat F\,\mat J\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\vek q}\), we have \(\mat A_2 = \mat F_2^\T\mat F_2 = \mat J^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\mat J = \mat J^\T\mat A\,\mat J\), because the order of a product is reversed under transposition.

Source: Item 1 is Lagrange's identity from lemma 2.34. Item 2 is our proof with the chain rule. VK §11.3 (PDF p. 313) does not treat a change of description.

By item 1, \(\sqrt{\det\mat A} = |\vek N|\), the area of the parallelogram of the tangent vectors, which is the factor in the surface integral (4.34): the area of a surface follows from the first form. Now we can say what we compute from it.

Lemma 22.5 Length, angle and area on a surface (dolžina, kot in ploščina na ploskvi)

Let \(\vek r\) be a description of a surface \(S\) with first form \(\mat A\), and let \(q_1(t)\) and \(q_2(t)\) be continuously differentiable functions on an interval \([\alpha, \beta]\) with values in \(M\). A curve on the surface is \(\vek c(t) = \vek r\big(q_1(t), q_2(t)\big)\). Then:

  1. \(\vek c'(t) = q_1'(t)\,\vek a_1 + q_2'(t)\,\vek a_2\), every velocity of a curve on the surface lies in the tangent plane, and \(|\vek c'(t)|^2 = \vek q'(t)^\T\mat A\,\vek q'(t)\) for \(\vek q' = (q_1', q_2')\).
  2. The length of the curve, defined as the integral of the speed \(|\vek c'|\) (as in definition 8.5, with three components instead of two), is
    \[L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\vek q'(t)^\T\mat A\,\vek q'(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{22.5}\]
  3. Let a second curve on the surface have at the same point the velocity \(\vek d' = w_1\vek a_1 + w_2\vek a_2\) and the first \(\vek c' = u_1\vek a_1 + u_2\vek a_2\). The angle \(\gamma\) between the curves is the angle between these vectors, and
    \[\cos\gamma = \frac{\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek w}{\sqrt{\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek u}\,\sqrt{\vek w^\T\mat A\,\vek w}} . \tag{22.6}\]
  4. The area of the surface \(S\) is \(\int_{\mathrm{M}}\sqrt{\det\mat A}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  5. Length, angle and area do not depend on the description of the surface: the curve on the surface is the same, for a description \(\vek r_2 = \vek r\circ\tau\) from lemma 22.4 they give the same numbers.
Proof

We must show that the velocity of a curve is expressed with the tangent vectors, that all formulas follow from this, and that a change of description does not alter them.

  1. The components of the function \(\vek r\) are continuously differentiable, and so are the functions \(q_{\mathrm{i}}(t)\), so by the chain rule (lemma 4.43, the version with an interval) \(\vek c'(t) = q_1'\,\partial\vek r/\partial q_1 + q_2'\,\partial\vek r/\partial q_2\) for each component. This is the diagonal of the parallelogram of figure 22.5.
  2. The square of the length of the velocity is \(|\vek c'|^2 = \vek c'\cdot\vek c' = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} q_{\mathrm{i}}'q_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek a_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek q'^\T\mat A\,\vek q'\) by the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12). This is the law of cosines from the figure, written with scalar products. This proves item 1 and (22.5).
  3. The angle between nonzero vectors, such as the angle \(\gamma\) between \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\), is the angle whose cosine is the scalar product divided by the product of the lengths (chapter 2). The scalar product \(\vek c'\cdot\vek d' = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}u_{\mathrm{i}}w_{\mathrm{j}}\,a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek w\) as in step 2, and the lengths are the roots of \(\vek u^\T\mat A\,\vek u\) and \(\vek w^\T\mat A\,\vek w\).
  4. By (4.34) with \(f = 1\) the area is \(\int_{\mathrm{M}} |\vek N|\,\mathrm{d}A\), and \(|\vek N| = \sqrt{\det\mat A}\), the area of the parallelogram, by item 1 of lemma 22.4.
  5. The function \(\vek c(t)\), which gives the point of the curve in space, is the same whichever description of the surface we write it with, so it has the same velocity \(\vek c'(t)\). If \(\vek r_2 = \vek r\circ\tau\) and \(\vek q = \tau(\tilde{\vek q})\), then \(\vek c(t) = \vek r_2(\tilde{\vek q}(t))\) with exactly the same velocity, and the formula (22.5), which is a computation of this velocity, gives the same number. For the angle the velocities of both curves are the same vectors. For the area this is stated by corollary 4.64. The matrix \(\mat A_2 = \mat J^\T\mat A\,\mat J\) is only another way of writing the same value: \(\tilde{\vek q}'^\T\mat A_2\,\tilde{\vek q}' = (\mat J\tilde{\vek q}')^\T\mat A\,(\mat J\tilde{\vek q}') = \vek q'^\T\mat A\,\vek q'\), because \(\vek q' = \mat J\tilde{\vek q}'\) by the chain rule.

Source: VK §11.3 (PDF p. 313-314): the first quadratic form for lengths, areas and angles. VK uses the arc length with differentials \(ds\) and \(d\alpha\), we use the velocity of a curve. The extension of the definition of the length of a curve from the plane to space is ours: the justification with segments between points does not use the plane. We also do not have a proof that polygonal lines converge to this integral, even in the plane (see definition 8.5).

The lemma says that the first form, the ruler and the protractor of the net, is all we need about a surface to measure on it, and that this does not depend on the chosen description. We took the length of a curve in space as the integral of the speed, as in the plane: this is a simplification that the book makes also for a plane curve, and the full treatment (the limit of polygonal lines) is in KREYSZIG §9.5 (PDF p. 411). That the integral gives the right number is checked by example 22.8 below: for one turn of a helix it gives the same length as we measure with a ruler on the unrolled cylinder.

When the coordinate lines are perpendicular at every point, the angle \(\gamma\) is a right angle, \(\cos\gamma = 0\), so \(a_{12} = |\vek a_1||\vek a_2|\cos\gamma = 0\), and the first form has only two numbers, the diagonal entries \(a_{11}\) and \(a_{22}\). Their roots get a name of their own.

Definition 22.6 Scale factors of a surface (skalirna faktorja ploskve)

Let \(a_{12} = 0\) on \(M\) (orthogonal coordinates on the surface, definition 22.2). The scale factors (skalirna faktorja) of the surface are the functions \(A_1 = \sqrt{a_{11}} = |\vek a_1|\) and \(A_2 = \sqrt{a_{22}} = |\vek a_2|\), with the unit of length per unit of parameter, and \(\mat A = \mathrm{diag}(A_1^2, A_2^2)\). The unit vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{i}}/A_{\mathrm{i}}\) with \(\vek n\) form a local frame (as in lemma 11.14).

Source: VK §11.3 (11.12), (11.13) (PDF p. 313) calls them the Lamé parameters \(A\) and \(B\). We write \(A_1\), \(A_2\) so as not to clash with the thickness \(h\) and with the scale factors \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\) of definition 11.13, which are in space, not on a surface.

The scale factor \(A_{\mathrm{i}}\) is like \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\) of chapter 11: it is the length of the vector \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\) and tells how much straight length falls on a unit of the parameter. From section 22.3 on we will always choose the coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) of the shell so that \(a_{12} = 0\). That such a choice is possible is not self-evident. For the surfaces of revolution below, symmetry gives it. For a general surface it is given by the system of lines of curvature (definition 22.16), whose existence we state after VK and do not prove (section 22.2.3). That the choice matters is shown by example 22.8: on the same cylinder another net gives \(a_{12} \ne 0\).

As examples let us first look at three surfaces that we will use most in the chapter, and for which the coordinate lines are perpendicular.

We draw a dome, made by rotating a plane curve about the axis. The position of the curve in one of the planes through the axis is a meridian, as on a globe, where the meridians connect the poles and all places on one meridian have noon at the same time. Every point of the curve describes in the rotation a circle that is parallel to the others, and we call it a parallel, like a parallel on the globe. Through the point \(P\) we take one meridian, to which \(\vek a_1\) is the tangent, and one parallel with the tangent \(\vek a_2\). At \(P\) we also draw the normal \(\vek n\), perpendicular to both vectors. The point \(P\) is at the distance \(\rho\) from the axis, the radius of the parallel. On the right is the meridian plane in section with the arc of the meridian and the point \(P\). In it is the angle \(\varphi\) between the axis and the line from the centre to \(P\), of length \(R\). The distance \(\rho\) is the leg opposite the angle \(\varphi\), so \(\rho = R\sin\varphi\). Since the meridian and the parallel are perpendicular at \(P\), the net is not oblique as in the previous figure.

The three surfaces of revolution that we will use are drawn in figure 22.8 to the same scale, with the dimensions of the example below.

Example 22.7 Surfaces of revolution: cylinder, sphere, cone (vrtenine: valj, krogla, stožec)

Let the meridian be a curve given by the functions \(\rho(q_1)\) (distance from the axis \(z\)) and \(\zeta(q_1)\) (height), and let \(\theta\) be the angle of rotation about the axis. A surface of revolution (vrtenina) has the description \(\vek r(q_1, \theta) = \big(\rho\cos\theta,\ \rho\sin\theta,\ \zeta\big)\). Then

\[\vek a_1 = (\rho'\cos\theta,\ \rho'\sin\theta,\ \zeta') , \quad \vek a_2 = \rho\,(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta,\ 0) , \quad \mat A = \begin{pmatrix} \rho'^2 + \zeta'^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \rho^2 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{22.7}\]

\(\vek N = \rho\,(-\zeta'\cos\theta,\ -\zeta'\sin\theta,\ \rho')\) and \(|\vek N| = \rho\sqrt{\rho'^2 + \zeta'^2}\). Perpendicularity follows from \(a_{12} = 0\). The scale factors (definition 22.6) are \(A_1 = \sqrt{\rho'^2 + \zeta'^2}\) and \(A_2 = \rho\). They tell how much length in space falls on a unit of the parameter along a coordinate line.

  1. Cylinder of radius \(R = 50\) mm about the axis: \(\rho = R\), \(\zeta = q_1 = z\), so \(A_1 = 1\), \(A_2 = 50\) mm, and \(\vek N = -R\,(\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) points toward the axis.
  2. Sphere of radius \(R = 50\) mm with the angle \(\varphi = q_1\) from the axis: \(\rho = R\sin\varphi\), \(\zeta = R\cos\varphi\), so \(A_1 = R = 50\) mm and \(A_2 = R\sin\varphi\). On the meridian about the axis, at \(\varphi = 60^\circ\) the distance from the axis is \(A_2 = 43{,}30\) mm, and \(\vek N = R^2\sin\varphi\,(\sin\varphi\cos\theta, \sin\varphi\sin\theta, \cos\varphi)\) points outward.
  3. Cone about the axis with the half-angle \(\alpha = 30^\circ\) at the apex, \(s\) measured along the generator from the apex: \(\rho = s\sin\alpha\), \(\zeta = s\cos\alpha\), so \(A_1 = 1\) and \(A_2 = s\sin\alpha\), at \(s = 20\) mm \(A_2 = 10\) mm and at \(s = 80\) mm it is \(40\) mm.

For the cylinder and the cone \(q_1\) is a length along the meridian, for the sphere an angle, so \(A_1\) equals 1 and \(R\) respectively. The direction of the normal depends on the order of the coordinates and on the direction of the meridian: for the cylinder with \(z\) upward it points toward the axis, for the sphere with \(\varphi\) from the axis outward (SymPy, num-01.py). Swapping the order of \(q_1\), \(\theta\) or reversing the meridian reverses the normal, as in definition 4.61.

For the cylinder the test with the first form is simple: the meridian is a straight line parallel to the axis, and \(\vek a_1\) is the unit vector along it. An arc of a parallel with the angle \(\Delta\theta\) has the length \(R\,\Delta\theta\), so \(A_2 = R\). For the sphere an arc of a meridian with the angle \(\Delta\varphi\) has the length \(R\,\Delta\varphi\), and an arc of a parallel with the angle \(\Delta\theta\) the length \(R\sin\varphi\,\Delta\theta\), which is less the closer the parallel is to the axis. That the net of meridians and parallels is not uniform is shown by \(A_2 = R\sin\varphi\): at \(\varphi = 60^\circ\) the parallel is a circle of radius \(43{,}30\) mm, \(2\pi \cdot 43{,}30 = 272{,}07\) mm long, at \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) a circle of radius \(50\) mm, \(314{,}16\) mm long.

All three surfaces of revolution have \(a_{12} = 0\), so the coordinate lines are perpendicular. Let us take one more example that does not have this property, and see what the first form tells about an oblique net.

We draw a cylinder of radius \(R\) and on it two families of helices. One family is blue and climbs with a rise \(c\) per radian, the other orange and descends equally steeply, with a rise \(-c\). Through the chosen point goes one helix of each family, the first with the tangent vector \(\vek a_1\), the second with the vector \(\vek a_2\). On the right we cut the cylinder along a generator and unroll it into a rectangle of width \(2\pi R\), because that is the circumference. Unrolling does not change lengths on the cylinder, and the helices of both families become straight lines. The two helices through the point become a rising and a falling straight line through the same point, with the vectors \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\). The angle \(\gamma\) between them is the angle between the helices. One turn of a helix is the hypotenuse of a triangle with the horizontal leg \(2\pi R\) and the vertical leg \(2\pi c\).

We draw the same cylinder with a second net. On the left is the cylinder with the net of helices \((u, v)\) through a chosen point, and in it the normal of this description, pointing toward the axis. In the middle is the same cylinder with the net of circles and generators \((\theta, z)\) through the same point, and its normal points outward. On the right is the square \([0, \pi/2]^2\) of the plane \((u, v)\) and beside it the parallelogram to which the change to \((\theta, z)\) maps it.

Example 22.8 A helical grid on the cylinder (vijačna mreža na valju)

Let the cylinder be the one of example 22.7 with radius \(R = 50\) mm and let the description be \(\vek r(u, v) = \big(R\cos(u + v),\ R\sin(u + v),\ c\,(u - v)\big)\) with \(c = 25\) mm and angles \(u\), \(v\) in radians. The line \(v = \) const. is a helix with a rise \(c\) per radian, the line \(u = \) const. a helix with a rise \(-c\), so of the other hand. The tangent vectors are \(\vek a_1 = (-R\sin(u + v),\ R\cos(u + v),\ c)\) and \(\vek a_2 = (-R\sin(u + v),\ R\cos(u + v),\ -c)\), and

\[\mat A = \begin{pmatrix} R^2 + c^2 & R^2 - c^2 \\ R^2 - c^2 & R^2 + c^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3125 & 1875 \\ 1875 & 3125 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{mm}^2 . \tag{22.8}\]
  1. The coordinates are not orthogonal (definition 22.6): \(a_{12} = 1875\ \text{mm}^2 \neq 0\). The test of the definition fails, although the surface is the same cylinder as in example 22.7, where \(a_{12} = 0\).
  2. The angle between the lines by (22.6) with \(\vek u = (1, 0)\) and \(\vek w = (0, 1)\) is \(\cos\gamma = a_{12}/\sqrt{a_{11}a_{22}} = 1875/3125 = 0{,}6\), \(\gamma = 53{,}13^\circ\). Each helix climbs at the angle \(\arctan(c/R) = 26{,}57^\circ\) to the parallel, which is a horizontal straight line on the unrolled cylinder. Both helices are equally steep, one upward and one downward, so the parallel bisects the angle between them and \(\gamma = 2 \cdot 26{,}57^\circ = 53{,}13^\circ\), the same as from the first form.
  3. The length of one turn of the first helix (\(u\) from 0 to \(2\pi\), \(v = 0\)) is by (22.5) \(\sqrt{3125}\cdot 2\pi = 55{,}90 \cdot 6{,}283 = 351{,}24\) mm. On the developed cylinder (right side of the figure) this is the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs \(2\pi R = 314{,}16\) mm and \(2\pi c = 157{,}08\) mm, \(\sqrt{314{,}16^2 + 157{,}08^2} = 351{,}24\) mm, the same number.
  4. The description \(\vek r_2(\theta, z) = (R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, z)\), which is the description of the cylinder of example 22.7 with the order of the coordinates swapped, has \(\theta = u + v\), \(z = c(u - v)\), the matrix of derivatives \(\mat J = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ c & -c\end{pmatrix}\) with determinant \(-2c = -50\) mm and \(\mat A_2 = \mathrm{diag}(R^2, 1)\) in the order \((\theta, z)\). By lemma 22.4 \(\mat J^\T\mat A_2\,\mat J = \mat A\), which SymPy confirms. The area of the square \([0, \pi/2]^2\) in \((u, v)\) is by lemma 22.5 \(\sqrt{\det\mat A}\,(\pi/2)^2 = 2Rc\,(\pi/2)^2 = 6168{,}50\ \text{mm}^2\) and in \((\theta, z)\), where the image of the square is a parallelogram of area \(|\det\mat J|\,(\pi/2)^2 = 2c\,(\pi/2)^2\) and where \(\sqrt{\det\mat A_2} = R\), it is \(R\cdot 2c\,(\pi/2)^2\), again \(6168{,}50\ \text{mm}^2\).
  5. Since \(\det\mat J < 0\), the normal in the description \((u, v)\) points toward the axis, in the description \((\theta, z)\) outward. Lengths and areas do not change, the direction of the normal does, as corollary 4.64 says.

What we found: the first form distinguishes the two nets on the same surface, but each net gives the same length and area. For later expressions we need an orthogonal net, because \(\mat A\) will then be diagonal.

The last example is special. The net of meridians and parallels on the sphere is orthogonal, but the description fails at two points, the poles.

Example 22.9 The poles of a sphere and the apex of a cone (pola krogle in vrh stožca)

For the sphere of example 22.7 \(|\vek N| = R^2\sin\varphi\) (SymPy, num-01.py), so at \(\varphi = 0\), at the pole, where all meridians meet, \(\vek N = \vek 0\) and the description there does not satisfy definition 4.61. The parallel with \(\varphi = 0\) is a point: \(\vek a_2 = \vek 0\). The same holds for the apex of the cone at \(s = 0\) (\(A_2 = s\sin\alpha = 0\)). For the sphere this is a fault of the description, not of the surface: the sphere has a normal at the pole, pointing along the axis, and another description gives it, for example the graph \(z = \sqrt{R^2 - x^2 - y^2}\), as with the description \(\vek r(s, t) = (s^3, t, 0)\) of a flat square in chapter 4, which fails on the line \(s = 0\), although the plane has a normal there. For the cone it is different: at the apex there is no tangent plane, because it would have to contain the directions of all generators through the apex, and these do not lie in any plane, and a shell reaching to the apex has no unit normal of the middle surface. So we will always treat conical shells as a truncated cone and not take them up to the apex.

A shell is thus described by its middle surface, which at every point has two tangent vectors, a normal and a first form, and by its thickness \(h\). On three surfaces of revolution we computed the scale factors, on the helical grid we saw that the first form distinguishes a non-orthogonal net from an orthogonal one, and at the poles of the sphere that a description can fail where the surface itself is not at fault. One thing is missing: the tangent vectors say how a surface is stretched, but not how it curves in space. The cylinder with the description \(\vek r_2(\theta, z)\) has the first form \(\mathrm{diag}(R^2, 1)\), and exactly the same one has the flat rectangle with the description \((\theta, z) \mapsto (R\theta, z, 0)\), which is the cylinder unrolled into the plane. In space the two surfaces differ, but the first form does not tell them apart. The next section therefore introduces the second fundamental form and the curvature.

Notation in this chapter. The thickness of a shell is the total \(h\), not the half as in the generalized plane stress state of chapter 11 (\(-h \le z \le h\)) and not the scale factor \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\) (there, in space, here we write \(A_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the factors of the surface and \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the factors in the space of the shell). The normal vector of the surface \(\vek N\) is bold, the internal forces of the shell in section 22.3 have indices (\(N_1\), \(N_2\)). The letter \(K\) is not used for the bulk modulus of chapter 11 but for the Gaussian curvature, and \(D\) is the bending stiffness of the shell, which we introduce in section 22.3, and is not the same as other letters \(D\) of the earlier chapters.

22.2 Curvature of a surface

We roll a sheet of paper into a tube. The tube is stiff when we try to bend it across the roll, and along the roll it bends without effort. The same sheet does not go over a ball without creases, because a ball bends in both directions at once and a tube in one only. Even for the tube that we use in this chapter (mid radius \(R = 50\) mm), it is therefore not enough to say that the surface is curved: along the axis it is straight, and around the circumference it is a circular arc of radius \(R\). How much the surface is curved depends on the direction in which we look. This section answers three questions. How do we measure the curvature of a surface in one direction? How does it change with the direction? And with how many numbers do we state it completely at a point? We need the answer in the following sections, because there we take the coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) along the directions of largest and smallest curvature.

First the curvature of a curve. For the beam we already had it as \(\kappa = v''\) (definition 5.16), but under the condition of a small slope. A curve in a surface can have a large slope with respect to any axis, so we need a curvature that does not depend on the axis. We describe the curve by its arc length \(s\) (length of a curve, definition 8.5, for a curve on a surface lemma 22.5): the point \(\vek c(s)\) is on the curve at the distance \(s\) from the start, measured along the curve.

Definition 22.10 Curvature of a curve (ukrivljenost krivulje)

A curve in space is given by a twice continuously differentiable map \(\vek c(s)\) whose output for every \(s\) is a point with three coordinates, and it is described by arc length, which means \(|\vek c'(s)| = 1\). The vector \(\vek t = \vek c'(s)\) is the unit tangent vector (enotski tangentni vektor). The curvature (ukrivljenost) is the number \(\kappa\), the length of the vector \(\vek c''(s)\), so \(\kappa = |\vek c''(s)|\), with unit 1/mm. Where \(\kappa \ne 0\), the radius of curvature (polmer ukrivljenosti) is \(1/\kappa\) and the centre of curvature (središče ukrivljenosti) is the point \(\vek c(s) + \vek c''(s)/\kappa^2\). The circle with this centre and radius is the osculating circle.

Source: VK section 11.2 (PDF p. 310) introduces the radius of curvature of a normal section as the distance from the point to the centre of curvature and the curvature as its reciprocal. The form with the second derivative with respect to arc length is not from the source.

Why is it so? Two reasons, both checked. First: \(\vek c''\) is perpendicular to \(\vek c'\). Since \(|\vek c'|^2 = \vek c'\cdot\vek c' = 1\) at every \(s\), the derivative of the left side by the product rule is \(2\,\vek c'\cdot\vek c'' = 0\), so \(\vek c' \perp \vek c''\). Second: for a circle of radius \(R\), \(\vek c(s) = \big(R\cos(s/R),\ R\sin(s/R),\ 0\big)\), we have \(|\vek c'| = 1\) and \(\vek c'' = -\tfrac1R\big(\cos(s/R), \sin(s/R), 0\big)\), so \(\kappa = 1/R\) and the centre of curvature \(\vek c + \vek c''R^2 = \vek 0\) is the centre of the circle (theorem on the derivatives of sine and cosine, 8.13). The curvature is thus the number that a circle of radius \(1/\kappa\) has. Figure 5.57 of chapter 5 shows the same: the osculating circle with the same \(\kappa\) fits the curve at the point.

The link with the beam is a lemma. The graph \(y = v(x)\) is described by arc length. On a piece of arc the horizontal step is \(\mathrm{d}x\), the vertical one \(v'\mathrm{d}x\), and by Pythagoras the length of the piece is \(\mathrm{d}s = \sqrt{1 + v'^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The arc length is the sum of the pieces, so we take the parameter \(s(x) = \int_0^x\sqrt{1 + v'^2}\,\mathrm{d}\xi\) (definition 8.5).

Lemma 22.11 Curvature of a graph (ukrivljenost grafa)

Let \(v\) be a twice continuously differentiable function on an interval. The curvature of the curve \(y = v(x)\) at the point \(x\) is

\[\kappa = \frac{|v''|}{(1 + v'^2)^{3/2}} . \tag{22.9}\]

For \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) the curvature \(\kappa\) is smaller than \(|v''|\) by at most \(1{,}5\) %.

Proof

We must show the form (22.9) and the estimate of the factor. We write the curve by arc length, compute \(\vek c''\) and, because of the perpendicularity to \(\vek c'\), take only its component along the normal.

  1. Let \(w(x) = \sqrt{1 + v'(x)^2} \ge 1\). The function \(s(x)\) has derivative \(s' = w > 0\), so it has an inverse \(x(s)\) with derivative \(x' = 1/w\) (theorem on the derivative of an inverse function). The curve is \(\vek c(s) = \big(x(s), v(x(s))\big)\) and by the chain rule (lemma 8.30) \(\vek c' = (1, v')/w\), of length \(\sqrt{1 + v'^2}/w = 1\).
  2. The derivative with respect to \(s\) is the derivative with respect to \(x\) multiplied by \(x' = 1/w\) (chain rule). With \(w' = v'v''/w\), \(\vek c''\) has two terms, a vertical one and one parallel to \(\vek c'\):
    \[\vek c'' = \frac1w\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\!\left[\frac{(1, v')}{w}\right] = \frac{(0, v'')}{w^2} - \frac{v'v''}{w^4}\,(1, v') .\]
  3. The vector \(\vek \nu = (-v', 1)/w\) is a unit vector perpendicular to \(\vek c'\), since \((1, v')\cdot(-v', 1) = 0\). Because \(\vek c' \perp \vek c''\), we have \(|\vek c''| = |\vek c''\cdot\vek \nu|\). The second term of step 2 is parallel to \(\vek c'\) and gives zero in the scalar product with \(\vek\nu\), the first gives \(v''/w^3\). So \(\kappa = |v''|/w^3\), which is (22.9).
  4. For \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\), \(w^3 = (1 + v'^2)^{3/2} \le 1{,}01^{3/2} = 1{,}0150\), so \(\kappa \ge |v''|/1{,}0150 = 0{,}985\,|v''|\).

Source: The same relation is stated in the source line of definition 5.16 (SADD, PDF p. 578, formula below (D.7)). The proof with a curve of arc length is not from the source.

We took the limit \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) in the chapter on beams because with it the factor stays above \(0{,}985\) and every expression with \(v''\) stays within \(1{,}5\) %. Let us see what happens without it, on the same beam as in the figure cited there, \(v = 0{,}12\,x^2\) (lengths in an arbitrary unit, \(v'' = 0{,}24\) per that unit). At \(x = 0\) we have \(v' = 0\) and \(\kappa = 0{,}2400\). At \(x = 1\) we have \(v'^2 = 0{,}058\) and \(\kappa = 0{,}2207\), which is \(8\) % less than \(v''\). At \(x = 3\) we have \(v'^2 = 0{,}518\) and \(\kappa = 0{,}1283\), almost half less (SymPy). At a large slope the equation \(\kappa = v''\) no longer holds, and for a surface where we do not control the slope with respect to a chosen axis, we must take the curvature from definition 22.10.

22.2.1 Normal section and the second fundamental form

At a point \(P\) the surface \(S\) has a tangent plane spanned by the tangent vectors \(\vek a_1 = \partial\vek r/\partial q_1\) and \(\vek a_2 = \partial\vek r/\partial q_2\) (definition 22.2), and a normal \(\vek n = \vek a_1\times\vek a_2/|\vek a_1\times\vek a_2|\) ((4.33)). Let the description \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\) be twice continuously differentiable. How is the surface curved in the direction of a unit tangent vector \(\vek t\)? We cut it with the plane through \(P\) that contains \(\vek t\) and the normal \(\vek n\). Such a section is a plane curve. Its curvature is the answer as we feel it when we move along the surface in the direction \(\vek t\).

We build the figure as at a board. We take the tube with axis \(x\) and on it the point \(P\) at the top, where the tangent plane \(T\) is horizontal. Through \(P\) we show the normal \(\vek n\), which looks into the tube, toward the axis. In the tangent plane we draw three directions: \(\vek t_0\) along the axis, \(\vek t_{90}\) around the circumference and \(\vek t_{45}\) between them. Through each direction and the normal we lay a plane. The plane through \(\vek t_0\) and \(\vek n\) cuts the tube in a straight line, along which the curvature is zero. The plane through \(\vek t_{90}\) and \(\vek n\) is the cross section of the tube perpendicular to the axis, and we get it as a circle of radius \(R\). When we move in the plane at \(45^\circ\) from \(P\) by a distance \(\lambda\) in the direction \(\vek t_{45}\), we move perpendicular to the axis by only \(\lambda\sin 45^\circ\). So this plane cuts the tube in an ellipse with the semi-axis \(R\) along \(\vek n\) and the semi-axis \(R/\sin 45^\circ = \sqrt2\,R\) along \(\vek t_{45}\). The ellipse is thus wider than the circle and flatter at \(P\), so its curvature is smaller: the centre of curvature \(C_{45}\) is twice as far from \(P\) as \(C_{90}\) (computed in example 22.14 below).

Definition 22.12 Normal curvature and the second fundamental form (normalna ukrivljenost in druga osnovna forma)

Let \(S\) be a surface with a twice continuously differentiable description \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\) and \(\vek n\) the unit normal at a point \(P\). For a unit tangent vector \(\vek t\), the normal section (normalni prerez) is the curve in which the plane through \(P\) that contains \(\vek t\) and \(\vek n\) cuts \(S\) near \(P\). Its description by arc length \(\vek c(s)\) with \(\vek c(0) = P\), \(\vek c'(0) = \vek t\) is a plane curve, so \(\vek c''(0)\) lies in that plane and is perpendicular to \(\vek t\) (definition 22.10), hence \(\vek c''(0) = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek n\) for a number \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\). This number is the normal curvature (normalna ukrivljenost) in the direction \(\vek t\), with unit 1/mm and a sign: positive when the curve bends toward \(\vek n\). Let

\[b_{11} = \vek n\cdot\frac{\partial^2\vek r}{\partial q_1^2} , \quad b_{12} = b_{21} = \vek n\cdot\frac{\partial^2\vek r}{\partial q_1\,\partial q_2} , \quad b_{22} = \vek n\cdot\frac{\partial^2\vek r}{\partial q_2^2} \tag{22.10}\]

and let \(\mat B\) be the symmetric matrix with these elements. The second fundamental form (druga osnovna forma) at \(P\) is the map that assigns to a pair of tangent vectors \(\vek u = u_1\vek a_1 + u_2\vek a_2\) and \(\vek v = v_1\vek a_1 + v_2\vek a_2\) the number \(\mathrm{II}(\vek u, \vek v) = (u_1, u_2)\,\mat B\,(v_1, v_2)^\T\).

Source: VK section 11.2 (PDF pp. 309-310) defines the normal section and its radius of curvature, section 11.3 (PDF pp. 313-315) the two quadratic forms with equations (11.16) to (11.18). The orientation of \(\vek n\) and the notation with the matrix \(\mat B\) are not from the source, VK uses the inward normal \(\vek e_3\), toward the centre of curvature of the shell (PDF p. 316). The existence of the section near \(P\) is stated after VK, not proved.

The first form, that is the matrix \(\mat G\) with elements \(a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek a_{\mathrm{j}}\) of definition 22.3, gave lengths and angles on the surface. The second gives curvature. Both are fundamental, because by VK (PDF pp. 314-315) together they determine the surface up to its position in space: surfaces with the same first and second form coincide and can differ only in position (stated, not proved). The first alone does not suffice, because we roll the paper into a tube and all lengths stay the same. Both are a quadratic expression in the components of a vector (\(|\vek v|^2 = (v_1, v_2)\,\mat G\,(v_1, v_2)^\T\) and \(\mathrm{II}(\vek v, \vek v)\)), and both appear in every following formula. If we replace \(\vek n\) by \(-\vek n\), all \(b_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) change sign. So we choose \(\vek n\) as needed, as a rule toward the centre of curvature, and say how at every example.

Is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) really given by \(\mat B\)? A lemma says so, and it holds for every curve on the surface, not only for the normal section. Through the point \(P\) on the surface with the normal \(\vek n\) there goes in the direction \(\vek v\), besides the normal section, also an oblique curve with the same tangent. Its \(\vek c''\) has a tangential component as well, but the component along \(\vek n\) is the same as for the normal section. With the lemma we shall also compute, in the examples, the curvature of curves that are not normal sections.

For the proof and for the Gaussian curvature we need the tangent plane with its basis. In the plane lie the vectors \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\). The parallelogram they span has an area \(|\vek a_1\times\vek a_2|\) that is not zero, because the vectors are independent. Every tangent vector \(\vek v\) is the sum \(v_1\vek a_1 + v_2\vek a_2\). In the orthonormal basis \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) the vectors \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) have components. The normal \(\vek n\) is perpendicular to the plane. On the right we step along the coordinate line \(q_{\mathrm{j}}\): \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\) stays perpendicular to \(\vek n\) at both points, \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\) changes by \(\partial\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek n\) tilts by \(\vek n_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the tangent plane.

Lemma 22.13 Normal curvature from the second form (normalna ukrivljenost iz druge osnovne forme)

Let \(\vek v = v_1\vek a_1 + v_2\vek a_2\) be a tangent vector at \(P\) with \(|\vek v| = 1\). For every curve \(\vek c(s)\) on the surface \(S\) with arc length, \(\vek c(0) = P\), \(\vek c'(0) = \vek v\),

\[\vek c''(0)\cdot\vek n = \mathrm{II}(\vek v, \vek v) = b_{11}v_1^2 + 2\,b_{12}v_1v_2 + b_{22}v_2^2 . \tag{22.11}\]

Hence the normal curvature is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek v) = \mathrm{II}(\vek v, \vek v)\), the same for all such curves, and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(-\vek v) = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\vek v)\).

Proof

We must show that the scalar product \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n\) depends only on the point and the direction. We write the curve as \(\vek c(s) = \vek r(q_1(s), q_2(s))\) and get the second derivative by differentiating the condition that \(\vek c'\) is tangent to \(S\) and hence perpendicular to \(\vek n\).

  1. By the chain rule (lemma 8.30), \(\vek c' = \vek a_1 q_1' + \vek a_2 q_2'\). At \(s = 0\) we have \(\vek c'(0) = \vek v\), so \(q_1'(0) = v_1\) and \(q_2'(0) = v_2\), since \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) are linearly independent (the area of the parallelogram is not zero, \(\vek a_1\times\vek a_2 \ne \vek 0\)).
  2. The vector \(\vek c'\) lies in the tangent plane, so \(\vek c'\cdot\vek n = 0\) at every \(s\), where \(\vek n = \vek n(q_1(s), q_2(s))\) is continuously differentiable because \(\vek r\) is twice continuously differentiable. The derivative with respect to \(s\), by the product rule, gives \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n + \vek c'\cdot\vek n' = 0\), where \(\vek n' = \vek n_1 q_1' + \vek n_2 q_2'\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{j}} = \partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) (chain rule). So \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n = -\vek c'\cdot\vek n'\).
  3. We differentiate the condition \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek n = 0\) with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{j}}\), as we step along the coordinate line (\(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\) changes, \(\vek n\) tilts): \(\dfrac{\partial\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}}\cdot\vek n + \vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\). Since \(\partial\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} = \partial^2\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\), we have \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{j}} = -b_{\mathrm{ij}}\). At the same time, by the symmetry of mixed derivatives (theorem 8.31), \(b_{12} = b_{21}\).
  4. In step 2 we insert \(\vek c' = \vek a_1 q_1' + \vek a_2 q_2'\) and \(\vek n'\) and use step 3: \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n = -\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{j}})\,q_{\mathrm{i}}'q_{\mathrm{j}}' = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} b_{\mathrm{ij}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}}'q_{\mathrm{j}}'\), where the sum runs over \(i, j \in \{1, 2\}\). At \(s = 0\) this is (22.11). For the normal section \(\vek c'' = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n\) and \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  5. The replacement \(\vek v \to -\vek v\) reverses the components \(v_1, v_2\), and the quadratic expression does not change.

Source: VK (11.16), (11.17) (PDF p. 314) give the normal curvature as the quotient of the two quadratic forms, with the direction given by the ratio of the components, for us \(v_2/v_1\). The proof with a curve of arc length is not from the source.

Example 22.14 Tube: curvature in a direction (cev: ukrivljenost v smeri)

We describe the tube of mid radius \(R = 50\) mm by the coordinates \(q_1 = x\) (along the axis) and \(q_2 = \varphi\) (angle around the axis), \(\vek r = (R\cos\varphi,\ R\sin\varphi,\ x)\) (SymPy). Then \(\vek a_1 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\vek a_2 = R(-\sin\varphi, \cos\varphi, 0)\), \(\vek a_1\times\vek a_2 = R\,(-\cos\varphi, -\sin\varphi, 0)\) and \(\vek n = (-\cos\varphi, -\sin\varphi, 0)\) looks toward the axis. The second derivatives are \(\vek r_{\mathrm{xx}} = \vek 0\), \(\vek r_{\mathrm{x}\varphi} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek r_{\varphi\varphi} = -R(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, 0)\), so \(b_{11} = b_{12} = 0\) and \(b_{22} = R\). The elements of the first form are \(a_{11} = 1\), \(a_{12} = 0\), \(a_{22} = R^2\). The unit vector at the angle \(\psi\) to the axis is \(\vek v = \cos\psi\,\vek a_1 + (\sin\psi/R)\,\vek a_2\), and by equation (22.11)

\[\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = b_{22}\,\frac{\sin^2\psi}{R^2} = \frac{\sin^2\psi}{R} . \tag{22.12}\]

At \(R = 50\) mm we get \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(0{,}0050\), \(0{,}0100\), \(0{,}0150\) and \(0{,}0200\) 1/mm at \(\psi = 0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(60^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), so the radius of curvature of the normal section is \(\infty\), \(200\), \(100\), \(66{,}67\) and \(50\) mm (SymPy). At \(0^\circ\), \(45^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) these are the blackwhite, blue and orange curves of figure 22.15, and for the section at \(45^\circ\) the centre of curvature \(C_{45}\) is indeed at the distance \(100\) mm \(= 2R\).

A curve that is not a normal section gives the same number. The helix \(\vek c(s) = \big(R\cos(s\sin\psi/R),\ R\sin(s\sin\psi/R),\ s\cos\psi\big)\) lies on the tube and has \(|\vek c'| = 1\), tangent at the angle \(\psi\) to the axis and \(\vek c''(0) = -(\sin^2\psi/R)(1, 0, 0)\). At the point \(s = 0\), where \(\vek n = (-1, 0, 0)\), we have \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n = \sin^2\psi/R\), as lemma 22.13 says (SymPy). The curvature of the helix itself is \(\kappa = |\vek c''| = \sin^2\psi/R\), because \(\vek c''\) is parallel to \(\vek n\).

22.2.2 Principal curvatures

For the tube \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = \sin^2\psi/R\), with the largest value at \(\psi = 90^\circ\) and the smallest at \(0^\circ\) (figure 22.20, left). Does every surface have such a largest and smallest value at every point, and are the two directions perpendicular? We had the same question for stresses: the largest and smallest normal stress at a point is in the principal directions (theorem 2.83). The normal curvature is the same quadratic form in two dimensions. Theorem 2.83 holds for three rows, and our plane case needs only two and gives the formulas as well, so we write out the proof for two rows.

We read the theorem from a figure. In the tangent plane we take the orthonormal basis \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and a direction \(\vek t\) at the angle \(\psi\). We draw the normal curvature as a graph against \(\psi\): it oscillates about the mean \(m\) with amplitude \(\rho\), the largest value \(\kappa_1\) is in the direction \(\vek t_1\) and the smallest \(\kappa_2\) in the direction \(\vek t_2\), perpendicular to \(\vek t_1\). The angle from \(\vek t_1\) to \(\vek t\) is \(\theta\), and the value between \(\kappa_2\) and \(\kappa_1\) lies according to the weights. The cosine of the double angle comes from a point on the unit circle, given by the angle \(2\psi_0\) and the point \((u/\rho, q/\rho)\). If we reverse the direction (\(\psi \to -\psi\)), we get the mirror graph.

Theorem 22.15 Principal curvatures and Euler's formula (glavne ukrivljenosti in Eulerjeva formula)

Let \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) be perpendicular unit vectors in the tangent plane of the surface at \(P\) and \(\mat S\) the symmetric matrix with elements \(S_{\mathrm{kl}} = \mathrm{II}(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\), that is \(p\), \(q\) in the first and \(q\), \(r\) in the second row. The normal curvature in the direction \(\vek t = \cos\psi\,\vek e_1 + \sin\psi\,\vek e_2\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = p\cos^2\psi + 2q\sin\psi\cos\psi + r\sin^2\psi\) (lemma 22.13). Let \(m = (p + r)/2\) and \(\rho = \sqrt{((p - r)/2)^2 + q^2}\). Then:

  1. The largest value of \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) over all directions is \(\kappa_1 = m + \rho\) and the smallest is \(\kappa_2 = m - \rho\). These are the principal curvatures (glavni ukrivljenosti), \(\kappa_1 \ge \kappa_2\), and they are the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat S\).
  2. If \(\rho > 0\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) has its extrema in exactly two perpendicular directions \(\vek t_1\) and \(\vek t_2\) (a direction and its opposite count as one), the principal directions (glavni smeri), which are eigenvectors of the matrix \(\mat S\). If \(\rho = 0\), then \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = m\) in every direction and every direction is principal.
  3. For \(\theta\), the angle from \(\vek t_1\) to \(\vek t\), we have \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = \kappa_1\cos^2\theta + \kappa_2\sin^2\theta\) (Euler's formula).
Idea

As with Mohr's circle: we write the quadratic form on a circle with the double angle and turn it into a single cosine, which has the largest value \(+1\) and the smallest \(-1\).

Proof
  1. By the addition formulas (corollary 8.16, \(\alpha = \beta = \psi\)) \(2\sin\psi\cos\psi = \sin 2\psi\) and \(\cos 2\psi = \cos^2\psi - \sin^2\psi\). With \(\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi = 1\) we have \(\cos^2\psi = (1 + \cos 2\psi)/2\) and \(\sin^2\psi = (1 - \cos 2\psi)/2\), so \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the sum of the mean \(m\) and an oscillation with the double angle, and for the tube it is \(\sin^2\psi\):
    \[\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = m + u\cos 2\psi + q\sin 2\psi , \qquad u = \tfrac{p - r}{2} .\]
  2. Let \(\rho > 0\). The point \((u/\rho, q/\rho)\) is on the unit circle, since \(u^2 + q^2 = \rho^2\), so there is a \(\psi_0\) with \(\cos 2\psi_0 = u/\rho\) and \(\sin 2\psi_0 = q/\rho\) (definition 8.10). By the addition formula
    \[\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = m + \rho\,(\cos 2\psi_0\cos 2\psi + \sin 2\psi_0\sin 2\psi) = m + \rho\cos 2(\psi - \psi_0) .\]
  3. The cosine has values between \(-1\) and \(1\), the value \(+1\) at \(2(\psi - \psi_0) = 0\) and \(-1\) at \(\pi\) (lemma 8.11). The directions \(\psi\) and \(\psi + \pi\) are the same direction. So among the directions \(\psi \in [\psi_0, \psi_0 + \pi)\) the largest value is \(m + \rho\) at \(\psi = \psi_0\) and the smallest is \(m - \rho\) at \(\psi = \psi_0 + \pi/2\), and nowhere else, since \(\cos 2\theta = \pm 1\) only at multiples of \(\pi/2\) for \(\theta\). This is point 1 and the first part of point 2.
  4. Euler's formula: with \(\theta = \psi - \psi_0\) we have \(\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta\), so \(m + \rho\cos 2\theta = (m + \rho)\cos^2\theta + (m - \rho)\sin^2\theta\), since \(m = m\,(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)\). This is point 3.
  5. Eigenvalues: in the basis \(\vek t_1\), \(\vek t_2\) the form has elements \(S'_{11} = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi_0) = \kappa_1\), \(S'_{22} = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi_0 + \pi/2) = \kappa_2\) and \(S'_{12} = q'\). The computation of step 1 in this basis gives \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = (\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)/2 + \tfrac{\kappa_1 - \kappa_2}{2}\cos 2\theta + q'\sin 2\theta\). By point 3 the same \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) equals \(m + \rho\cos 2\theta\) with \(m = (\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)/2\) and \(\rho = (\kappa_1 - \kappa_2)/2\). At \(\theta = \pi/4\) we have \(\cos 2\theta = 0\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 1\), so \(q' = 0\). The expansion in the orthonormal basis \(\vek t_1\), \(\vek t_2\) gives \(\mat S\,\vek t_1 = (\vek t_1\cdot\mat S\,\vek t_1)\,\vek t_1 + (\vek t_2\cdot\mat S\,\vek t_1)\,\vek t_2 = \kappa_1\vek t_1 + q'\,\vek t_2 = \kappa_1\vek t_1\) and likewise \(\mat S\,\vek t_2 = \kappa_2\vek t_2\). Hence \(\kappa_1\), \(\kappa_2\) are the eigenvalues.
  6. If \(\rho = 0\), then \(p = r\) and \(q = 0\), so \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = m\) at every \(\psi\).

Source: VK section 11.4 (PDF p. 315) shows that the extrema of \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) are in two perpendicular directions (equations (11.19) to (11.21), the perpendicularity is proved with appendix C.2). The proof with the double angle and Euler's formula are not from the source.

For the tube \(p = 0\), \(q = 0\), \(r = 1/R\) in the basis \(\vek e_1 = \vek a_1\), \(\vek e_2 = \vek a_2/R\) (example 22.14), so \(m = 1/(2R)\), \(\rho = 1/(2R)\), \(\kappa_1 = 1/R\) at \(\psi_0 = 90^\circ\) and \(\kappa_2 = 0\) at \(0^\circ\). Euler's formula with \(\theta = \psi - 90^\circ\) gives \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = \cos^2\theta/R = \sin^2\psi/R\), as equation (22.12).

The horizontal axes carry the direction \(\psi\) from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\), the vertical ones the normal curvature multiplied by \(R\) or by \(c\), so that the number has no unit. The graph of the tube is \(\sin^2\psi\): at the principal directions it has a horizontal tangent, which means that a small error of the direction gives an error of the curvature of second order. The blue dot is the value \(1/(2R)\) at \(45^\circ\), the curvature of the ellipse in which the plane at \(45^\circ\) cuts the tube. For the saddle (example 22.23 below) the graph is \(\sin 2\psi\), which changes sign.

If \(\kappa_1 = \kappa_2\) (\(\rho = 0\)), every direction is principal. An example is the sphere: every normal section is a circle of radius \(R\) with the same centre on the normal, so the graph of \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a horizontal line. The computation: with the inward normal and coordinates \(q_1 = \varphi\), \(q_2 = \theta\) (the angles of lemma 11.15) we have \(a_{11} = R^2\), \(a_{22} = R^2\sin^2\varphi\), \(b_{11} = R\), \(b_{22} = R\sin^2\varphi\) and \(b_{12} = 0\) (SymPy). For a direction \(\vek v\) with components \(v_1 = \cos\psi/R\), \(v_2 = \sin\psi/(R\sin\varphi)\) we have \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = (R\cos^2\psi + R\sin^2\psi)/R^2 = 1/R\) for every \(\psi\). The theorem holds but does not find two distinct directions, and this is not a fault of the theorem: a sphere is just as exactly described by a single radius. This is why point 2 of the theorem is conditional on \(\rho > 0\).

22.2.3 Lines of curvature and the Gaussian curvature

In the next section the coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) will lie along the principal directions: through the point \(P\) there pass the coordinate lines, their tangents \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) are the principal directions and are perpendicular. Such a curve is a line of curvature.

Definition 22.16 Line of curvature (črta ukrivljenosti)

A line of curvature is a curve on a surface whose tangent is a principal direction at every point (theorem 22.15). A coordinate system \((q_1, q_2)\) on a part of the surface is a system of lines of curvature if the two coordinate lines through every point are perpendicular and are principal directions.

Source: VK section 11.2 (PDF pp. 311-312). VK states there that at least two perpendicular lines of curvature pass through every point, and that such a system is in general not simple to determine, but the existence of the coordinates is not proved. We also cite, not prove, the existence of a system of lines of curvature near a point where \(\kappa_1 \ne \kappa_2\) (VK PDF p. 312, the paragraph before section 11.3).

For the surfaces we need, the lines of curvature are known, so existence is not a problem. But are the two forms in such coordinates really simple?

Lemma 22.17 Both forms are diagonal (obe formi sta diagonalni)

Let \(q_1\), \(q_2\) be coordinates of lines of curvature, so that \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) are in the principal directions of theorem 22.15. Let \(A_1 = \sqrt{a_{11}} = |\vek a_1|\) and \(A_2 = \sqrt{a_{22}} = |\vek a_2|\) (in the orthogonal coordinates of definition 11.13 these are the scale factors \(h_1\), \(h_2\), here we write them \(A_1\), \(A_2\), because \(h\) means the thickness of the shell, and \(H_1\), \(H_2\) will be the scale factors through the thickness). Then \(a_{12} = 0\), \(b_{12} = 0\) and the principal curvatures in the directions \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) are

\[\kappa_1 = \frac{b_{11}}{A_1^2} = \frac1{R_1} , \qquad \kappa_2 = \frac{b_{22}}{A_2^2} = \frac1{R_2} . \tag{22.13}\]

The quantities \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are the principal radii of curvature (glavna polmera ukrivljenosti). Here the index tells the coordinate line, not the size: \(\kappa_1\) is in the direction \(\vek a_1\) and may be smaller than \(\kappa_2\), regardless of the convention \(\kappa_1 \ge \kappa_2\) of theorem 22.15.

Proof

We must show that \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) are perpendicular and that \(\mat B\) has no off-diagonal element. The first follows from the perpendicularity of the principal directions, the second from the diagonal form of the matrix \(\mat S\).

  1. The vectors \(\vek a_1\) and \(\vek a_2\) lie along principal directions, which are perpendicular (definition 22.16, for \(\kappa_1 \ne \kappa_2\) by point 2 of theorem 22.15). So \(a_{12} = \vek a_1\cdot\vek a_2 = 0\).
  2. By lemma 22.13 the normal curvature in the direction \(\vek a_1/A_1\) equals \(b_{11}/A_1^2\) (components \(v_1 = 1/A_1\), \(v_2 = 0\)), and since \(\vek a_1\) is a principal direction by assumption, this is the principal curvature \(\kappa_1\) in the direction \(\vek a_1\). Likewise \(\kappa_2 = b_{22}/A_2^2\).
  3. By step 5 of theorem 22.15 the matrix \(\mat S\) in the basis of principal directions \(\vek a_1/A_1\), \(\vek a_2/A_2\) is diagonal (for \(\rho = 0\) in every basis, by step 6), and its element \(S_{12} = \mathrm{II}(\vek a_1/A_1, \vek a_2/A_2) = b_{12}/(A_1A_2) = 0\).

Source: VK (11.21), (11.22) (PDF p. 315). The proof is not from the source.

For a surface of revolution we do not need to look for the lines of curvature, because symmetry gives them. A surface of revolution (vrtenina) arises when a plane curve, the meridian (meridian), is rotated about an axis. A point of the meridian describes a circle, a parallel (vzporednik). Figure 22.23 shows the plane of the meridian through a point \(P\).

We build the figure starting from the axis \(z\). We draw the meridian and its point \(P\). From \(P\) to the axis we measure the radius of the parallel \(r\). Through \(P\) we draw the normal inward, perpendicular to the tangent of the meridian, and extend it to the axis. The angle \(\varphi\) is the one this normal makes with the axis. The centres of curvature, \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), lie on the normal: \(O_1\) for the meridian, \(O_2\) where the normal cuts the axis.

For the proof we need the reflection. The plane of the meridian through \(P\) is a mirror plane of the surface of revolution. In it the meridian, the normal and the point \(P\) stay, and the parallel is reversed: the direction \(\vek t\) at the angle \(\psi\) from the meridian goes to the direction at \(-\psi\).

Lemma 22.18 Lines of curvature of a surface of revolution (črte ukrivljenosti vrtenine)

On a surface of revolution the meridian and the parallel through every point are lines of curvature. Let \(\varphi\) be the angle between the normal and the axis, \(r\) the radius of the parallel and \(\vek n\) the normal toward the interior. With index 1 for the meridian and 2 for the parallel (lemma 22.17), the principal curvatures are \(\kappa_1 = 1/R_1\), the normal curvature in the direction of the meridian, that is the curvature of the meridian as a plane curve with the sign plus when it bends toward \(\vek n\), and

\[\kappa_2 = \frac{\sin\varphi}{r} = \frac1{R_2} , \qquad R_2 = \frac{r}{\sin\varphi} , \tag{22.14}\]

where \(R_2\) is the distance from the point to the axis, measured along the normal.

Proof

We must show that the meridian is a principal direction and compute the curvature along the parallel. The first follows from mirror symmetry, the second from lemma 22.13.

  1. The reflection in the plane of the meridian through \(P\) maps the surface of revolution onto itself, leaves \(P\), \(\vek n\) and the meridian in place and reverses the direction of the parallel. It preserves lengths, so it preserves the curvature of a curve: the normal section in the direction at the angle \(\psi\) from the meridian goes to the section in the direction at \(-\psi\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(-\psi)\).
  2. By theorem 22.15, for \(\rho > 0\) the function is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = m + \rho\cos 2(\psi - \psi_0)\). The condition \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = \kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(-\psi)\) at \(\psi = \pi/4\) gives, by the addition formula, \(\cos(\pi/2 - 2\psi_0) = \cos(\pi/2 + 2\psi_0)\), so \(2\sin(\pi/2)\sin 2\psi_0 = 0\), that is \(\sin 2\psi_0 = 0\) and \(\psi_0\) is a multiple of \(\pi/2\): the meridian is a principal direction, and so is the perpendicular parallel. For \(\rho = 0\) every direction is principal.
  3. The meridian is a normal section (the plane of the meridian contains the axis and \(\vek n\)), so its curvature is the principal curvature \(\kappa_1\).
  4. The parallel is a circle of radius \(r\) on the surface, with arc length, \(\vek c'' = -\tfrac1r\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) pointing away from the axis and \(|\vek c''| = 1/r\) (definition 22.10). The component of the unit normal \(\vek n\) perpendicular to the axis has size \(\sin\varphi\) and points toward the axis, so \(\vek c''\cdot\vek n = \sin\varphi/r\).
  5. For \(\varphi \ne 90^\circ\) the parallel is not a normal section, because the plane of the circle does not contain \(\vek n\). But it has the same tangent as the second principal section, so by lemma 22.13 \(\kappa_2 = \vek c''\cdot\vek n = \sin\varphi/r\). The normal, the axis and the parallel (\(r\) horizontal) form a right triangle with hypotenuse \(|PO_2|\) and the leg \(r\) opposite the angle \(\varphi\) at \(O_2\), so \(\sin\varphi = r/|PO_2|\) and \(|PO_2| = r/\sin\varphi = R_2\).

Source: VK section 11.2 (PDF pp. 311-312): the meridian is one line of curvature and a principal normal section, the parallel is the other line of curvature and is not a principal normal section, the second radius \(R_2\) is the distance along the normal to the axis. The proof with symmetry and lemma 22.13 is not from the source.

For the tube \(\varphi = 90^\circ\), \(r = R\), \(\kappa_2 = 1/R\) and the meridian (a straight line) has \(\kappa_1 = 0\), as in example 22.14. Here \(\kappa_1 < \kappa_2\), because the index tells the direction of the meridian. For the sphere \(r = R\sin\varphi\) and \(\kappa_2 = 1/R\) at every \(\varphi\). For a cone with half angle \(\alpha\) at the apex, \(\varphi = 90^\circ - \alpha\) and the distance along the normal to the axis is \(R_2 = r/\cos\alpha\): at \(r = 50\) mm and \(\alpha = 45^\circ\) we have \(R_2 = 70{,}71\) mm, \(\kappa_2 = 0{,}01414\) 1/mm, and the meridian (a straight line) has \(\kappa_1 = 0\) (SymPy). The same \(\kappa_2\) also follows from \(b_{22}/a_{22}\) on the cone \(\vek r = s(\sin\alpha\cos\theta, \sin\alpha\sin\theta, \cos\alpha)\) with the inward normal.

22.2.4 Gaussian curvature and kinds of surface

Two numbers at a point, \(\kappa_1\) and \(\kappa_2\), are more than we need for classifying points. The sign of their product tells whether the surface near the point lies on one side of the tangent plane (the product is positive, as for the dome) or pierces it (the product is negative, as for the saddle), as we show below.

Definition 22.19 Gaussian curvature (Gaussova ukrivljenost)

The Gaussian curvature of a surface at a point is the product of the principal curvatures \(K = \kappa_1\kappa_2\) with unit 1/mm\(^2\): for the dome both are positive, for the saddle they have opposite signs. It does not depend on the choice of \(\vek n\), because \(-\vek n\) reverses the sign of both \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Source: VK section 11.6 (PDF p. 317), (11.28). A note on notation: \(K\) here is the Gaussian curvature and not the bulk modulus of theorem 11.30.

The curvature bears the name of Gauss. VK (PDF p. 317) does not give the origin of the name, but says that the concept of Gaussian curvature is fundamental in the theory of surfaces and that \(K\) appears in the equation it calls the condition of Gauss (11.27b). In coordinates of lines of curvature it reads

\[K = \frac1{R_1R_2} = -\frac1{A_1A_2}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial q_1}\!\left(\frac1{A_1}\frac{\partial A_2}{\partial q_1}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial q_2}\!\left(\frac1{A_2}\frac{\partial A_1}{\partial q_2}\right)\right] , \tag{22.15}\]

so \(K\) is determined by the scale factors \(A_1\), \(A_2\) alone, that is by lengths on the surface, although we defined it by curvature in space. So a sheet rolled into a tube has the same \(K = 0\) as a flat sheet. VK also gives the conditions of Codazzi, (11.27a), and says that the conditions of Codazzi and Gauss are necessary for four functions \(A_1\), \(A_2\), \(R_1\), \(R_2\) to belong to a surface. Both are stated after the source, not proved in this section, and we do not need them in the following ones.

Lemma 22.20 Computing the Gaussian curvature (izračun Gaussove ukrivljenosti)

In arbitrary coordinates

\[K = \frac{b_{11}b_{22} - b_{12}^2}{a_{11}a_{22} - a_{12}^2} = \frac{\det\mat B}{\det\mat G} , \tag{22.16}\]

and in coordinates of lines of curvature \(K = b_{11}b_{22}/(A_1^2A_2^2) = 1/(R_1R_2)\). Here \(\det\mat G\) is the square of the area of the parallelogram of \(\vek a_1\), \(\vek a_2\).

Proof

We must show that \(\det\mat S\), which is \(\kappa_1\kappa_2\), differs from \(\det\mat B\) by the same factor as \(\det\mat G\). The factor is the square of the ratio of the areas of the parallelogram of \(\vek a_1\), \(\vek a_2\) and the unit square of \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\).

  1. Let \(\mat E\) be the matrix whose columns are the components of the vectors \(\vek a_1\), \(\vek a_2\) in the orthonormal basis \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\). Then \(a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek a_{\mathrm{j}}\) is exactly the element of the matrix \(\mat E^\T\mat E\), so \(\mat G = \mat E^\T\mat E\) and \(\det\mat G = (\det\mat E)^2\), where \(\det\mat E \ne 0\) because \(\vek a_1\), \(\vek a_2\) are independent and the parallelogram has an area that is not zero.
  2. The second form is bilinear, so \(b_{\mathrm{ij}} = \mathrm{II}(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}, \vek a_{\mathrm{j}})\) is the element of the matrix \(\mat E^\T\mat S\,\mat E\):
    \[\mat B = \mat E^\T\mat S\,\mat E .\]
    The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants:
    \[\det\mat B = \det\mat S\,(\det\mat E)^2 .\]
  3. The quotient is \(\det\mat B/\det\mat G = \det\mat S\). By theorem 22.15, \(\kappa_1\), \(\kappa_2\) are the eigenvalues of \(\mat S\), so \(\det\mat S = \kappa_1\kappa_2\) (in the basis of eigenvectors \(\mat S\) is diagonal, and the determinant is preserved under a rotation). By lemma 22.17 the last form follows.

Source: VK (11.28) and (11.30) (PDF p. 317). The proof is not from the source.

The sign of \(K\) tells how the surface lies with respect to the tangent plane. Let us see where it lies near \(P\).

We measure the height in a figure. We draw the tangent plane and the surface that touches it at the point \(P\). In the plane we move from \(P\) by \(\lambda\), and the surface is there \(\zeta\) above it, measured along \(\vek n\). On the right we follow the height along the path from \(P\): \(f(\tau)\) starts with a horizontal tangent and ends at \(f(1)\).

For the proof we need the plane of parameters. On the left a line goes from \(\vek 0\) to the offset \(\vek\delta\). On the right is the tangent plane with the principal directions. The vector \(\vek u = \delta_1\vek a_1 + \delta_2\vek a_2\) has the components \(x_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{u}}\). The surface point is projected orthogonally onto the plane, it differs from the end of \(\vek u\) by a small difference of order \(|\vek\delta|^2\), and its distance \(\lambda\) from \(P\) is almost \(|\vek u|\).

Lemma 22.21 Shape of a surface near a point (oblika ploskve ob točki)

Let \(x\), \(y\) be coordinates in the tangent plane along the principal directions \(\vek t_1\), \(\vek t_2\) from \(P\) and \(\lambda\) the distance to \(P\) in this plane. The height of a point of the surface above the plane, measured in the direction \(\vek n\), is

\[\zeta = \tfrac12\,(\kappa_1x^2 + \kappa_2y^2) + \varepsilon(\lambda)\,\lambda^2 , \qquad \varepsilon(\lambda) \to 0 \text{ as } \lambda \to 0 . \tag{22.17}\]
Proof

We must show that the first nonzero term of the height is the second form, which Taylor's theorem on a line in the plane of parameters gives us, and that the correction from the conversion to the coordinates \(x\), \(y\) does not change the leading term.

  1. For an offset \(\vek\delta = (\delta_1, \delta_2)\) in the parameters, the height \(f(\tau) = \vek n\cdot\big(\vek r(\tau\vek\delta) - \vek r(\vek 0)\big)\) with \(\tau \in [0, 1]\) is a function of one variable, where \(\vek n\) is the normal at \(P\) and does not change. Its first derivative at \(\tau = 0\) is \(\vek n\cdot(\vek a_1\delta_1 + \vek a_2\delta_2) = 0\), since the \(\vek a_{\mathrm{i}}\) are perpendicular to \(\vek n\).
  2. The second derivative is \(f''(\tau) = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}\big(\vek n\cdot\partial^2\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\big)(\tau\vek\delta)\,\delta_{\mathrm{i}}\delta_{\mathrm{j}}\). Taylor's theorem (theorem 8.68) gives \(f(1) = \tfrac12 f''(c)\) for some \(c \in (0, 1)\). The functions \(\vek n\cdot\partial^2\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous and equal \(b_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at \(\vek 0\), so \(f(1) = \tfrac12\mathrm{II}(\vek u, \vek u) + \varepsilon_1|\vek\delta|^2\), with \(\varepsilon_1 \to 0\) as \(\vek\delta \to \vek 0\), where \(\vek u = \delta_1\vek a_1 + \delta_2\vek a_2\).
  3.
