The orthogonal projection of the point \(\vek r(\vek\delta)\) onto the tangent plane has coordinates \((x, y)\) that differ from the coordinates of the vector \(\vek u\) along the principal directions by \(O(|\vek\delta|^2)\), since \(\vek r(\vek\delta) - \vek r(\vek 0) = \vek u + O(|\vek\delta|^2)\) (Taylor's theorem for every component). The quadratic form therefore changes by \(O(|\vek\delta|^3)\). It remains to bound \(|\vek\delta|\) by \(\lambda\). We have \(|\vek u|^2 = \vek\delta^\T\mat G\,\vek\delta \ge g\,|\vek\delta|^2\), where \(g\) is the smallest value of \(\vek e^\T\mat G\,\vek e\) over unit \(\vek e\) (point 1 of theorem 22.15, whose computation uses only the symmetry of the matrix, so it holds for \(\mat G\) too). The number \(g\) is positive, because \(\vek e^\T\mat G\,\vek e = |e_1\vek a_1 + e_2\vek a_2|^2\) and \(\vek a_1\), \(\vek a_2\) are independent. So for small enough \(\vek\delta\) also \(\lambda \ge |\vek u| - O(|\vek\delta|^2) \ge \tfrac12\sqrt g\,|\vek\delta|\), and the terms \(\varepsilon_1|\vek\delta|^2\) of step 2 and \(O(|\vek\delta|^3)\) are both of the form \(\varepsilon_2\lambda^2\) with \(\varepsilon_2 \to 0\) as \(\lambda \to 0\).
  4. In principal coordinates, by lemma 22.17 and theorem 22.15, \(\mathrm{II}(\vek u, \vek u) = \kappa_1x_{\mathrm{u}}^2 + \kappa_2y_{\mathrm{u}}^2\) with the components \(x_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the vector \(\vek u\) along \(\vek t_1\), \(\vek t_2\). Together with steps 2 and 3 this is (22.17).

Source: The form \(\tfrac12(\kappa_1x^2 + \kappa_2y^2)\) is also described in VK section 11.6 (PDF pp. 317-318) by the positions of the centres of curvature. The proof with Taylor's theorem is not from the source.

For the tube at \(R = 50\) mm this means the following. We take a point of the circle of the cross section whose distance from \(P\) in the tangent plane is \(\lambda\) in the direction of the circumference. By Pythagoras' theorem in the cross section it lies exactly \(\zeta = R - \sqrt{R^2 - \lambda^2}\) below the tangent plane, while formula (22.17) with \(\kappa = 1/R\) in the direction of the circumference gives \(\lambda^2/(2R)\). At \(\lambda = 5\), \(10\), \(20\) and \(30\) mm the formula gives \(0{,}2500\), \(1{,}0000\), \(4{,}0000\) and \(9{,}0000\) mm, and the exact value is \(0{,}2506\), \(1{,}0102\), \(4{,}1742\) and \(10{,}0000\) mm. The formula is thus too small by \(0{,}25\) %, \(1{,}0\) %, \(4{,}2\) % and \(10\) % (NumPy). The term \(\varepsilon\lambda^2\) is here below \(1{,}5\) % of the height as long as \(\lambda \le 12{,}2\) mm, which is about \(0{,}24R\). This bound is exact, because the relative error here equals \(\zeta/(2R)\): from \(\zeta = \lambda^2/(R + \sqrt{R^2 - \lambda^2})\) follows \(1 - \lambda^2/(2R\zeta) = (R - \sqrt{R^2 - \lambda^2})/(2R)\).

From equation (22.17) we read three kinds of point by the sign of \(K\). Figure 22.27 shows all three: above, a piece of surface with the principal sections, below, these two sections as profiles with the same tangent.

On each piece there is the point \(P\) with the normal \(\vek n\), and through \(P\) go the blue and the orange principal section. Below we draw them as profiles that touch the tangent at \(P\). At the dome both curves bulge on the same side, in both planes the surface bends toward \(\vek n\), and the point is elliptic. At the tube one section is a straight line, the point is parabolic. At the saddle one section bends toward \(\vek n\) and the other away from it, and the point is hyperbolic.

Definition 22.22 Elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic point (eliptična, parabolična in hiperbolična točka)

A point of a surface is elliptic (eliptična) if \(K > 0\), parabolic (parabolična) if \(K = 0\) and at least one principal curvature is not zero, and hyperbolic (hiperbolična) if \(K < 0\). A surface is singly curved (enojno ukrivljena) if every point of it is parabolic, and doubly curved (dvojno ukrivljena) if \(K \ne 0\) at every point of it.

Source: VK section 11.6 (PDF p. 317) uses the names elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic point by the position of the centres of curvature, section 11.7.2 (PDF pp. 320-321) singly curved shells (zero Gaussian curvature) and doubly curved shells of positive or negative Gaussian curvature. The condition that one principal curvature is not zero is ours, because a plane also has \(K = 0\). We explain the names in the text below.

The names fit the curve that we get from equation (22.17) when we cut the surface with a plane \(\zeta = \zeta_0 \ne 0\) parallel to the tangent plane: \(\kappa_1x^2 + \kappa_2y^2 = 2\zeta_0\) is an ellipse for \(K > 0\), a hyperbola for \(K < 0\), and for \(K = 0\) with \(\kappa_2 = 0\) two parallel lines, as a plane cutting a tube parallel to its axis gives. The parabola is the limiting case between ellipse and hyperbola, as \(K = 0\) is the border between \(K > 0\) and \(K < 0\). VK does not give the history of the names, so we do not claim it here. For \(K > 0\) the quadratic form in equation (22.17) has the same sign in every direction, and for small enough \(\lambda\) it prevails over the correction, so near \(P\) the surface lies on one side of the tangent plane, like the dome. For \(K < 0\) the form has opposite signs in the principal directions, so the surface pierces the tangent plane, like the saddle.

Example 22.23 Saddle with straight lines (sedlo z ravnimi črtami)

The hyperbolic paraboloid \(z = xy/c\) with \(c = 10\) m is described by \(\vek r = (x, y, xy/c)\). At the origin \(\vek a_1 = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek a_2 = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(b_{11} = b_{22} = 0\), \(b_{12} = 1/c\) (SymPy). The matrix \(\mat S = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1/c\\ 1/c & 0\end{pmatrix}\) has the eigenvalues \(\pm 1/c = \pm 0{,}1000\) 1/m with the eigenvectors \((1, 1)/\sqrt2\) and \((-1, 1)/\sqrt2\), so the principal directions are at \(45^\circ\) and \(135^\circ\). The normal curvature is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(\psi) = \sin 2\psi/c\) (figure 22.20, right): \(0{,}0866\) 1/m at \(30^\circ\) and \(0\) at \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). The Gaussian curvature is \(K = \det\mat B/\det\mat G = -c^2/(x^2 + y^2 + c^2)^2\), at the origin \(-0{,}0100\) 1/m\(^2\), and at the point \((5, 5)\) m it is \(-0{,}00444\) 1/m\(^2\).

The surface contains straight lines (for constant \(y\), \(z = (y/c)\,x\) is a straight line), and the coordinate line \(y = 0\), which at the origin is in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), is straight, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\). Is this line a line of curvature? No. A line of curvature has a principal direction at every point (definition 22.16), and here the principal direction is at \(45^\circ\), not at \(0^\circ\). For the tube the straight line along the axis is at the same time a line of curvature, because \(\kappa_{\mathrm{n}}(0) = 0\) is an extremum. For the saddle a straight line is only a curve with zero curvature, and the coordinate system along the straight lines is not a system of lines of curvature: \(b_{12} = 1/c \ne 0\) (lemma 22.17). So from straight lines on a surface we must not conclude that they are lines of curvature.

Three more examples with \(K\): the dome and the sphere (\(K = 1/R^2 > 0\), every point elliptic), the tube and the cone (\(K = 0\), every point parabolic), and a surface of revolution whose meridian curves away from the axis, such as the hyperboloid of one sheet of a cooling tower. For the hyperboloid \(r^2 = a^2 + z^2/c^2\) (\(c\) is a number without unit) we have \(K = -a^2c^6/(a^2c^4 + c^2z^2 + z^2)^2\) (SymPy), and at the throat (\(z = 0\)) \(K = -1/(a^2c^2)\): the parallel has \(\kappa_2 = 1/a\) and the meridian \(\kappa_1 = -1/(ac^2)\) with the opposite sign, because the meridian curves away from the axis. At \(a = 20\) m and \(c = 1\) we have \(K = -0{,}00250\) 1/m\(^2\) at the throat and \(-0{,}00028\) 1/m\(^2\) at \(z = 20\) m. The hyperboloid is thus hyperbolic at every point, although at first sight it resembles a tube.

We draw the hyperboloid in the plane of the meridian. From the axis we measure the meridian, a hyperbola that is nearest to the axis at the throat. At the point \(P\) of the throat the normal points toward the axis, and the parallel with \(r = a\) cuts the axis at the centre \(O_2\). There the meridian bends away from the axis, and its osculating circle has its centre \(O_1\) on the other side of the surface from \(O_2\).

A table gives everything in one place. The index follows the coordinate lines as in lemma 22.17: for surfaces of revolution 1 is the meridian and 2 the parallel, for the saddle 1 is the direction at \(45^\circ\) and 2 the direction at \(135^\circ\).

surface \(\kappa_1\) \(\kappa_2\) \(K\) point
sphere \(R\) \(1/R\) \(1/R\) \(1/R^2\) elliptic
tube \(R\) \(0\) \(1/R\) \(0\) parabolic
cone, radius \(r\), angle \(\alpha\) \(0\) \(\cos\alpha/r\) \(0\) parabolic
saddle \(z = xy/c\), origin \(1/c\) \(-1/c\) \(-1/c^2\) hyperbolic
hyperboloid, throat \(-1/(ac^2)\) \(1/a\) \(-1/(a^2c^2)\) hyperbolic

Does the sign of \(K\) have a mechanical meaning? By VK (section 11.7.3, PDF p. 321) a singly curved surface can be developed into a plane without stretching the middle surface, a doubly curved one cannot, and therefore such shells need more energy to deform and are in general stronger and more stable. We do not prove this. The sheet of paper at the start of the section therefore went into a tube and not over a ball.

Stated and not proved in this section: the existence of a system of lines of curvature near a point (VK section 11.2, PDF pp. 311-312), the conditions of Codazzi and Gauss (VK (11.27), PDF p. 317, appendix C.4), the perpendicularity of the principal directions after the source (we prove it in theorem 22.15), the existence of a normal section near a point (VK PDF p. 309), the developability of surfaces (VK PDF p. 321).

22.3 Displacements, strains and internal forces of a shell (pomiki, deformacije in notranje sile lupine)

A steel tube with mid radius \(R = 50\) mm and thickness \(h = 2\) mm is closed with plugs and holds oil at pressure \(p = 3\) MPa. It is the thin tube of section 22.1, our shell (definition 22.1). At a diameter of one hundred millimetres the wall is two millimetres thick, so in a first approximation its behaviour is the behaviour of a surface. Can a three-dimensional body really be replaced by a curved surface carrying only three displacements, and how much do we lose by it? We need the answer before we can set up equilibrium (section 22.4) and energy. The section takes three steps: it says what we assume about the wall (definition 22.24), shows that the strains of the wall are fixed by six functions on the middle surface (theorem 22.26), and turns the stresses into forces and moments per unit length, which the whole chapter then uses (definition 22.27, theorems 22.28 and 22.29).

22.3.1 Assumptions and coordinates (predpostavke in koordinate)

As for the beam (section 5.3.4), we assume how a fibre lying perpendicular to the middle surface moves. Take a short fibre from a point \(P\) of the middle surface along the unit normal \(\vek n\), of length \(h\), which we call the normal fibre of the wall (normala stene). When the shell is loaded, the fibre moves and turns. For the beam we prescribed that the fibres stay straight and perpendicular to the axis. The shell repeats this on a surface.

Definition 22.24 Kirchhoff-Love assumptions (predpostavke Kirchhoffa in Love)

Let a shell (definition 22.1) have middle surface \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\), normal \(\vek n\) (equation (4.33)), thickness \(h\) and points \(\vek r + z\,\vek n\), \(-h/2 \le z \le h/2\). Let it be of an isotropic, homogeneous, linearly elastic material, and let the displacements be small compared with the thickness. A displacement of the shell is in the Kirchhoff-Love model (model Kirchhoffa in Love) a field for which, at every interior point:

  1. the fibre along the normal does not lengthen, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\),
  2. the fibre stays perpendicular to the deformed middle surface, that is the shear strains of the normal with the tangents vanish, \(\varepsilon_{1\mathrm{n}} = \varepsilon_{2\mathrm{n}} = 0\) (local components, definition 11.19),
  3. the stress along the normal is negligible, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\).

The last item is an assumption about stress, not about displacement, and only Hooke's law uses it (theorem 22.28).

Source: VK section 12.1 (PDF p. 330-331) states Kirchhoff's two assumptions (normals straight and normal without extension, negligible transverse normal stress) and says that together with small displacements and a thin wall they are called the Kirchhoff-Love assumptions. We used the same idea, straight and perpendicular cross sections, for the beam (section 5.3.4). The name is after Kirchhoff because the assumptions come from his theory of plates (VK, PDF p. 330), and after Love, who started his work in the theory of elasticity with thin shells and treated their bending by Kirchhoff's method (TIMO, PDF p. 281).

We look at each of the three assumptions on a normal fibre of the wall of our tube (figure 22.29) and say for each why it is justified here, when it fails and what it does to the result.

The first assumption: the normal fibre keeps its length. We draw the wall before loading with the grey dashed normal fibre, of length \(h\). The pressure pushes the wall outwards by \(w\), and in the model the orange normal fibre after the move is again of length \(h\). Why may we do this? A fibre shortens only if something compresses it or if it narrows because of tension in the plane of the wall, as a bar narrows when we pull it (Poisson's ratio \(\nu\)). Only the pressure compresses it, and the pressure is small (third assumption), while the narrowing is the in-plane strain times \(\nu\). For our tube with the hoop stress \(75\) MPa and the axial stress \(pR/(2h) = 37{,}5\) MPa (a tube with closed ends), Hooke's law with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) gives the strain of the normal fibre \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = -\nu\,(\sigma_{\theta\theta} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})/E = -0{,}3\cdot(75 + 37{,}5)/196\,000 = -1{,}7\cdot 10^{-4}\) (VK (12.39), PDF p. 342, which admits this as an approximation of the theory). The real fibre of thickness 2 mm therefore shortens by \(2\ \mathrm{mm}\cdot 1{,}7\cdot 10^{-4} = 0{,}34\ \mu\)m, and by the exact solution of the tube by \(0{,}35\ \mu\)m (section 22.3.2). That is \(2\,\%\) of the displacement of the wall \(w = 16\ \mu\)m. So the assumption does not claim that the normal fibre does not shorten at all, but that the shortening is negligible next to the displacement of the wall. What it does to the result: the displacement along the normal is the same through the whole thickness, \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = w\) (theorem 22.26). It fails for a thick wall: for a tube with \(h/R = 0{,}4\) the displacements of the inner and the outer face differ by \(27\,\%\).

The second assumption: the normal fibre stays perpendicular. Grey dashed are the middle line and the normal fibre before loading. When the wall bends, the middle line tilts, and in the model the normal fibre turns with it, so that the right angle between them stays. A blackwhite fibre that lagged behind the perpendicular by the angle \(\gamma\) would mean a shear strain between the normal fibre and the middle line. Why may we neglect it? Shear strain is caused by the transverse force, and its share in the deflection falls with the square of the slenderness, as we measured for the beam: for the slender cantilever it contributed \(0{,}125\,\%\) of the bending deflection, for the short one with \(L/h = 2\) it was \(19{,}5\,\%\) (section 5.3.4). For a shell, \(L\) is the distance over which the bending of the wall changes. The assumption fails when this distance is not large compared with the thickness. Then a model with shear deformation is needed (section 5.13 shows the idea for a beam), which this book does not develop for shells. What it does to the result: the normal fibre has no rotation of its own, its rotation is the slope of the middle surface, so the displacements in the whole wall are fixed by functions on the middle surface (equation (22.19)).

The third assumption: the transverse stress is negligible. On the normal fibre we draw both stresses to the same scale. The transverse stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = -p = -3\) MPa on the inner face, because the oil presses there, and zero on the outer, free face. The hoop stress is by the equilibrium of half a tube (equation (11.35)) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} \approx pR/h = 75\) MPa. The blue wedge is hardly visible next to the blackwhite rectangle: the ratio \(p/\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 3/75 = 0{,}04 = h/R\) says that the transverse stress is smaller than the hoop stress by the factor \(R/h = 25\). The reason is geometry: the pressure pushes on the whole width of the tube, but only the thin wall holds it, so the stress in the wall is \(R/h\) times the pressure. The assumption fails for a thick wall: for the thick tube of chapter 11 the pressure is \(30\) MPa next to a hoop stress of \(24\cdot(1 + 60^2/40^2) = 78\) MPa at the bore (theorem 11.28), a factor of only \(2{,}6\). What it does to the result: every layer of the wall is in plane stress and Hooke's law of the shell (theorem 22.28) is the law of that state. The error of the theory is by VK (PDF p. 330) of order \(h/R\) compared with one, for us \(0{,}04\).

The first and the third assumption do not fully agree, as for the beam: if \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\), then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = -1{,}7\cdot 10^{-4} \ne 0\), as we have just computed on the real fibre. The kinematics does not contain this shortening, Hooke's law accounts for it in the stress.

To compute strains we need coordinates in which the wall with its thickness is also an orthogonal system, as in chapter 11. Take coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) along the lines of curvature of the middle surface (definition 22.16) and a third coordinate \(z\) along the normal. Let \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) be the unit vectors of the tangents to the coordinate lines (definition 22.2), \(A_{\mathrm{i}} = |\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}|\) the scale factors of the middle surface, and \(R_1\), \(R_2\) the principal radii of curvature (theorem 22.15), signed so that \(R_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) when the centre of curvature lies on the side of the vector \(-\vek n\), that is \(1/R_{\mathrm{i}} = -\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the principal curvature \(\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the same normal \(\vek n\) (equation (22.13)). In section 22.2 the normal usually points towards the centre and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{i}} = 1/R_{\mathrm{i}}\) there, here the normal is the outward one. A spherical shell with outward normal thus has \(R_1 = R_2 = R > 0\), a tube with outward normal \(R_2 = R\) and \(R_1 = \infty\). Two warnings: the scale factors \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\) of chapter 11 are called \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\) here, because \(h\) is the thickness, and VK uses the axis \(z\) towards the centre of curvature, so its factor is \(1 - z/R_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Lemma 22.25 Shell coordinates (koordinate lupine)

Let \(\vek r(q_1, q_2)\) be a three times continuously differentiable middle surface on an open set whose coordinate lines are lines of curvature, and let \(|z| \le h/2\) with \(h/2 < |R_{\mathrm{i}}|\) for \(i = 1, 2\). Let \(\Phi(q_1, q_2, z) = \vek r(q_1, q_2) + z\,\vek n(q_1, q_2)\) be injective. Then \(q_1\), \(q_2\), \(z\) are orthogonal coordinates (definition 11.13) with scale factors

\[H_1 = A_1\Big(1 + \frac{z}{R_1}\Big) , \qquad H_2 = A_2\Big(1 + \frac{z}{R_2}\Big) , \qquad H_3 = 1 \tag{22.18}\]

and local frame \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek n\).

Proof

We must show the three conditions of definition 11.13. We compute the columns of the matrix of derivatives from the derivatives of the normal.

  1. Let \(b_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek n\cdot\partial^2\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\) be the second fundamental form (definition 22.12). The derivative of \(\vek n\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) gives \(\partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} = -b_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The derivative of the unit normal is perpendicular to it (the derivative of \(\vek n\cdot\vek n = 1\) is \(2\,\vek n\cdot\partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\)), so it lies in the tangent plane and in the basis \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) equals \(\partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (b_{\mathrm{ij}}/A_{\mathrm{j}})\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. On lines of curvature \(b_{12} = 0\), and the normal curvature in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{i}} = b_{\mathrm{ii}}/A_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = -1/R_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the agreed sign (centre of curvature on the side of \(-\vek n\): for a sphere with outward normal \(b_{\mathrm{ii}} = -A_{\mathrm{i}}^2/R\)). Hence \(\partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = (A_{\mathrm{i}}/R_{\mathrm{i}})\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\). This is Rodrigues' relation, for a sphere with outward normal \(\partial\vek n/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = (\partial\vek r/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}})/R\).
  3. The columns along the normal and the arc are \(\partial\Phi/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}} = A_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + z\,(A_{\mathrm{i}}/R_{\mathrm{i}})\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}} = H_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(i = 1, 2\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z = \vek n\). They are perpendicular because \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek n\) are pairwise perpendicular (definition 22.2). This is condition 3.
  4. The Jacobian determinant is by lemma 11.14 \(J = H_1 H_2 > 0\), because \(1 + z/R_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\ge 1 - h/(2|R_{\mathrm{i}}|) > 0\) and \(\vek e_1\times\vek e_2 = \vek n\). Conditions 1 and 2 are the conditions of three times differentiability of \(\vek r\) and injectivity of \(\Phi\).

Source: VK sections 11.3 to 11.5 and 12.2 (PDF p. 312-316 and 331-337) introduce the scale factors \(A(1 \mp z/R)\) for a shell. The proof from the definition of orthogonal coordinates is not from the source.

The condition \(h/2 < |R_{\mathrm{i}}|\) is not a formality. Take a solid rod, that is a tube with \(h = 2R\). The inner arc of radius \(R - h/2\) then shrinks to a point. At \(z = -R\) the point lies on the axis, where \(1 + z/R_2 = 0\), the Jacobian determinant is zero and the coordinates fail: the fibres of all directions \(\theta\) meet in the same point. For our tube (\(h/2 = 1\) mm, \(R = 50\) mm) and for the thick tube of chapter 11 (\(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, \(h/2 = 10\) mm) the condition holds, since \(1 + z/R \ge 0{,}8\).

We look at the factors \(1 + z/R_{\mathrm{i}}\) in figure 22.30. We draw the two radii at angles \(\theta\) and \(\theta + \Delta\theta\), which enclose the angle \(\Delta\theta\), and between them the wall of the tube. The fibres along the normal join the inner and the outer face. The middle arc has length \(R\,\Delta\theta\) (a step \(\Delta\theta\) along a circle of radius \(R\), as in lemma 11.15). The inner arc has radius \(R - h/2\) and is therefore shorter, the outer one has radius \(R + h/2\) and is longer. At the distance \(z\) from the middle surface the arc has length \((R + z)\,\Delta\theta = R\,(1 + z/R)\,\Delta\theta\), in agreement with \(H_2 = R\,(1 + z/R)\) of lemma 22.25 (\(A_2 = R\), \(R_2 = R\)). For the thick tube the outer and inner arcs are in the ratio \(60 : 40\), for ours \(51 : 49\), which is \(1{,}041\).

22.3.2 Strains across the thickness (deformacije po debelini)

Now we can look for the strains of the wall. VK states the general form for arbitrary lines of curvature as (12.22) to (12.25) (PDF p. 336), and we only quote it without proof. We prove it for shells that are loaded axisymmetrically, which covers the cylinder, sphere, cone and every shell of revolution.

We cut the shell of revolution with a plane through the axis (figure 22.31, left). In this plane the middle surface is a curve, the meridian, and the whole surface arises when we turn it around the axis. As coordinates we take the arc length \(s\) along the meridian and the angle \(\theta\) around the axis. At the point \(P\) we draw the normal and extend it grey dashed back to the axis. The angle between the axis and the normal is \(\varphi(s)\) (for a sphere this is \(\varphi\) of lemma 11.15). Two centres lie on this line. The first is the centre of the circle that fits the meridian best at \(P\): the distance to it is \(R_1\), the radius of curvature of the meridian. When we move along the meridian by \(\Delta s\), the normal turns by \(\Delta\varphi \approx \Delta s/R_1\), as on a circle of radius \(R_1\), so \(\varphi' = 1/R_1\). Derivatives with respect to \(s\) are marked by a prime. The second centre is the point where the normal meets the axis: the distance to it is \(R_2\), the second principal radius. The distance of the point \(P\) from the axis is \(\rho(s)\). In the right triangle with the axis, the normal and \(\rho\) we have \(\rho = R_2\sin\varphi\), so \(R_2 = \rho/\sin\varphi\). The tangent of the meridian \(\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\) is perpendicular to the normal \(\vek n\), so its component in the direction away from the axis is \(\cos\varphi\) and \(\rho' = \cos\varphi\). The fibre along the normal reaches from \(z = -h/2\) to \(h/2\). Its point at height \(z\) is farther from the axis than \(P\) by \(z\sin\varphi\), that is at \(\rho + z\sin\varphi = \rho\,(1 + z/R_2)\). For a cylinder \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) and \(1/R_1 = 0\), for a sphere \(R_1 = R_2 = R\). The vectors of the local frame \(\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\vek e_\theta\), \(\vek n\) are differentiable with respect to \(s\), \(\theta\) by a table that we derive in the proof.

The displacement has a tangential component \(u_{\mathrm{s}}\) and a normal one \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\), and no component along \(\theta\) (axial symmetry). The right side of figure 22.31 shows it on the middle surface: a point of the meridian before loading moves by \(u^0\) along the meridian and by \(w\) along the normal onto the orange meridian. Its distance from the axis was \(\rho\). The first displacement moves it away by \(u^0\cos\varphi\), the second by \(w\sin\varphi\), together by \(\Delta\rho\). The parallel through the point is a circle of radius \(\rho\) and circumference \(2\pi\rho\). After the displacement its circumference is \(2\pi(\rho + \Delta\rho)\), so it lengthens by the fraction \(\Delta\rho/\rho\). This is the hoop strain, which the theorem will give as \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\).

Theorem 22.26 Strains of a shell of revolution (deformacije lupine vrtenine)

Let a shell of revolution be as above with \(h/2 < |R_{\mathrm{i}}|\) (lemma 22.25) and let \(u^0(s)\), \(w(s)\) be twice continuously differentiable functions.

  1. An axisymmetric displacement field with \(u_\theta = 0\) has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{sn}} = 0\) if and only if
    \[u_{\mathrm{s}} = u^0\,\Big(1 + \frac{z}{R_1}\Big) - z\,w' , \qquad u_{\mathrm{n}} = w . \tag{22.19}\]
  2. For such a field \(\varepsilon_{\theta \mathrm{n}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}\theta} = 0\) and
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{s}} + z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{s}}}{1 + z/R_1} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\theta} = \frac{\varepsilon^0_\theta + z\,\kappa_\theta}{1 + z/R_2} \tag{22.20}\]
    with the strains of the middle surface and the changes of curvature
    \[\begin{aligned} &\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{s}} = u^{0\prime} + \frac{w}{R_1} , \qquad \varepsilon^0_\theta = \frac{u^0\cos\varphi + w\sin\varphi}{\rho} , \\ &\kappa_{\mathrm{s}} = \beta' , \qquad \kappa_\theta = \frac{\beta\cos\varphi}{\rho} , \qquad \beta = \frac{u^0}{R_1} - w' . \end{aligned} \tag{22.21}\]
  3. If we drop the factors \(1 + z/R_{\mathrm{i}}\), then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{KL}} = \varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{i}} + z\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{KL}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}} = (z/R_{\mathrm{i}})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the error is at most \(h/(2|R_{\mathrm{i}}|)\) of the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}\).
Proof

We must show that the field (22.19) satisfies both conditions and that the strains are as stated. We use theorem 11.20 with the local frame of lemma 22.25.

  1. Derivatives of the frame: the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{s}} = (\cos\varphi\cos\theta, \cos\varphi\sin\theta, -\sin\varphi)\), \(\vek n = (\sin\varphi\cos\theta, \sin\varphi\sin\theta, \cos\varphi)\), \(\vek e_\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\) are differentiable by the theorem on derivatives of sine and cosine. Their derivatives are \(\partial\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}/\partial s = -\vek n/R_1\), \(\partial\vek n/\partial s = \vek e_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1\), \(\partial\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}/\partial\theta = \cos\varphi\,\vek e_\theta\), \(\partial\vek n/\partial\theta = \sin\varphi\,\vek e_\theta\), \(\partial\vek e_\theta/\partial\theta = -\sin\varphi\,\vek n - \cos\varphi\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\), all the others are zero. From \(\partial\vek n/\partial s = \varphi'\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\partial\vek n/\partial q_1 = \vek e_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1\) (lemma 22.25) we get \(\varphi' = 1/R_1\) (the normal turns by \(\Delta s/R_1\)), and the last three equalities are the same as in the table of spherical coordinates (lemma 11.15). The scale factors are \(H_{\mathrm{s}} = 1 + z/R_1\) and \(H_\theta = \rho + z\sin\varphi = \rho\,(1 + z/R_2)\), the distance of a point of the fibre from the axis.
  2. For \(\vek u = u_{\mathrm{s}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}} + u_{\mathrm{n}}\,\vek n\) the second equality of (11.26) and step 1 give \(\partial\vek u/\partial s = (u_{\mathrm{s}}' + u_{\mathrm{n}}/R_1)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}} + (u_{\mathrm{n}}' - u_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1)\,\vek n\), \(\partial\vek u/\partial\theta = (u_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\varphi + u_{\mathrm{n}}\sin\varphi)\,\vek e_\theta\) (the bracket is the shift away from the axis) and \(\partial\vek u/\partial z = u_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{s}} + u_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{z}}\,\vek n\), where \(u_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{z}}\) means the derivative with respect to \(z\).
  3. The first equality of (11.26) gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = u_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sn}} = \tfrac12\big(u_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{z}} + (u_{\mathrm{n}}' - u_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1)/H_{\mathrm{s}}\big)\). The first is zero if and only if \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) does not depend on \(z\), that is \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = w(s)\): both ends of the normal fibre move by the same amount. The second is zero if and only if \(u_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{z}}H_{\mathrm{s}} - u_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1 = -w'\), that is \(\partial(u_{\mathrm{s}}/H_{\mathrm{s}})/\partial z = -w'/H_{\mathrm{s}}^2\), since \(\partial(u_{\mathrm{s}}/H_{\mathrm{s}})/\partial z = (u_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{z}}H_{\mathrm{s}} - u_{\mathrm{s}}/R_1)/H_{\mathrm{s}}^2\).
  4. Since \(\partial(z/H_{\mathrm{s}})/\partial z = 1/H_{\mathrm{s}}^2\), the solution is \(u_{\mathrm{s}}/H_{\mathrm{s}} = u^0 - w'z/H_{\mathrm{s}}\) with the function \(u^0(s) = u_{\mathrm{s}}(s, 0)\), that is \(u_{\mathrm{s}} = u^0H_{\mathrm{s}} - w'z\). Conversely, this \(u_{\mathrm{s}}\) satisfies the equation of step 3. This is item 1.
  5. Insert (22.19) into step 2: \(u_{\mathrm{s}}' + w/R_1 = H_{\mathrm{s}} u^{0\prime} + z\,u^0\,(1/R_1)' - z\,w'' + w/R_1\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}} = A_{\mathrm{ss}} = (u_{\mathrm{s}}' + w/R_1)/H_{\mathrm{s}}\) equals \(\big[\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{s}} + z\,(u^{0\prime}/R_1 + u^0(1/R_1)' - w'')\big]/H_{\mathrm{s}}\). The expression in the bracket is \(\beta'\), since \(\beta' = (u^0/R_1)' - w''\). This is the first equality of (22.20).
  6. The hoop strain \(\varepsilon_\theta = (u_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\varphi + w\sin\varphi)/H_\theta\) is the shift away from the axis divided by the distance from the axis, as for the circumference of a circle. In the numerator \(u_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\varphi + w\sin\varphi = (u^0\cos\varphi + w\sin\varphi) + z\cos\varphi\,(u^0/R_1 - w')\), and with \(H_\theta = \rho\,(1 + z/R_2)\) this is the second equality. The shear components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{s}\theta}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\theta \mathrm{n}}\) are zero, because \(\partial\vek u/\partial\theta\) has no components in \(\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek n\) and because \(\partial\vek u/\partial s\) and \(\partial\vek u/\partial z\) have no component in \(\vek e_\theta\).
  7. Dropping the factor: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{KL}} = \varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{i}} + z\kappa_{\mathrm{i}} = (1 + z/R_{\mathrm{i}})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the difference is \((z/R_{\mathrm{i}})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(|z/R_{\mathrm{i}}| \le h/(2|R_{\mathrm{i}}|)\). This is item 3. On the inner arc \(z/R_{\mathrm{i}} < 0\) and the model underestimates the strain, on the outer one it overestimates it.

Source: VK (12.22) to (12.25) (PDF p. 336) for general lines of curvature, without proof. The proof for a shell of revolution is ours. VK has the exact forms (22.20) as (12.10) and (12.21) (PDF pp. 334-335). We checked the computation numerically on a shell with varying \(R_1(s)\) and \(R_2(s)\) and arbitrary \(u^0\), \(w\): the difference between the formulas and the strains from Cartesian derivatives is \(6\cdot 10^{-12}\) at strains of order \(10^{-3}\) (NumPy, num-03.py).

Special cases are seen at once. For a cylinder (\(1/R_1 = 0\), \(\varphi = 90^\circ\), \(\rho = R\)) we have \(\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{x}} = u^{0\prime}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = -w''\), \(\varepsilon^0_\theta = w/R\) and \(\kappa_\theta = 0\), and the circumference of the tube lengthens from \(2\pi R\) to \(2\pi(R + w)\), that is by the fraction \(w/R\) (for a cylinder \(\Delta\rho = w\)), as for the expanded ring in chapter 11. Along a generator the tube is a beam with the deflection \(v = w\), and the change of curvature \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = -w''\) is the curvature \(v''\) of a beam (definition 5.16) with the opposite sign. The sign is reversed because for the beam \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v''\) (equation (5.17)), while here \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} = u^{0\prime} + z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\). Figure 22.32 shows it.

We draw first the wall before the load: the middle line and both faces with lines of the normals, of thickness \(h\), and the axes \(x\) and \(z\) along the generator and along the normal. Then we take a function \(w(x)\) for which the middle line rises in its middle part by \(w\) and draw it in orange. By theorem 22.26 the faces and normals move like this: each normal moves with the point of the middle line to which it is attached and turns, so that it stays perpendicular to the new middle line. The angle of rotation is to first order \(-w'\), which gives the term \(-z\,w'\) in the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{s}}\) (cylinder, \(R_1 = \infty\)): a point on the upper face, \(z = h/2\), moves along the axis by \(-w'\,h/2\). A fibre lengthens or shortens only if this axial shift changes along the axis, that is, if \(w'\) changes. Where \(w'\) grows (\(w'' > 0\), at the foot of the bump) the upper fibres shorten and the lower ones lengthen, at the top of the bump (\(w'' < 0\)) it is the other way round. We measure this in the figure: the two normals next to the top were \(\Delta x\) apart before loading. After it they open like a fan, the upper ends are \(1{,}13\,\Delta x\) apart and the lower ones \(0{,}85\,\Delta x\), while on the middle line the distance stays \(\Delta x\). The strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} = u^{0\prime} - z\,w''\) is linear in \(z\) and vanishes on the middle surface if \(u^{0\prime} = 0\).

We test the dropping of the factor \(1 + z/R_{\mathrm{i}}\) on two tubes of chapter 11. For the thin tube (\(R = 50\) mm, \(h = 2\) mm) \(h/(2R) = 0{,}020\), the factor \(1/(1 + z/R)\) is \(1{,}0204\) on the inner face and \(0{,}9804\) on the outer one. The reason is the same lengthening \(2\pi w\) of the circumference on a shorter or a longer arc. So the exact strain is \(2{,}04\,\%\) larger than \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\) on the inner face and \(1{,}96\,\%\) smaller on the outer one, and the bound relative to \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\) is \((h/2R)/(1 - h/2R) = 0{,}0204\). Relative to the exact strain the error is \(z/R\), at most \(h/(2R) = 0{,}02\) (theorem 22.26, item 3). The hoop strain \(w/R\) is thus accurate to \(2\,\%\) through the whole thickness. For the thick tube (\(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, \(R = 50\) mm, \(h = 20\) mm) \(h/(2R) = 0{,}2\) and the factor is \(1{,}25\) on the inner and \(0{,}833\) on the outer face, so the exact strain differs from \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\) by \(+25\,\%\) and \(-16{,}7\,\%\) (bound \(0{,}25\), relative to the exact strain \(0{,}2\)). Figure 22.30 is drawn for exactly this ratio \(h/R = 0{,}4\). For the same displacement \(w\) the inner face has the hoop strain \(w/40\) and the outer one \(w/60\), a ratio of \(1{,}5\). The Kirchhoff-Love strain \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\), equal through the whole thickness, is not usable here.

The assumption about the normal also has its price. By Lamé (theorem 11.28, closed ends, equation (11.38)) the thin tube at \(p = 3\) MPa has the displacement \(u(a) = 16{,}281\ \mu\)m on the inner face and \(u(b) = 15{,}931\ \mu\)m on the outer one. The normal fibre shortens by the difference \(0{,}350\ \mu\)m, which is \(2{,}2\,\%\) of the mean displacement, and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = -1{,}85\cdot 10^{-4}\) is not zero. The assumption \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = w\) through the thickness is thus accurate to \(2\,\%\). For the thick tube (\(p = 30\) MPa) \(u(a) = 16{,}286\ \mu\)m, \(u(b) = 12{,}490\ \mu\)m, a difference of \(27\,\%\), and the hoop strain is \(4{,}07\cdot 10^{-4}\) on the inner face and \(2{,}08\cdot 10^{-4}\) on the outer one, a ratio of \(1{,}96\) (num-03.out). The price of the second assumption, the dropped shear strain of the normal fibre, was estimated at the assumption itself (section 22.3.1).

22.3.3 Forces and moments per unit length (sile in momenti na enoto dolžine)

The strains in the wall are linear in \(z\), so the stresses will be too, and we would have to describe every cross section by a function. Equilibrium of the shell will be simpler if we add the stresses through the thickness into forces and moments on the middle surface, as for the beam we added the stresses over the cross section into \(N\), \(V\), \(M\). Take a cut of the wall along the coordinate line \(q_2\) at \(q_1 = a\) (figure 22.33), with outward normal \(+\vek e_1\) and stress vector \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_1 = \sigma_{11}\,\vek e_1 + \sigma_{12}\,\vek e_2 + \sigma_{1\mathrm{n}}\,\vek n\) (definition 11.19). By lemma 11.14 (surface vector \(\vek N_1 = H_2 H_3\,\vek e_1\)) the force on the part of the cut \(c \le q_2 \le d\) equals the integral

\[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d\!\!\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} \ten\sigma\,\vek e_1\;A_2\Big(1 + \frac{z}{R_2}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}q_2 .\]

The factor \(1 + z/R_2\) is the same as in lemma 22.25: a strip of the cross section at height \(z\) is longer or shorter than the strip on the middle surface, so it carries more or less force. As in theorem 22.26 we drop it, with an error of at most \(h/(2|R_2|)\). For our tube that is \(0{,}02\). For the thick tube it is \(0{,}2\) and dropping it is no longer justified. After dropping it the resultants become simple integrals of the stresses through the thickness.

Definition 22.27 Stress resultants and stress couples of a shell (notranje sile in momenti lupine)

Let a shell be as in lemma 22.25 with a stress field \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) in the local frame \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek n\), continuous through the thickness. The forces per unit length of a coordinate line of the middle surface (unit N/mm) are functions of the point of the middle surface, which are integrals over the thickness

\[\begin{aligned} &N_1 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{11}\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad N_2 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{22}\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad N_{12} = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{12}\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ &Q_1 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{1\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad Q_2 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{2\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}z , \end{aligned} \tag{22.22}\]

and the moments per unit length (unit N mm/mm)

\[M_1 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{11}\,z\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad M_2 = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{22}\,z\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad M_{12} = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\!\sigma_{12}\,z\,\mathrm{d}z . \tag{22.23}\]

On a cut with normal \(+\vek e_1\) the force \(N_1\,\vek e_1 + N_{12}\,\vek e_2 + Q_1\,\vek n\) and the moment \(M_1\,\vek e_2 - M_{12}\,\vek e_1\) act per unit length, on a cut with normal \(+\vek e_2\) the force \(N_2\,\vek e_2 + N_{12}\,\vek e_1 + Q_2\,\vek n\) and the moment \(-M_2\,\vek e_1 + M_{12}\,\vek e_2\), because \(\sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21}\). The forces and moments are the resultant and the moment of the stress vector about a point of the middle surface, with an error of the factor \(1 + z/R_{\mathrm{j}}\) of at most \(h/(2|R_{\mathrm{j}}|)\).

Source: VK (12.35) and (12.36) (PDF p. 340), with the exact form that has the factor \(1 \mp z/R_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the integrand (PDF p. 339-340), and the simplification by dropping (PDF p. 344). In the exact form VK has \(N_{12} \ne N_{21}\) and \(M_{12} \ne M_{21}\) (12.43, PDF p. 343), after dropping the factor they are equal (12.48, PDF p. 345). The sign of \(M_1\) is as for the curved beam (definition 11.59, \(M > 0\) when the outer fibres are in tension), and \(Q_1\) has the opposite sign to its \(V\).

We look at the figure as at a board. We draw the wall of thickness \(h\) with the middle line dashed, and a cut at its end, with the directions \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek n\). On the cut there is the stress \(\sigma_{11}\): the blue arrows show how it changes through the thickness, it is largest at the upper face (tension) and compressive at the lower one. Its sum over the thickness is \(N_1\), the force along \(\vek e_1\) through the middle surface, and its moment about the middle surface is \(M_1\), a couple of forces pulling above and pushing below (so \(M_1 > 0\) when the outer fibres are in tension). The shear stress \(\sigma_{1\mathrm{n}}\) is gathered by \(Q_1\) along \(\vek n\). All three forces are drawn on the same wall to the right of the equivalence sign \(\equiv\). The units are N/mm and N mm/mm, per unit length, not as for the beam, where \(N\) and \(M\) are whole forces of the cross section (section 5.2.1).

For the tube from the start of the section, \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = pR/h = 75\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = pR/(2h) = 37{,}5\) MPa are constant through the wall (axisymmetric membrane), so the sums over the thickness are \(N_\theta = \sigma_{\theta\theta}h = pR = 150\) N/mm, \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = pR/2 = 75\) N/mm, and all moments are zero (section 22.5 derives them).

22.3.4 Wall, plate and shell (stena, plošča in lupina)

The shell has two flat relatives, and the difference between them and the shell is the reason why the shell has a theory of its own. We cut all three out of a structure and look at them from the side (figure 22.34). VK (section 10.2, PDF p. 298) says that a shell has all the characteristics of a plate and one more, curvature, and that a plate is the limiting case of a shell without curvature.

The first piece is a wall (stena): flat and thin, loaded only in its own plane, like a sheet that we pull at two edges. Each of its layers is in plane stress (definition 11.36) and the stresses are the same through the thickness. Of the eight quantities of definition 22.27 only the in-plane forces are therefore non-zero, these are \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{xy}}\). There are no moments, because for a stress that is the same through the thickness \(\int\sigma z\,\mathrm{d}z = \sigma\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\). There are no transverse forces, because nothing loads the wall perpendicular to its plane.

The second piece is a plate (definition 18.1): flat as well, but loaded perpendicular to its plane. Why can the in-plane forces not carry this load? The forces \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the two cuts would lie in the plane of the plate, as for the wall, so perpendicular to the load, and they contribute nothing in the direction of the load. The load is therefore carried by the transverse forces on the cuts. These grip the piece at its edges, while the load acts along its whole length, so without the bending moments the piece would turn and bend. A plate thus carries with the moments \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the transverse forces \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) (definitions 18.5 and 18.9), and a Kirchhoff plate has no in-plane forces (definition 18.2, item 4).

The third piece is a shell, here a piece of the wall of our tube between two radii that enclose the angle \(\Delta\theta\). The pressure \(p\) pushes perpendicular to the wall, like the load on the plate. But the cuts are no longer parallel: the hoop forces \(N_\theta\) are tangent to the middle surface and therefore inclined towards each other by the angle \(\Delta\theta\). We put them together in a triangle of forces. Their resultant \(2N_\theta\sin(\Delta\theta/2)\) points to the centre of the tube, straight against the pressure. The resultant of the pressure on the piece is the pressure times the chord \(2R\sin(\Delta\theta/2)\), because the components of the pressure along the chord cancel (the same calculation as for half a tube before equation (11.35), where the chord is the diameter). The equilibrium of forces in the direction of the centre, per unit length of the tube, is therefore

\[2\,N_\theta\sin\frac{\Delta\theta}{2} = 2\,p\,R\sin\frac{\Delta\theta}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{N_\theta}{R} = p . \tag{22.24}\]

For our tube and the angle \(50^\circ\) of the figure both sides are \(2\cdot 150\cdot\sin 25^\circ = 2\cdot 3\cdot 50\cdot\sin 25^\circ = 126{,}8\) N/mm, and \(N_\theta = pR = 150\) N/mm is the force we obtained from half a tube. The pressure is carried by a tensile force in the surface, without a transverse force and without a moment. This is the essence of a shell: because of the curvature, a force in the surface has a component perpendicular to the surface, \(N_\theta/R\) per unit area. For a flat piece \(R = \infty\), this component vanishes and only \(Q\) and \(M\) are left for the load. VK (section 10.4, PDF p. 304) compares this with an arch and a straight beam: an arch carries a transverse load with its axial force, a straight beam with bending.

In general a shell has all eight quantities on a cut at once, also the moment and the transverse force, that is \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(N_\theta\), \(N_{\mathrm{x}\theta}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_\theta\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}\theta}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_\theta\), and the curvature ties them together in the same equations of equilibrium. So for a shell bending cannot be separated from stretching (VK, PDF p. 298), as it can for a flat piece, where the wall and the plate each solve their own problem. Where the tube cannot expand freely, for example at a clamped edge, the term \(N_\theta/R\) does not balance the whole pressure and bending takes the difference. This will be the equation of the cylinder (22.42) in section 22.6, in which this term stands written with the displacement: \(N_\theta/R = (Eh/R^2)\,w + \nu N_1/R\).

A comparison shows how much the curvature is worth. Let the same pressure \(p = 3\) MPa be carried, instead of the tube, by a flat strip of plate of the same thickness \(h = 2\) mm, as wide as the diameter of the tube, \(L = 2R = 100\) mm, and simply supported on both long edges (corollary 18.26, item 1, with the load \(q = p\) and the bending stiffness \(D = Eh^3/(12(1 - \nu^2)) = 143\,590\) N mm of definition 18.6).

tube (shell) flat strip (plate)
force on the cut \(N_\theta = pR = 150\) N/mm, in the surface \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = pL/2 = 150\) N/mm, transverse
largest moment \(0\) \(pL^2/8 = 3750\) N mm/mm
largest stress \(pR/h = 75\) MPa \(6\cdot 3750/h^2 = 5625\) MPa
largest displacement \(16{,}3\ \mu\)m \(5pL^4/(384D) = 27{,}2\) mm

Both structures carry the same force, \(2pR = 300\) N per millimetre of length, so the forces on the cuts are equally large, \(150\) N/mm. The difference is in the direction. In the tube the force lies in the surface of the wall and the whole thickness carries it evenly. In the plate the force is transverse and comes with a moment, which only the layers near the faces carry. The ratio of the stresses is

\[\frac{6\,pL^2/(8h^2)}{pR/h} = \frac{3L^2}{4Rh} = \frac{3R}{h} = 75 \qquad\text{for } L = 2R .\]

The numbers for the plate are not a prediction but a proof that such a strip cannot do the job: \(5625\) MPa is far above the strength of steel, and the deflection \(27{,}2\) mm is \(13{,}6\) thicknesses, while a Kirchhoff plate allows at most \(h/5 = 0{,}4\) mm (definition 18.2, item 2). A tube of the same sheet carries the same pressure with \(75\) MPa and expands by \(16\ \mu\)m.

The flat pieces have one more simplification. For \(R = \infty\) the factor \(1 + z/R\) is exactly one, so the integrals of definition 22.27 are exact resultants for the wall and the plate. For a shell they are an approximation with the error \(h/(2R)\). In the lectures the forces and moments per unit length are called unit forces and moments (enotske sile in momenti). For the wall and the plate the book writes them with the indices \(x\), \(y\) (\(N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\)), for a general shell with the indices \(1\), \(2\) of the coordinates of the middle surface.

22.3.5 Hooke's law for a shell (Hookov zakon za lupino)

How are \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{i}}\) related to the strains \(\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}\)? The material of every fibre is in plane stress (theorem 11.37), because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) (definition 22.24, item 3). Hooke's law in local components (corollary 11.27) gives by theorem 11.37 with \(E' = E\), \(\nu' = \nu\) the relation of stresses and strains, from which integration over the thickness gives the relation of the resultants.

Theorem 22.28 Hooke's law for a shell (Hookov zakon za lupino)

Let a shell be as in definition 22.24, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{ij}} + z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with \(i, j = 1, 2\) (strains in the surface, theorem 22.26, item 3) and \(E\), \(\nu\) from theorem 3.64. Let

\[C = \frac{E\,h}{1 - \nu^2} , \qquad D = \frac{E\,h^3}{12\,(1 - \nu^2)} . \tag{22.25}\]

Then

\[\begin{aligned} &N_1 = C\,(\varepsilon^0_1 + \nu\,\varepsilon^0_2) , \quad N_2 = C\,(\varepsilon^0_2 + \nu\,\varepsilon^0_1) , \quad N_{12} = C\,(1 - \nu)\,\varepsilon^0_{12} , \\ &M_1 = D\,(\kappa_1 + \nu\,\kappa_2) , \quad M_2 = D\,(\kappa_2 + \nu\,\kappa_1) , \quad M_{12} = D\,(1 - \nu)\,\kappa_{12} . \end{aligned} \tag{22.26}\]

The forces depend only on the strains of the middle surface, the moments only on the changes of curvature.

Proof

We must show that the integral over the thickness separates \(\varepsilon^0\) from \(\kappa\).

  1. By theorem 11.37 (item 1, equations (11.50) inverted) at every point through the thickness \(\sigma_{11} = E\,(\varepsilon_{11} + \nu\,\varepsilon_{22})/(1 - \nu^2)\), \(\sigma_{22} = E\,(\varepsilon_{22} + \nu\,\varepsilon_{11})/(1 - \nu^2)\) and \(\sigma_{12} = E\,\varepsilon_{12}/(1 + \nu)\) (equations (3.27) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\)).
  2. Insert \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{ij}} + z\kappa_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and integrate over \(z\) from \(-h/2\) to \(h/2\). The integral \(\int\mathrm{d}z\) is \(h\), \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\) and \(\int z^2\,\mathrm{d}z = h^3/12\). The middle one is zero because every layer above the middle surface has an equal layer below it with the opposite \(z\): the part of the stress that is linear in \(z\) pulls above as much as it pushes below.
  3. In \(N_1\) \(= \int\sigma_{11}\,\mathrm{d}z\) what remains is \(E\,h\,(\varepsilon^0_1 + \nu\varepsilon^0_2)/(1 - \nu^2)\), because the term with \(\kappa\) multiplies \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\). The same for \(N_2\). For \(N_{12}\) it is \(E\,h\,\varepsilon^0_{12}/(1 + \nu) = C\,(1 - \nu)\,\varepsilon^0_{12}\).
  4. In \(M_1\) \(= \int\sigma_{11}z\,\mathrm{d}z\) the term with \(\kappa\) remains, because the term with \(\varepsilon^0\) multiplies \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\), and it is \(E\,(h^3/12)(\kappa_1 + \nu\kappa_2)/(1 - \nu^2) = D\,(\kappa_1 + \nu\kappa_2)\). The same for \(M_2\) and \(M_{12}\).

Source: VK (12.45) to (12.47) (PDF p. 344), proof as in VK by integrating (12.33) over the thickness. VK calls \(D\) the flexural rigidity of the shell. The plate has the same \(D\) (chapter 18). The symbol \(D\) in this book is not the amplification factor of the chapter on plane equations. The proof from \(\varepsilon^0_{12}\), \(\kappa_{12}\) as tensor components is ours.

Numbers for our tube (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(h = 2\) mm): \(C = 430\,769\) N/mm and \(D = 143\,590\) N mm, the ratio \(D/C = h^2/12 = 0{,}333\) mm\(^2\). Under pressure \(N_\theta = 150\) N/mm and \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = 75\) N/mm. The inverted first line gives \(\varepsilon^0_\theta = (N_\theta - \nu N_{\mathrm{x}})/(E\,h) = 3{,}2526\cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{x}} = 7{,}653\cdot 10^{-5}\), the displacement \(w = R\,\varepsilon^0_\theta = 16{,}263\ \mu\)m. In section 22.7 we compare this membrane displacement of the tube with that of a hemispherical head, which expands less. Check: \(C\,(\varepsilon^0_\theta + \nu\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{x}}) = 150{,}00\) N/mm.

The theorem held because we took the reference surface for the integrals in the middle, \(z \in [-h/2, h/2]\), where \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\). What happens if we take the inner face as the reference surface? Let \(z' = z + h/2 \in [0, h]\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon'_{\mathrm{ij}} + z'\kappa_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Then \(\int z'\,\mathrm{d}z' = h^2/2 \ne 0\) and

\[N_1 = \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2}\,\Big[h\,(\varepsilon'_1 + \nu\varepsilon'_2) + \frac{h^2}{2}\,(\kappa_1 + \nu\kappa_2)\Big] = C\,\Big[(\varepsilon'_1 + \nu\varepsilon'_2) + \frac{h}{2}\,(\kappa_1 + \nu\kappa_2)\Big] ,\]

so the force depends on the curvature too, and the moment on the stretching. Test it on pure bending with \(\kappa_1 = 5\cdot 10^{-4}\) mm\(^{-1}\) (\(\kappa_2 = 0\)) at \(h = 2\) mm, that is on a cross section that carries only the couple \(M_1\). The force \(N_1\) in the cross section is zero, since the bending is pure, so the strain of the inner face is \(\varepsilon'_1 = -\kappa_1h/2 = -5\cdot 10^{-4}\). The law of theorem 22.28 without the term in \(\kappa\), applied at the inner face, \(N_1 = C\,\varepsilon'_1\) (with \(\varepsilon'_2 = 0\)), would give \(N_1 = -215\) N/mm, that is a mean stress of \(-107{,}7\) MPa through the whole thickness, while the true value is zero. Without symmetry through the thickness (the middle surface) the membrane and bending parts do not separate. So we take as the reference surface the middle surface \(z = 0\), which halves the wall.

22.3.6 Energy of a shell (energija lupine)

The last step is the energy, on which sections 22.6 and 22.8 will rely. The strain energy of a body is the integral of the energy density over the volume (definition 4.85). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{1\mathrm{n}} = \varepsilon_{2\mathrm{n}} = 0\) the energy density, which we denote here by \(\mathcal W\) because \(w\) is a displacement in this chapter, is \(\mathcal W = \tfrac12(\sigma_{11}\varepsilon_{11} + \sigma_{22}\varepsilon_{22} + 2\sigma_{12}\varepsilon_{12})\): the terms with the normal have either zero stress or zero strain. So the energy density that we take here is that of plane stress, not that from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) (this would give the constant \(E\,(1 - \nu)/((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu))\) instead of \(E/(1 - \nu^2)\), for \(\nu = 0{,}3\) larger by the factor \((1 - \nu)^2/(1 - 2\nu) = 1{,}225\)).

Why the energy will split into two parts is shown already by the square of the strain through the thickness \(h\) (figure 22.35). The energy is proportional to the square of the strain, added up through the thickness. In stretching the strain is the same \(\varepsilon_0\) through the whole thickness, its square as well, and the mean of the square is \(1\cdot\varepsilon_0^2\). In bending with the same largest strain the strain goes linearly from \(-\varepsilon_0\) on one face to \(\varepsilon_0\) on the other and is zero on the middle surface. Its square is a parabola, full only at the faces, with the mean

\[\frac{1}{h}\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\Big(\frac{2z}{h}\Big)^2\mathrm{d}z = \frac{1}{h}\cdot\frac{4}{h^2}\cdot\frac{h^3}{12} = \frac13 .\]

The grey dashed line bounds a rectangle with the same area as the parabola. The material near the middle surface does almost no work in bending, so bending with the same largest strain stores only a third of the energy of stretching. The mixed term, the strain of stretching times the strain of bending, is zero on average through the thickness, because the linear part is positive above and equally negative below.

Theorem 22.29 Strain energy of a shell (energija lupine)

Let a shell be as in theorem 22.28 and \(S\) the middle surface with area \(A = \iint_{\mathrm{S}} A_1 A_2\,\mathrm{d}q_1\,\mathrm{d}q_2\). The strain energy is, up to the factor \((1 + z/R_1)(1 + z/R_2)\) of lemma 22.25, which we drop, the sum \(U = U_{\mathrm{m}} + U_{\mathrm{b}}\) with

\[\begin{aligned} U_{\mathrm{m}} &= \frac{C}{2}\iint_{\mathrm{S}} \Big[(\varepsilon^0_1)^2 + (\varepsilon^0_2)^2 + 2\nu\,\varepsilon^0_1\varepsilon^0_2 + 2\,(1 - \nu)\,(\varepsilon^0_{12})^2\Big]\,A_1A_2\,\mathrm{d}q_1\,\mathrm{d}q_2 , \\ U_{\mathrm{b}} &= \frac{D}{2}\iint_{\mathrm{S}} \Big[\kappa_1^2 + \kappa_2^2 + 2\nu\,\kappa_1\kappa_2 + 2\,(1 - \nu)\,\kappa_{12}^2\Big]\,A_1A_2\,\mathrm{d}q_1\,\mathrm{d}q_2 . \end{aligned} \tag{22.27}\]

The membrane part \(U_{\mathrm{m}}\) is proportional to the thickness \(h\), the bending part \(U_{\mathrm{b}}\) to \(h^3\).

Proof

We must show that the density separates \(\varepsilon^0\) from \(\kappa\). By the change of variables theorem (theorem 4.59) the volume is an integral with \(J = H_1H_2 = A_1A_2\,(1 + z/R_1)(1 + z/R_2)\).

  1. By Hooke's law (step 1 of the proof of theorem 22.28) the density is \(\mathcal W = \tfrac{E}{2(1 - \nu^2)}\,\big[\varepsilon_{11}^2 + \varepsilon_{22}^2 + 2\nu\,\varepsilon_{11}\varepsilon_{22} + 2(1 - \nu)\,\varepsilon_{12}^2\big]\).
  2. Denote the expression in the bracket by \(G(\varepsilon_{11}, \varepsilon_{22}, \varepsilon_{12})\). It is a quadratic form, so \(G(\varepsilon^0 + z\kappa) = G(\varepsilon^0) + 2z\,G(\varepsilon^0, \kappa) + z^2\,G(\kappa)\) with the bilinear form \(G(\cdot, \cdot)\).
  3. Drop the factor \((1 + z/R_1)(1 + z/R_2)\). The integral over \(z\) from \(-h/2\) to \(h/2\) gives \(h\,G(\varepsilon^0) + 2\cdot 0\cdot G(\varepsilon^0, \kappa) + (h^3/12)\,G(\kappa)\), since \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\). The first term is the rectangle, the third the parabola, since \(h^3/12 = h\cdot(h/2)^2\cdot\tfrac13\). Multiplied by \(\tfrac{E}{2(1 - \nu^2)}\) the terms give \(\tfrac{C}{2}G(\varepsilon^0)\) and \(\tfrac{D}{2}G(\kappa)\), which is equation (22.27).

Source: VK section 12.4 (12.49) to (12.51) (PDF p. 345-346): membrane and bending energy. The proof is ours.

What part of the energy is bending energy? Take the tube from the start of the section. Under pressure the energy per unit area is \(U_{\mathrm{m}}/A = \tfrac12(N_\theta\varepsilon^0_\theta + N_{\mathrm{x}}\varepsilon^0_{\mathrm{x}}) = 0{,}027264\) N mm/mm\(^2\), on a piece of tube of length \(100\) mm (area \(2\pi R\cdot 100 = 31\,416\) mm\(^2\)) \(856{,}5\) N mm. If the same tube were bent in the hoop direction so that the strain on the outer face equalled the hoop strain \(\varepsilon^0_\theta\), then \(\kappa = 2\varepsilon^0_\theta/h = 3{,}25\cdot 10^{-4}\) mm\(^{-1}\) and \(M = D\kappa = 46{,}7\) N mm/mm, and the energy is \(U_{\mathrm{b}}/(\tfrac12 C\,\varepsilon^{0\,2}_\theta) = (D/C)\,\kappa^2/\varepsilon^{0\,2}_\theta = (h^2/12)\,(2/h)^2 = 1/3\) of the membrane energy at the same hoop strain, independent of \(h\). This is the third of figure 22.35. Stretching and bending at equal strain \(\varepsilon\) and curvature \(\kappa\) have the stiffness ratio \(C/D = 12/h^2\) (for \(h = 2\) mm it is \(3\) mm\(^{-2}\)), so a shell is stiff in stretching and soft in bending. Section 22.5 uses this separation.

22.3.7 What we have shown (kaj smo pokazali)

We replaced the shell by a surface: in the Kirchhoff-Love model (definition 22.24) the strains are linear through the thickness (theorem 22.26), together with the coordinates (lemma 22.25) this was proved for a shell of revolution and quoted for general lines of curvature. We added the stresses through the thickness into forces and moments per unit length (definition 22.27). A wall has of them only the in-plane forces, a plate only the moments and transverse forces, a shell all at once, and because of its curvature it carries pressure with a tensile force, \(N_\theta/R = p\) (section 22.3.4). By Hooke's law the forces depend only on the strains of the middle surface and the moments only on the changes of curvature, because \(\int z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\) (theorem 22.28), and the energy splits into a part \(\propto h\) and a part \(\propto h^3\) (theorem 22.29). The idealizations had limits: \(h/(2|R_{\mathrm{i}}|) = 0{,}02\) for our tube and \(0{,}2\) for the thick one (where it does not hold), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) with the error \(h/R = 0{,}04\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nn}} = 0\) with the strain \(1{,}7\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the dropped shear strain.

22.4 Membrane theory of shells of revolution

A steel tube with mean radius \(R = 50\) mm and wall thickness \(h = 2\) mm is closed at both ends and filled with oil at pressure \(p = 3\) MPa. What does its wall carry? Do we need to know how the wall bends, or is it enough that the wall only pulls, like a rubber inner tube inflated with air? The pressure acts perpendicular to the wall, and the forces in the wall lie along it. So we ask what forces the wall must carry for every part of the tube to be in equilibrium.

The model is a thin shell (lupina, section 22.1) of isotropic elastic steel, \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). The wall is so thin that we add the stresses over the thickness into forces per unit length, and the pressure acts on the middle surface. We shall name both simplifications and give each a bound when we meet numbers.

We cut the tube in two ways. Figure 22.36 shows the cross section perpendicular to the axis (left) and the longitudinal section (right).

In the left picture we keep the upper arc of the tube and cut it along the axis. From inside, the pressure \(p\) pushes on it perpendicular to the wall. The surface of the arc is curved and the pressure points in a different direction at every point, so we find the resultant (the sum of all forces) by components. Horizontal components cancel in every pair of points that are symmetric about the vertical axis. Vertical components add up to a force equal to the pressure times the area of the horizontal projection of the arc. The reason lies in a small piece of wall: if it is tilted by an angle \(\alpha\), the pressure force \(p\,\mathrm{d}A\) has the vertical component \(p\,\mathrm{d}A\cos\alpha\), and \(\mathrm{d}A\cos\alpha\) is exactly the area of the shadow of the piece on a horizontal plane. The sum of the shadows of all pieces is the shadow of the whole arc. The projection is a rectangle of length \(L\) (perpendicular to the paper, hence drawn obliquely) and width \(2R\), so the resultant of the pressure upward is \(p\cdot 2R\cdot L\). The body is at rest, so the wall below the cut must balance it. The wall pulls the upper arc downward in both cuts with a force \(N_\theta\) per unit length, together \(2N_\theta L\). From \(2N_\theta L = 2pRL\) it follows that \(N_\theta = pR = 150\) N/mm. We call \(N_\theta\) the hoop force (obročna sila), because it is the force in the iron hoops that hold a barrel together: it pulls along the circumference.

In the right picture we cut the tube across the axis and keep the left part. It is bounded by the end (dno), on which the oil pushes outward with the force \(p\pi R^2\) (pressure times the area of the end, a circle of radius \(R\)). The body is at rest, so the wall at the cut must hold it back with an equal force in the axial direction. The cut has circumference \(2\pi R\), and the wall pulls with a force \(N_\varphi\) per unit length of circumference. From \(N_\varphi\cdot 2\pi R = p\pi R^2\) it follows that \(N_\varphi = pR/2 = 75\) N/mm. For now we call \(N_\varphi\) the axial force, because it pulls along the tube axis. For a general shell we shall find it a name that holds there too. At \(h = 2\) mm the stresses are \(N_\theta/h = 75\) MPa and \(N_\varphi/h = 37{,}5\) MPa.

How good is this calculation? The cut goes through the wall and the pressure acts on its inner side, at the radius \(a\), which is smaller than \(R\) by half the wall thickness: \(a = R - h/2 = 49\) mm (the thickness is exaggerated in the figure). The exact balance of half the tube is therefore \(2L\int\sigma\,\mathrm{d}r = p\cdot 2aL\), so the true force per unit length is \(pa = 147\) N/mm. Our \(pR = 150\) N/mm differs from it by \(2\) %, which is exactly \(h/(2R) = 0{,}02\). This is the size of the error we make by treating the wall as a surface of radius \(R\) (the explanation is in section 22.3, where we dropped the factor \(1 + z/R\)). For a thicker wall, for example the tube with radii 40 and 60 mm of theorem 11.28 (\(h/R = 0{,}4\)), the error is \(20\) %, and the calculation is no longer good (the thick wall is drawn on the right of the figure: the inner radius \(a = 40\) mm is \(R/5\) below \(R = 50\) mm, that is \(20\) %, and the pressure acts on a clearly smaller radius than the middle surface has).

From history

Navier's book on the strength of materials first appeared in print in 1826, and copies of his lectures had been given to his students since 1819 (TIMO, PDF p. 81). The last chapter of the book deals with thin shells (TIMO, PDF p. 86). Navier begins with a string that is perfectly flexible and inextensible and is loaded in the plane of the curve by a pressure \(p\) perpendicular to it. From the equilibrium of a piece of the string he finds that the tension \(S\) in the string is constant and that \(S/\rho = p\), where \(\rho\) is the radius of curvature: the curvature is proportional to the pressure at every point (TIMO, PDF p. 87). We see the reason in figure 22.37. We cut out the arc of the string with radius \(\rho\) and angle \(\psi\) between the radii to its ends. The string pulls at both ends with a force \(S\) along the tangent, which is perpendicular to the radius. Each force has a component toward the center \(S\sin(\psi/2)\) and a component along the chord, which cancels the other one. So the resultant of the two forces is \(2S\sin(\psi/2)\) toward the center. The pressure \(p\) on the arc points in a different direction at every point, but for the same reason as in the tube its resultant equals the pressure times the length of the chord, \(p\cdot 2\rho\sin(\psi/2)\). The string is at rest, so \(2S\sin(\psi/2) = p\cdot 2\rho\sin(\psi/2)\) and \(S = p\rho\). An assumption enters here: the string is perfectly flexible, so its force lies only along the string. If the string had bending stiffness, every cross section would also carry a transverse force and a moment, and the equation \(S = p\rho\) would not hold. This is in miniature the same assumption as the membrane state below.

He uses the same idea as for the arc of string for a channel full of liquid, held up by uniformly distributed forces \(S\). He asks when the wall is not bent and answers that this happens when the curvature at a point is proportional to the depth \(y\) (TIMO, PDF p. 87). This is the same law, because the pressure of a liquid grows with depth.

Finally he treats a thin shell. Figure 22.38 shows a piece of the shell, curved in two perpendicular directions with radii \(\rho\) and \(\rho_1\). The pressure \(p\) pushes on it from inside, and on all four edges the tension \(S\) pulls it equally in both directions. From equilibrium he obtains the equation

\[S\Big(\frac1\rho + \frac1{\rho_1}\Big) = p ,\]

in which \(\rho\) and \(\rho_1\) are the radii of curvature of the shell in two directions. For a sphere he derives from it the stress \(\sigma = S/h = p\rho/(2h)\) for thickness \(h\) (TIMO, PDF p. 87). Navier also did an experiment. He loaded thin iron spheres of about 1 ft diameter (about 30 cm) and \(0{,}1\) in thickness (about 2,5 mm) with internal pressure up to rupture, and found that the breaking strength of the material was about the same as in a simple tension test (TIMO, PDF p. 87). The comparison is made possible by the equation \(\sigma = p\rho/(2h)\), which gives from the bursting pressure the stress in the wall at rupture, in the wall of a sphere the same in every direction of the plane. The agreement tells that the wall broke when this stress reached the same value as in a bar in a tension test, although the wall was stretched in two directions and the bar in only one. For his spheres the radius is \(6\) in and the thickness \(0{,}1\) in, so \(R/h = 60\) (our calculation).

Back to the tube. For a sphere of radius \(R\), Navier's equation has \(\rho = \rho_1 = R\), so \(S\cdot 2/R = p\) and \(S = pR/2\). This is the same force as the axial force of the tube \(N_\varphi = pR/2\), which we obtained with the cut across the axis. The tube has two different forces, \(N_\theta = pR\) is twice as large as \(N_\varphi = pR/2\), and for each we needed its own cut. For a general shell, where the radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) differ from point to point and the load is not the same everywhere, we cannot guess such cuts. We ask when the forces in the wall follow from equilibrium alone, without any equations for displacements. This is possible when the wall carries no bending moments and no transverse shear forces.

Definition 22.30 Membrane state of a shell (membransko stanje lupine)

A shell (section 22.1) has at every point its internal forces per unit length (definition 22.27): membrane forces \(N_1\), \(N_2\), \(N_{12}\) (along the middle surface, in N/mm), transverse shear forces \(Q_1\), \(Q_2\) and moments \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(M_{12}\) (N mm/mm). The shell is in a membrane state (membransko stanje) if at every point all three moments and both transverse forces are zero,

\[M_1 = M_2 = M_{12} = 0 , \qquad Q_1 = Q_2 = 0 , \tag{22.28}\]

so that only \(N_1\), \(N_2\) and \(N_{12}\) can be nonzero. The adjective membrane has the same meaning as for a skin: Latin membrana is a thin skin, and the skin of a drum carries a load only by pulling in its own plane, not by bending.

Source: VK section 13.1 (PDF p. 354) and equations (13.1), (13.3) (PDF p. 355): membrane theory neglects all moments and with them also the transverse forces. The definition follows this source, the notation is from section 22.3.

Is it then possible for the wall to be in this state? Figure 22.39 shows each condition on its own. VK (PDF p. 357) lists four conditions under which it is possible and gives them without proof. They share one reason: a membrane force lies in the tangent plane of the shell, so it cannot carry anything that does not run along the wall. (1) The edge must not carry a transverse force or a moment, because exactly \(Q\) and \(M\), which the membrane state does not have, would have to carry them. (2) The normal displacement and the rotation of the edge must be free: if a support prevents them, it gives a reaction perpendicular to the wall and a bending zone arises at the edge, treated in section 22.6. (3) The surface must be smooth, because at a crease the direction of the tangent jumps and the equilibrium of the joint demands a transverse force. (4) The load must be continuous, because a point force has no tangential support in the wall. We shall meet each condition while working the examples, and for each we shall show how much bending appears when it is violated.

Before we state the theorem we fix the shell on which we shall prove it. Take two families of lines on the middle surface that we know from a globe. A vertical plane through the axis \(z\) cuts the surface in a curve that we call a meridian (meridian). The name comes from the Latin word for midday: all points on the same meridian have the sun at its highest at the same time. A horizontal plane cuts the surface in a circle that we call a parallel (vzporednik), because all such circles are parallel to each other. The surface obtained by rotating a meridian about the axis \(z\) is a surface of revolution, and a thin shell on it a shell of revolution (lupina vrtenine).

Every meridian lies in its own plane of the axis, so we describe it in the plane \((r, z)\), where \(r\) is the distance from the axis. Figure 22.40 shows this for a sphere, where the meridian is a circular arc.

On the meridian, which turns about the axis \(z\), we measure the arc length \(s\) from a starting point \(s_0\). Let the unit tangent vector of the meridian be \(\vek e_\varphi\), the outward unit normal of the surface (definition 2.17) \(\vek n\), and the angle between the normal and the axis \(z\) be \(\varphi(s)\). The normal is the outward one, as in section 22.3 (there the tangent vector is called \(\vek e_{\mathrm{s}}\), here \(\vek e_\varphi\), because \(\varphi\) is the main variable of our calculation). In section 22.2 the normal points inward for the sign of the curvature, and every formula there holds here too. As in spherical coordinates (lemma 11.15), in the plane \((r, z)\)

\[\vek e_\varphi = (\cos\varphi,\ -\sin\varphi) , \qquad \vek n = (\sin\varphi,\ \cos\varphi) . \tag{22.29}\]

Since \(\vek e_\varphi\) is the derivative of the meridian point with respect to arc length, \(r'(s) = \cos\varphi\) and \(z'(s) = -\sin\varphi\) (a prime is the derivative with respect to \(s\)). The radius of curvature \(R_1\) of the meridian is fixed by the definition of the curvature of a curve (section 22.2) through \(1/R_1 = \varphi'(s)\): the angle of the tangent turns at the rate \(1/R_1\). The second principal radius \(R_2\) is the distance along the normal from the surface to the axis (lemma 22.18), so in the right triangle formed by the axis, the normal and the parallel, the radius of the parallel is \(r = R_2\sin\varphi\). For a sphere \(R_1 = R_2 = R\), for a cylinder \(\varphi = \pi/2\), \(1/R_1 = 0\) and \(R_2 = r = R\).

Before we write the definition, look at the load in figure 22.41: on the meridian lies the point \(P\). We split the load at a point of the meridian into the component \(p_\varphi\) along the tangent and the component \(p_{\mathrm{n}}\) along the outward normal. Under it the point moves by the displacement \(\vek U\), which we write with the components \(u\) and \(w\) in the same basis. Axial symmetry means that on the parallel everything is the same at every point: the load, the forces and the displacement do not contain the angle \(\theta\).

Definition 22.31 Axisymmetric state of a shell of revolution (osnosimetrično stanje lupine vrtenine)

Let a shell of revolution be given by a meridian \(s \mapsto (r(s), z(s))\), \(s \ge s_0\), with a continuously differentiable angle \(\varphi(s)\) and \(\sin\varphi > 0\), \(r > 0\) for \(s > s_0\). The load per unit area of the middle surface has a component \(p_\varphi\) along \(\vek e_\varphi\) and a component \(p_{\mathrm{n}}\) along the outward normal \(\vek n\), both continuous functions of the arc length \(s\), and no circumferential component. The shell is in an axisymmetric state (osnosimetrično stanje) if its membrane forces and displacements do not depend on the angle \(\theta\) that fixes the meridian: \(N_\varphi(s)\), \(N_\theta(s)\) and \(N_{\varphi\theta}(s)\), where \(N_\varphi = N_1\) is the force in the meridian direction, \(N_\theta = N_2\) the force in the parallel direction and \(N_{\varphi\theta} = N_{12}\), and \(N_\varphi\) and \(N_\theta\) are continuous. The displacement of a point is then the vector \(\vek U = u\,\vek e_\varphi + w\,\vek n\) with no circumferential component.

Source: Notation after VK section 13.4 (PDF p. 357-358) and section 13.5 (PDF p. 361-362), where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the normal and the axis and \(r = R_2\sin\varphi\). VK denotes the load components \(p_1\) and \(p_3\), and their directions differ from ours by a sign, so we derive all the equations below again.

We now call \(N_\varphi\) the meridional force (meridianska sila), because it acts along the meridian, and \(N_\theta\) the hoop force, as for the tube, because it acts along the parallel. For the tube the meridional force is the same as the axial one. The load can be weight, gas pressure or snow.

We find \(N_\varphi\) first with a cap. Figure 22.42 shows a shell that has its top on the axis, and one parallel below it.

We draw the axis \(z\) and then, in grey, the meridian of the shell, which in the picture is a circular arc of radius 3 cm (a sphere, so \(R_1 = R_2 = 3\) cm). We choose a parallel at the angle \(\varphi_0 = 50^\circ\) and call the part of the shell above it the cap (kapa). The word is the everyday one, like a cap on a head: the part that covers the top. We cut the cap off, and the wall below the cut must hold it. At the parallel of radius \(r_0\) (in the figure the distance \(r_0\)) the normal of the surface is the dashed line to the axis, its length is \(R_2\) and its angle with the axis is \(\varphi_0\), because this is the definition of the angle \(\varphi\) and because \(r_0 = R_2\sin\varphi_0\). The wall below the cut pulls the cap with a force \(N_\varphi\) per unit length along the tangent of the meridian, away from the cap, starting at the point of the cut. Only two vectors in the plane of the section are drawn. In reality the force \(N_\varphi\) acts all around the circle.

Its axial component is \(N_\varphi\sin\varphi_0\) downward, because by equation (22.29) the vector \(\vek e_\varphi\) has the axial component \(-\sin\varphi\). The horizontal component points outward at every point of the circle, as the view from above shows. In a pair of opposite points the two are equal and opposite, so around the whole circle they cancel. What remains is the axial component, which is the same along the whole length \(2\pi r_0\) of the circle. The total load on the cap has an axial component \(P_{\mathrm{z}}\): for a pressure \(p\) it is the pressure on a horizontal circle of the same radius, \(P_{\mathrm{z}} = p\pi r_0^2\). The body is at rest, so the sum of the forces on the cap in the direction \(z\) must be zero: \(P_{\mathrm{z}} - 2\pi r_0 N_\varphi\sin\varphi_0 = 0\). The pressure gives an axial force as at the end of the tube: pressure times the area of the horizontal projection. For a sphere with pressure this gives \(N_\varphi = p\pi r_0^2/(2\pi r_0\sin\varphi_0) = p R_2/2\), which agrees with the end of the tube and with Navier's sphere.

Does this hold for every load, not only for pressure? The cap does not suffice for the force \(N_\theta\), because \(N_\theta\) acts across a cut along a meridian, and the cut of the cap runs along a parallel. So we take a band between two parallels and two meridians. Figure 22.43 shows it.

On the left we draw again the axis \(z\) and the meridian, and choose the band (pas) between the angles \(\varphi_{\mathrm{a}} = 30^\circ\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{b}} = 65^\circ\). The load \(p_{\mathrm{n}}\) acts on the band in the direction of the outward normal, drawn as a pressure that pushes the wall outward from inside.
