Theorem 22.42 Equation of the cylinder under axisymmetric load (enačba valja pri osnosimetrični obtežbi)

Let a cylinder of radius \(R\) and thickness \(h\), both constant, be made of an isotropic, linearly elastic material with \(E\) and \(\nu\) (theorem 3.64). Let the Kirchhoff and Love assumptions hold (definition 22.24), let the pressure \(p(x)\) be a continuous function of the axial coordinate \(x\) only and let there be no axial surface load. Let the deformation be axisymmetric, the slope small, \(|w'| \le 10^{-2}\), and let the equilibrium be written on the undeformed band. Then:

  1. The axial force \(N_1\) is constant on the whole cylinder.
  2. The radial displacement \(w(x)\) of the middle surface, positive outward, solves the equation
    \[D\,w'''' + \frac{Eh}{R^2}\,w = p - \frac{\nu N_1}{R} , \qquad D = \frac{Eh^3}{12(1 - \nu^2)} . \tag{22.42}\]
  3. The moment, the shear force and the hoop force are \(M = D\,w''\), \(Q = -D\,w'''\) and \(N_2 = Eh\,w/R + \nu N_1\).

With \(\beta\) defined by \(4\beta^4 = Eh/(R^2 D)\), that is

\[\beta = \frac{\sqrt[4]{3(1 - \nu^2)}}{\sqrt{R h}} , \tag{22.43}\]

the equation (22.42) is \(w'''' + 4\beta^4 w = (p - \nu N_1/R)/D\).

Proof

We must show four things. The equilibrium of the band gives the relation between \(Q\), \(M\), \(N_2\) and \(p\), the axial equilibrium gives the constancy of \(N_1\), kinematics and Hooke's law express \(N_2\) and \(M\) by \(w\), then we substitute.

  1. Radial equilibrium of the band between \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), with the shear forces, the pressure and the radial part of the hoop forces and with the factors computed above: \(\Lambda\,Q(b) - \Lambda\,Q(a) + \Lambda\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b p\,\mathrm{d}x - \dfrac{\Lambda}{R}\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b N_2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). After division by \(\Lambda > 0\) we get \(Q(b) - Q(a) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\big(N_2/R - p\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\). The radial component of the axial force \(N_1\), the product \(N_1\,w'\) (axial force on the tilted wall), we neglected. We may, because the slope of the wall is small, for our tube at most \(1{,}35\cdot 10^{-3}\), and the error is \(1{,}6\) % (estimate in the section after theorem 22.43). For a large compressive axial force we may not, since the tube can buckle.
  2. The function \(N_2/R - p\) is continuous, because \(p\) is continuous by assumption and \(N_2\) by step 6. So by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55, item 2) the function \(Q\) is differentiable and \(Q' = N_2/R - p\).
  3. The band is a beam with radial load \(q = p - N_2/R\) per unit width, since the radial part of the hoop forces is just one more radial load. By corollary 5.11 (equation (5.13), \(m = 0\)) we have \(M' = -Q\) and therefore \(M'' = -Q' = p - N_2/R\).
  4. By the same corollary \(N_1'\) \(= -q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), because the axial load is zero, so \(N_1\) is constant. This is item 1.
  5. By theorem 22.26 on the deformations of the shell (equations (22.21)), for a cylinder the meridian is a straight line, \(1/R_1 = 0\), the normal is perpendicular to the axis, \(\varphi = \pi/2\), and \(\rho = R\). For an axisymmetric displacement \((u, w)\) of the middle surface the axial strain is therefore \(\varepsilon_1^0 = u'\) and the hoop strain \(\varepsilon_2^0 = w/R\) (corollary 11.21 gives the same with \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = w\) and \(r = R\)). The changes of curvature are \(\kappa_1 = (u/R_1 - w')' = -w''\), which is the curvature of the bent middle line in the longitudinal section with the opposite sign, and \(\kappa_2 = (u/R_1 - w')\cos\varphi/\rho = 0\), since \(\cos\varphi = 0\).
  6. By theorem 22.28 we have \(N_1 = C(\varepsilon_1^0 + \nu\varepsilon_2^0)\) and \(N_2 = C(\varepsilon_2^0 + \nu\varepsilon_1^0)\) with \(C = Eh/(1 - \nu^2)\). From the first, \(\varepsilon_1^0 = N_1/C - \nu w/R\). We substitute in the second: \(N_2 = C(1 - \nu^2)\,w/R + \nu N_1 = Eh\,w/R + \nu N_1\). The same theorem gives \(M_1 = D(\kappa_1 + \nu\kappa_2) = -D\,w''\). This moment, \(M_1 = \int\sigma_{11}z\,\mathrm{d}z\) (equation (22.23)), is positive when the outer face is in tension. The bending moment of the beam \(M\) (definition 5.8), however, is positive when the lower face, here the inner one, is in tension, since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -M\,y/I\) (theorem 5.35), here with \(y = z\) outward. So the moment on the faces of the band is \(M = -M_1 = D\,w''\), and with \(Q = -M'\) from step 3, \(Q = -D\,w'''\). This is item 3.
  7. We substitute \(M = D\,w''\) and \(N_2\) from step 6 into \(M'' = p - N_2/R\) from step 3. Since \(D\) is constant, \(D\,w'''' = p - Eh\,w/R^2 - \nu N_1/R\). This is the equation (22.42). From \(4\beta^4 = Eh/(R^2 D) = 12(1 - \nu^2)/(R^2h^2)\) we get \(\beta^4 = 3(1 - \nu^2)/(Rh)^2\), which is the equation (22.43).

Source: VK (15.35)-(15.45) (PDF pp. 426-427). VK measures the deflection \(w\) and the pressure \(p_3\) inward, \(\varepsilon_2 = -w/R\) (15.38), and has the shear force with the opposite sign, \(Q_1 = \mathrm{d}M_1/\mathrm{d}x\). Its equation (15.43) becomes ours with \(w \to -w\) and \(p_3 \to -p\). The proof from a band with angle \(\alpha\) and from corollary 5.11 is not literally from the source, VK takes the equilibrium equations from the general theory (12.41), (12.42).

Notation. The quantity \(\beta\) has the unit \(\mathrm{mm}^{-1}\), so \(1/\beta\) is a length. We call it the decay constant (konstanta upadanja), because theorem 22.43 will show that the disturbance at the edge decays as \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\). The symbol \(D\) is the bending stiffness of the shell per unit width from theorem 22.28, as \(EI\) is the bending stiffness of the beam. It is not the amplification factor of chapter 9 or the compliance matrix of chapter 4. The symbol \(N\) here means a force per unit length, for the beam a force through the whole cross-section, and the same holds for \(M\). The symbol \(h\) is the thickness of the shell, not the size of an element (\(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) in section 22.8).

The equation (22.42) has a form that we already know. The beam has \(EI\,v'''' = q\) (theorem 5.42), the band has \(D\,w'''' = p - k\,w - \nu N_1/R\) with \(k = Eh/R^2\). So the band acts like a beam on an elastic foundation, called the Winkler foundation (Winklerjeva podlaga). Winkler proposed the simplest model of a foundation, in which the reaction at every point is proportional to the deflection, \(q = k\,w\) (VK (3.65), PDF p. 81), hence the name. Let us draw this in figure 22.64, a. The band with bending stiffness \(D\) is clamped at the plate, the pressure pushes it outward from the undeformed position, and under it there are springs with stiffness \(k\), tied to the axis of the tube. The foundation here is not a new material. Each spring is a ring of the wall, which cannot widen without the hoop force pulling it back toward the axis, as we saw with the hoop forces at the plate. For our tube \(k = 156{,}80\ \mathrm{N/mm^3}\), \(D = 143\,590\) N mm and \(\beta = 0{,}12854\ \mathrm{mm^{-1}}\), so \(1/\beta = 7{,}780\) mm. Chapter 25 uses the same equation for a beam on a real foundation. Here we solve it completely, because we need it for the edge effect.

Why is the length of the bending proportional to \(\sqrt{Rh}\)? In figure 22.64, b, we bulge the band into a bump of length \(\lambda\) and height \(w\) in two ways. The short bump is strongly curved. The curvature is the second derivative of the deflection, the load of a beam the fourth, and each derivative divides by the length of the bump, so bending resists the bump with a load of about \(D\,w/\lambda^4\), the springs only with \(k\,w\). The long bump is almost straight and bending hardly resists it, but it stretches many springs, each pulling with \(k\,w\). The disturbance at the edge is therefore neither very short nor very long. It settles at the length where the two resistances are equal:

\[\frac{D}{\lambda^4} = k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \sqrt[4]{\frac{D}{k}} = \sqrt[4]{\frac{Eh^3}{12(1 - \nu^2)}\cdot\frac{R^2}{Eh}} = \frac{\sqrt{Rh}}{\sqrt[4]{12(1 - \nu^2)}} .\]

This is an estimate, the exact length from the equation (22.43) is \(1/\beta = \sqrt[4]{4D/k}\), longer by the factor \(\sqrt2\). For our tube the estimate gives \(5{,}50\) mm, the exact value is \(7{,}78\) mm. The thickness enters \(D\) with the third power and \(k\) with the first, so the length grows with \(\sqrt h\): for a wall twice as thick it would be \(1{,}41\) times longer, \(11{,}0\) mm. The radius enters only \(k\), which is a weaker spring for a larger radius, so the length grows with \(\sqrt R\).

We test the theorem on two extreme cases. If \(R \to \infty\), the springs would vanish, \(k \to 0\), the band would become a straight beam and the equation would be the beam equation (figure 22.64, c). A band of length \(100\) mm, clamped at one end, would deflect under the pressure \(3\) MPa by \(pL^4/(8D) = 261{,}2\) mm, which is absurd, since this is more than twice the length of the band and the linear theory of bending no longer holds there. For the tube \(\beta L = 12{,}85\) and the deflection is \(16{,}263\ \mu\)m. The curvature of the tube, that is the hoop forces, therefore changes the equation decisively. The second case is the free edge of an open tube above the axis, under pressure and without axial force (figure 22.64, d): \(N_1 = 0\), \(M = Q = 0\) and \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}} = pR^2/(Eh) = 19{,}133\ \mu\)m solves the equation and all boundary conditions. The wall only moves outward in parallel by \(19{,}133\ \mu\)m and there is no bending in it. Bending does not come from the pressure but from the edge not being allowed to do what the wall would do by itself.

22.6.2 Solution and edge effect

The equation (22.42) is an ordinary linear equation of the fourth order with constant coefficients. Its solution is the sum of one particular solution and the general solution of the homogeneous equation. The particular solution for constant \(p\) is the constant function \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = (p - \nu N_1/R)\,R^2/(Eh)\), which solves \(Eh\,w_{\mathrm{p}}/R^2 = p - \nu N_1/R\). This is the membrane solution: by lemma 22.36 \(N_1 = pR/2\), for our tube \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = 16{,}263\ \mu\)m and \(N_2 = Eh\,w_{\mathrm{p}}/R + \nu N_1 = pR = 150\) N/mm, which is the membrane hoop force. The homogeneous equation \(w'''' + 4\beta^4 w = 0\) remains.

What solutions does it have? We try \(\mathrm{e}^{sx}\). Substitution gives \(s^4 = -4\beta^4\). Since \((1 + \mathrm{i})^4 = (2\mathrm{i})^2 = -4\), the four solutions are \(s = \beta(\pm 1 \pm \mathrm{i})\). In figure 22.65, a, they lie in the plane with the axes \(\mathrm{Re}\,s\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,s\) on the circle of radius \(\sqrt2\,\beta\) at \(45^\circ\) to the axes. The fourth power of a complex number raises its absolute value to the fourth power and multiplies its angle by four, so \(s^4\) has the absolute value \(4\beta^4\) and the angle \(4\cdot 45^\circ = 180^\circ\), so it is indeed \(-4\beta^4\). So we have the real solutions \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\beta x}\cos\beta x\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\beta x}\sin\beta x\). The left roots have the real part \(-\beta\) and give the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\), which decays, the right ones the real part \(+\beta\) and the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\), which grows. The imaginary part \(\pm\beta\) gives in both cases the oscillation \(\cos\beta x\) and \(\sin\beta x\). Figure 22.65, b, shows the decaying solution: along the axis \(x\) from the edge it oscillates between the envelopes, which at \(x = \pi/\beta\) are only \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}c\) from the axis. Figure 22.65, c, shows the growing one, over the same axis. Which solutions belong in a long tube that starts at \(x = 0\)?

Theorem 22.43 Edge effect (robni učinek)

Let \(w\) be a solution of the equation (22.42) on \([0, \infty)\) with constant \(p\) and \(N_1\), \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = (p - \nu N_1/R)R^2/(Eh)\) and \(\beta\) from the equation (22.43). Then:

  1. The difference \(\omega = w - w_{\mathrm{p}}\) is a linear combination of the functions \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x\), \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\), \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\cos\beta x\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\sin\beta x\), and every such combination solves \(\omega'''' + 4\beta^4\omega = 0\).
  2. If \(w\) is bounded on \([0, \infty)\), the coefficients at \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\) are zero and
    \[w(x) = w_{\mathrm{p}} + \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\big(C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x\big) \tag{22.44}\]
    with constants \(C_1\), \(C_2\) determined by the edge.
  3. For \(c = \sqrt{C_1^2 + C_2^2}\) and \(\omega = w - w_{\mathrm{p}}\) the following holds for \(x \ge 0\): \(|\omega| \le c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\), \(|\omega''| \le 2\beta^2 c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\) and \(|\omega'''| \le 2\sqrt2\,\beta^3 c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\). The moment and the shear force, \(M = D\,\omega''\) and \(Q = -D\,\omega'''\), therefore decay as \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\).
Proof

We must show three items. The first comes from the roots of the characteristic polynomial and from the uniqueness theorem, the third from writing the solution as the real part of a complex function, the second from the growth of \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\).

  1. The function \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\) is constant, so \(w_{\mathrm{p}}'''' = 0\) and \(D\,w_{\mathrm{p}}'''' + (Eh/R^2)w_{\mathrm{p}} = p - \nu N_1/R\) by the choice of \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\). The difference \(\omega\) therefore solves \(D\,\omega'''' + (Eh/R^2)\,\omega = 0\), that is \(\omega'''' + 4\beta^4\omega = 0\).
  2. The characteristic polynomial is \(P(s) = D(s^4 + 4\beta^4)\) with roots \(s = \beta(\pm 1 \pm \mathrm{i})\), because \((\pm 1 \pm \mathrm{i})^4 = -4\). By theorem 9.34, item 3, and lemma 9.42 every function \(\mathrm{e}^{sx}\) for these four \(s\) is a solution. Their real and imaginary parts are solutions by linearity and they are exactly the four named functions.
  3. The vectors \((f, f', f'', f''')\) at \(x = 0\) for the four functions are \((1, -\beta, 0, 2\beta^3)\), \((0, \beta, -2\beta^2, 2\beta^3)\), \((1, \beta, 0, -2\beta^3)\), \((0, \beta, 2\beta^2, 2\beta^3)\). The determinant of the matrix made of them is \(32\beta^6 \ne 0\) (SymPy, num-06.out B). So from them we can build every initial vector \((\omega, \omega', \omega'', \omega''')(0)\), and by the uniqueness theorem (theorem 9.41) every solution on \([0, T]\) is such a combination, for every \(T\). This is item 1.
  4. Let \(\omega_- = \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x)\). With \(t = \beta x\) we have \(C_1\cos t + C_2\sin t = \mathrm{Re}\big[(C_1 - \mathrm{i}C_2)(\cos t + \mathrm{i}\sin t)\big]\), so \(\omega_- = \mathrm{Re}\big[(C_1 - \mathrm{i}C_2)\,\mathrm{e}^{(-1 + \mathrm{i})\beta x}\big]\) with the left root. By theorem 9.34, item 3, its \(j\)-th derivative is \(\mathrm{Re}\big[(C_1 - \mathrm{i}C_2)\,\beta^j(-1 + \mathrm{i})^j\,\mathrm{e}^{(-1 + \mathrm{i})\beta x}\big]\).
  5. The absolute value of the real part is not larger than the absolute value of the complex number, and that is the product of the absolute values. Since \(|\mathrm{e}^{(-1 + \mathrm{i})\beta x}| = \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\) (theorem 9.34, item 2), \(|C_1 - \mathrm{i}C_2| = c\) and \(|-1 + \mathrm{i}| = \sqrt2\), we have \(|\omega_-^{(j)}| \le c\,(\sqrt2\beta)^j\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\). With \(j = 0, 2, 3\) these are the estimates of item 3 when \(\omega = \omega_-\). For \(j = 0\) the estimate says that \(\omega_-\) lies between the envelopes \(\pm c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\).
  6. Let \(\omega = \omega_- + \omega_+\) with \(\omega_+ = \mathrm{e}^{\beta x}(C_3\cos\beta x + C_4\sin\beta x)\) and \(c' = \sqrt{C_3^2 + C_4^2} > 0\). Then \(\omega_+ = c'\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\cos(\beta x - \varphi)\) for some angle \(\varphi\), and at the points \(x_{\mathrm{k}} = (\varphi + 2k\pi)/\beta\) with natural \(k\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) we have \(\omega_+(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = c'\mathrm{e}^{\beta x_{\mathrm{k}}} \ge c'(1 + \beta x_{\mathrm{k}})\) (lemma 9.20, item 1), which is unbounded as \(k \to \infty\). Since \(|\omega_-| \le c\) by step 5, \(\omega\) would also be unbounded. A bounded \(w\) therefore requires \(C_3 = C_4 = 0\). This is item 2 and with it item 3.

Source: VK (15.47)-(15.49) and (15.53) (PDF pp. 428, 430). VK finds the solution with an ansatz and characteristic roots and sets \(A_3 = A_4 = 0\), because the deflection and its derivatives must be finite. The estimates of item 3 and the proof of boundedness are ours.

Figure 22.66 shows what the theorem says. In both parts of the figure the distance \(x\) from the edge runs to the right, the deflection \(w\) is at the top, the moment \(M\) at the bottom. On the left side, at I, is the clamped edge, where the wall is forced to stay at \(w = 0\). The dashed line is \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\), where the wall would widen by itself. The deflection grows from zero at the edge toward \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\), exceeds it by 4 % and then approaches it. Why does it exceed it? The deflection at the clamped edge is \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}}\big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta x)\big)\), which we derive in lemma 22.45. The factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\) decays, while the cosine and sine oscillate. The derivative of the deflection is \(2\beta w_{\mathrm{p}}\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\) and is zero for the first time at \(\beta x = \pi\), where \(\cos\pi + \sin\pi = -1\), so \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}}(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-\pi})\) with \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi} = 0{,}0432\). Below is the moment. It is largest at the edge, \(M_0 = 77{,}17\) N mm/mm, then it oscillates a few times and decays. The right part of the figure, II, shows the simply supported edge, like the simple support of a beam in definition 5.5: the edge does not move outward, but it may rotate. Its deflection exceeds the membrane value even more, by \(6{,}7\) %, while the moment at the edge is zero. Where the disturbance dies out is determined by the following corollary.

Corollary 22.44 Disturbance length (dolžina motnje)

Under the conditions of theorem 22.43 the edge disturbance \(\omega\) decays at the distance \(\ell = \pi/\beta\) from the edge to \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi} = 0{,}0432\) of its bound at the edge or less, and

\[\ell = \frac{\pi}{\beta} = \frac{\pi\sqrt{R h}}{\sqrt[4]{3(1 - \nu^2)}} = 2{,}444\,\sqrt{R h}\quad(\nu = 0{,}3) . \tag{22.45}\]

For a tube with \(R = 50\) mm and \(h = 2\) mm, \(\ell = 24{,}44\) mm, that is \(0{,}49\,R\) or \(12{,}2\,h\).

Proof
  1. By item 3 of theorem 22.43 \(|\omega(x)| \le c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\), at \(x = \ell\) we have \(\beta x = \pi\), so \(|\omega(\ell)| \le \mathrm{e}^{-\pi}c\).
  2. From the equation (22.43), \(1/\beta = \sqrt{R h}/\sqrt[4]{3(1 - \nu^2)}\). For \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(\sqrt[4]{3\cdot 0{,}91} = 1{,}2854\) and \(\pi/1{,}2854 = 2{,}444\) (SymPy, num-06.out A). For \(R = 50\) and \(h = 2\), \(\sqrt{Rh} = 10\) mm, so \(\ell = 24{,}44\) mm.

Source: VK (15.55) (PDF p. 431) and example 15.1 (PDF p. 433) give \(3/\beta \approx 2{,}3\sqrt{Rh}\). The length \(\pi/\beta\) is our choice, because it is the first point where the deflection at a clamped edge reaches its maximum.

The two bars of length \(\pi/\beta\) in figure 22.66 thus mark where the disturbance has almost died out. The whole region of bending is therefore a band of the wall only twelve thicknesses or half a radius long. We see this in figure 22.62, a, where the lengths and the radius are to scale: the region of bending reaches only to half the radius. The name edge effect comes from here: the bending is confined to the neighbourhood of the edge or of another place where membrane theory does not hold, and decays quickly in the direction perpendicular to it (VK §17.5, PDF p. 512). The edge may be a physical one or a contact with another shell (section 22.7).

What do the assumptions of theorem 22.42 cost? The first two cost at most 2 % for our tube, the third we do not estimate with a number. Let us show each in figure 22.67.

  1. Pressure on the middle surface (panel a). The pressure acts on the inner face with radius \(R - h/2\), and we stated it on the middle one. Between two radii that enclose the angle \(\mathrm{d}\theta\) the inner arc has length \((R - h/2)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\) and the middle one \(R\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). Per unit area of the middle surface the pressure therefore gives the force \(p\,(1 - h/(2R))\). The difference is \(h/(2R) = 0{,}02\), that is 2 % for our tube: we overestimate the load by about that much, and the deflection and the moment are too large by as much. The assumption is good because the wall is thin. For a thick-walled tube with \(h = R/2\) the difference would already be 25 %.
  2. Equilibrium on the undeformed shape (panel b). We treated the band on the undeformed shape, but the wall at the plate is inclined by \(w'\). The axial force \(N_1\) on the faces of the band therefore has the radial component \(N_1\,w'\) (step 1 of the proof). It would give the radial load \(N_1\,w'' = N_1\,\omega''\), since \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\) is constant. We compare it with \(D\,\omega''''\). By item 3 of theorem 22.43 \(N_1|\omega''| \le 2\beta^2N_1c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\) and because of \(\omega'''' = -4\beta^4\omega\) we have \(D|\omega''''| \le 4\beta^4Dc\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\). The ratio of the estimates is \(N_1/(2D\beta^2) = 0{,}016\) at \(N_1 = 75\) N/mm and \(D\beta^2 = 2372\) N/mm (num-06.out A), that is 1,6 %. For a tensile axial force the sign is such that the tube is slightly stiffened. For a compressive axial force the sign is opposite and the tube is slightly softened. For a large enough compressive force the ratio is no longer small and the tube can buckle, which the equation without this term does not capture.
  3. The Kirchhoff-Love assumption (panel c). By it a fibre of the wall stays perpendicular to the middle line, so we neglect the transverse shear deformation, as for the beam (definition 5.14). For the beam this error is small when the depth is small compared with the length over which the bending changes. Here that length is \(1/\beta = 7{,}78\) mm against the thickness \(h = 2\) mm, the ratio is \(h\beta = 0{,}26\). For a thick wall or a very short disturbance, when the ratio is close to \(1\), the assumption no longer holds. We do not estimate this error with a number, since that would need a shell theory with shear deformation.

22.6.3 Clamped and simply supported edge

Now we can finish the tube we started with. The pressure and the axial force are known and the edge is clamped, so we determine \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) from the boundary conditions.

Lemma 22.45 Clamped edge of a long pressurised tube (vpeti rob dolge cevi pod tlakom)

Let the tube of theorem 22.43 be closed, \(N_1 = pR/2\), with a clamped edge \(w(0) = 0\), \(w'(0) = 0\) and bounded deflection on \([0, \infty)\). Then

\[w = w_{\mathrm{p}}\Big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta x)\Big) , \qquad w_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{pR^2}{Eh}\Big(1 - \frac{\nu}{2}\Big) , \tag{22.46}\]
\[M(0) = \frac{p}{2\beta^2}\Big(1 - \frac{\nu}{2}\Big) , \qquad Q(0) = \frac{p}{\beta}\Big(1 - \frac{\nu}{2}\Big) . \tag{22.47}\]

The axial stress on the faces at the edge is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N_1/h \pm 6M(0)/h^2 = \dfrac{pR}{2h}\Big(1 \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt3\,(1 - \nu/2)}{\sqrt{1 - \nu^2}}\Big)\), with the plus sign on the inner face. The hoop stress at the edge on the middle surface is \(\nu N_1/h\).

Proof

First we determine \(C_1\), \(C_2\) from the boundary conditions, then \(M\) and \(Q\) with theorem 22.42.

  1. By lemma 22.36 \(N_1 = pR/2\), so \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\) = (p - \nu p/2)R^2/(Eh) = pR^2(1 - \nu/2)/(Eh)$.
  2. By theorem 22.43 \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}} + \omega\) with \(\omega = \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x)\). Its derivatives at the edge, at \(0\), are \(\omega(0) = C_1\), \(\omega'(0) = \beta(C_2 - C_1)\), \(\omega''(0) = -2\beta^2C_2\) and \(\omega'''(0) = 2\beta^3(C_1 + C_2)\) (SymPy, num-06.out B).
  3. From \(w(0) = 0\) we get \(C_1 = -w_{\mathrm{p}}\) and from \(w'(0) = 0\) we get \(C_2 = C_1 = -w_{\mathrm{p}}\), these are the two conditions of the clamped edge. This is the equation (22.46).
  4. By item 3 of theorem 22.42 \(M(0)\) = D,w''(0) = -2D\beta^2C_2 = 2D\beta^2w_p\(. From \)4D\beta^4 = Eh/R^2\( we get \)2D\beta^2 = Eh/(2R^2\beta^2)\(, so \)M(0) = Eh,w_p/(2R^2\beta^2) = p(1 - \nu/2)/(2\beta^2)$.
  5. Similarly \(Q(0)\) = -D,w'''(0) = -2D\beta^3(C_1 + C_2) = 4D\beta^3w_p = p(1 - \nu/2)/\beta$.
  6. By theorem 5.35 the stress due to the moment is \(-M\,y/I\) with \(I = h^3/12\) per unit width, on the face \(y = \mp h/2\) so \(\pm 6M/h^2\) (the bending part), and the axial force contributes \(N_1/h\) (the membrane part). From the equation (22.43) \(\beta^2 = \sqrt{3(1 - \nu^2)}/(Rh)\), so \(6M(0)/h^2 = 3p(1 - \nu/2)/(h^2\beta^2) = \sqrt3\,(1 - \nu/2)\,pR/(h\sqrt{1 - \nu^2})\), which is in the theorem.
  7. At the edge \(w = 0\), so \(N_2 = \nu N_1\) by item 3 of theorem 22.42 and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \nu N_1/h\) on the middle surface.

Source: VK example 15.2 (PDF pp. 433-434) for \(R = 1{,}2\) m, \(h = 0{,}01\) m has \(M_0 = p(1 - \nu/2)/(2\beta^2)\) and \(Q_0 = -p(1 - \nu/2)/\beta\). The sign of \(Q_0\) is opposite to ours, since VK has \(Q_1 = \mathrm{d}M_1/\mathrm{d}x\) and we have \(Q = -M'\).

The numbers for our tube (num-06.out C): \(M(0) = 77{,}167\) N mm/mm, \(Q(0) = 19{,}838\) N/mm and the bending stress \(6M(0)/h^2 = 115{,}75\) MPa. In figure 22.62, c, we add it across the wall thickness \(h\) to the membrane axial stress \(37{,}50\) MPa. The axial stress is therefore \(37{,}50 + 115{,}75 = 153{,}25\) MPa on the inner face and \(37{,}50 - 115{,}75 = -78{,}25\) MPa on the outer one. This is \(4{,}09\) times the membrane axial stress and \(2{,}04\) times the membrane hoop stress \(75\) MPa. The ratio of the bending stress to the membrane hoop stress, \(\sqrt3\,(1 - \nu/2)/\sqrt{1 - \nu^2} = 1{,}543\), does not depend on \(R\) and \(h\): a thin tube at a clamp is not safe merely because the membrane stress is small. The hoop stress at the edge is, because of \(w = 0\), only \(\nu N_1/h = 11{,}25\) MPa instead of \(75\) MPa. For a tube with \(R = 1{,}2\) m and \(h = 0{,}01\) m our formula gives \(M(0) = 3{,}087\cdot 10^{-3}\,p\) N m/m, which agrees with VK, who writes \(3{,}08\cdot 10^{-3}\,p\) (PDF p. 434) and cuts off the last digit. Besides the axial moment the wall has by Hooke's law also the hoop moment \(M_2 = D(\kappa_2 + \nu\kappa_1) = \nu M_1\) (theorem 22.28, \(\kappa_2 = 0\) by step 5 of the proof of theorem 22.42). The hoop bending stress is therefore \(\nu\) times the axial bending stress, with the same sign on each face, and at the edge it gives \(\pm 6\nu M(0)/h^2 = \pm 34{,}7\) MPa on the faces, tension on the inner face.

What about a support that does not clamp? For a tube that merely must not move outward but may rotate we have the following lemma.

Lemma 22.46 Simply supported edge of a long pressurised tube (členkasto podprt rob dolge cevi pod tlakom)

Let the tube be as in lemma 22.45 and let the edge have \(w(0) = 0\) and \(M(0) = 0\). Then

\[w = w_{\mathrm{p}}\big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x\big) , \qquad M(x) = -2D\beta^2w_{\mathrm{p}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x , \tag{22.48}\]

\(|M|\) reaches its maximum at \(\beta x = \pi/4\) and \(\max|M| = \mathrm{e}^{-\pi/4}\,M_{\mathrm{v}}/\sqrt2 = 0{,}322\,M_{\mathrm{v}}\), where \(M_{\mathrm{v}}\) is the moment at the clamped edge from lemma 22.45. The deflection is largest at \(\beta x = 3\pi/4\) and equals \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\big(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3\pi/4}/\sqrt2\big) = 1{,}067\,w_{\mathrm{p}}\).

Proof
  1. With \(\omega\) from theorem 22.43 and the derivatives from step 2 of lemma 22.45, \(w(0) = w_{\mathrm{p}} + C_1 = 0\), so \(C_1 = -w_{\mathrm{p}}\). The condition \(M(0) = D\,\omega''(0) = -2D\beta^2C_2 = 0\) gives \(C_2 = 0\). This is the first equality in (22.48).
  2. The second derivative of \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x\) is \(2\beta^2\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\) (theorem 9.34, item 3, twice), so \(M\)\( = D\,w'' = -2D\beta^2w_{\mathrm{p}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\).
  3. Let \(g(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-t}\sin t\) for \(t = \beta x\). The derivative \(g' = \mathrm{e}^{-t}(\cos t - \sin t)\) is positive on \([0, \pi/4)\) and negative on \((\pi/4, 5\pi/4)\). So \(g\) on \([0, \pi]\) is largest at \(\pi/4\) with the value \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi/4}/\sqrt2 = 0{,}3224\). For \(t \ge \pi\), \(|g| \le \mathrm{e}^{-\pi} = 0{,}0432 < 0{,}3224\). With \(2D\beta^2w_{\mathrm{p}} = M_{\mathrm{v}}\) (step 4 of lemma 22.45) this is the claim about the moment.
  4. Deflection: \(w' = w_{\mathrm{p}}\beta\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta x)\) and \(\cos t + \sin t = \sqrt2\sin(t + \pi/4)\). So the derivative is positive on \([0, 3\pi/4)\), zero at \(t = 3\pi/4\) and negative on \((3\pi/4, 7\pi/4)\). At \(t = 3\pi/4\), \(\cos t = -1/\sqrt2\), so \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}}\big(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3\pi/4}/\sqrt2\big) = 1{,}067\,w_{\mathrm{p}}\). For \(t \ge 7\pi/4\), \(w - w_{\mathrm{p}} = -w_{\mathrm{p}}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\cos t \le w_{\mathrm{p}}\mathrm{e}^{-7\pi/4} = 0{,}0041\,w_{\mathrm{p}}\), which is less. So this is the largest deflection.

Source: VK (15.57) (PDF p. 431) gives the deflection and the moment for general \(M_0\) and \(Q_0\) at the edge. The special case of the simply supported edge is our derivation from theorem 22.43.

For our tube \(\max|M| = 24{,}878\) N mm/mm at \(\beta x = \pi/4\), that is \(x = 6{,}11\) mm, the bending stress is \(37{,}32\) MPa, the shear force at the edge \(Q(0) = 2D\beta^3w_{\mathrm{p}} = 9{,}919\) N/mm and the deflection has its maximum \(1{,}067\,w_{\mathrm{p}}\) at \(18{,}33\) mm (num-06.out D). A simple support therefore does not remove bending. At the edge the moment is indeed zero, as we required, but a third of the clamped moment is reached already \(6{,}11\) mm away. The bending has moved into the interior of the wall.

22.6.4 The short tube

Theorem 22.43 held for a tube that starts at \(x = 0\) and does not end. How long must a real tube be for this to be good? Take a tube clamped at both ends, of length \(L\). Now we may no longer drop \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}\), because \(x\) does not reach infinity. We determine the solution with all four functions from four conditions (\(w\) and \(w'\) at \(0\) and \(L\)) and compare the moment at the edge with the value for the long tube, \(77{,}167\) N mm/mm.

\(L\) (mm) \(\beta L\) \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta L}\) \(M(0)\) (N mm/mm) \(M(0)/77{,}167\) \(w(L/2)\) (\(\mu\)m)
10 1,285 0,277 20,84 0,270 0,452
20 2,571 0,0765 65,32 0,847 5,463
30 3,856 0,0211 81,57 1,057 13,273
50 6,427 0,0016 77,10 0,999 17,659
100 12,854 \(2{,}6\cdot 10^{-6}\) 77,17 1,000 16,203

In figure 22.68 let us draw three tubes of the table, each between its two clamped edges and all on one scale of length. The dashed line in each row is \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\), to which the wall would widen without edges, the orange curve is the deflection. At \(L = 10\) mm the two edges are hardly \(1{,}3/\beta\) apart, the disturbances from both edges overlap and the short tube is so stiff that the moment is only 27 % of the value for the long tube and \(w(L/2) = 0{,}452\ \mu\)m: the wall hardly rises between the edges. The formula for the long tube would give \(w(L/2) = 4{,}291\ \mu\)m, so it does not hold there either. At \(L = 30\) mm the wall reaches \(0{,}82\,w_{\mathrm{p}}\) in the middle, and at \(100\) mm each edge has its own disturbance as in figure 22.66, I, and between them the wall is at \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\). At \(L = 30\) mm the error of \(M(0)\) is \(+5{,}7\) %, at \(50\) mm it is \(-0{,}09\) %. The error is not equal to \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta L}\) and it oscillates. From the computation for \(\beta L \in [1, 8]\) (num-06.out I) it is at most \(4{,}1\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta L}\), below \(5\) % for \(\beta L \ge 4{,}33\) and below \(1\) % for \(\beta L \ge 5{,}57\). VK (15.54), (15.55) (PDF p. 431) gives \(\beta L \ge 3\), that is \(L \ge 2{,}3\sqrt{Rh} = 23\) mm, for an error of 5 % in stresses. For the moment at the clamped edge, however, we get an error of \(2{,}8\) % at \(\beta L = 3\) and \(5{,}7\) % at \(\beta L = 3{,}86\), so for this quantity we take \(\beta L \ge 4{,}33\), that is \(L \ge 33{,}7\) mm or \(0{,}67\,R\). This is a result of a computation, not a proof. What is proved is only that the correction at the other edge comes from terms of size \(c\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta L}\) (theorem 22.43, item 3).

What have we shown? Bending appears in the wall because the clamp or support demands a different deflection than the membrane gives. The equation of the cylinder (theorem 22.42) is the equation of a beam on a Winkler foundation whose foundation is the hoop forces. The solution decays as \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\) from the edge (theorem 22.43) and the disturbance almost vanishes over the length \(\pi/\beta = 2{,}44\sqrt{Rh}\) (corollary 22.44). At the clamp the stress is \(153{,}25\) MPa, at the simple support \(37{,}32\) MPa of bending. A long tube has its two edges independent, a short one does not. We use the same edge effect in the next section at the junction of a tube and a hemisphere.

22.7 Junctions of shells

The wall of a pressure vessel has two parts that we know from sections 22.5 and 22.6: a cylinder and the hemisphere that closes it. We know each part alone: both by membrane theory, the cylinder also by the bending of the cylinder. What happens on the circle where they meet? Does the membrane state stay there, or does an edge effect appear as at a clamped edge? And if it appears, how large is it?

Take the vessel of section 22.5.1: a steel tube with mid-surface radius \(R = 50\) mm and thickness \(h = 2\) mm, closed by a hemisphere of the same radius and thickness, filled with oil at pressure \(p = 3\) MPa, which pushes the wall outward. The thickness becomes visible when we magnify the wall, and the middle surface \(S\) runs through the middle of the thickness. The steel has \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). An axisymmetric load means that everything repeats the same way around the axis. So the lower half of the section is the mirror image of the upper one, and the upper half of the axial section (osni prerez), the section by a plane through the axis, is enough.

We name four idealizations, each with why it holds here, when it does not and how much it changes the result.

  1. The joint of the two shells has no notch and no stiff ring: the cylinder passes into the hemisphere with the same thickness and without a step. This is the vessel we choose here. A stiff ring or a thick flat end would hold the end of the cylinder back, and the limiting case, a rigid clamp, is compared with the junction at the end of the section: the largest bending stress is \(10{,}5\) times larger there.
  2. The material is linearly elastic and homogeneous, with the same \(E\) and \(\nu\) in both shells. All stresses we compute in the example below are under \(80\) MPa, which is less than \(40\) % of the yield stress of steel, \(220\) MPa (chapter 3). At a pressure \(2{,}8\) times larger the largest stress near the junction would reach the yield stress, the steel would start to yield there, and the proportionality of force and displacement, on which everything below rests, would no longer hold.
  3. Displacements are small compared with the thickness. The largest displacement, \(w_\mathrm{c} = 16{,}263\) μm, is \(0{,}008\) of the thickness, in the magnified wall it is as thick as the orange line on the outer face. So we compute with the shape before loading. The radius changes by \(w_\mathrm{c}/R = 0{,}03\) %, and the hoop force \(pR\) computed with the old radius is wrong by that much. With displacements comparable with the thickness we would have to write equilibrium on the displaced shape.
  4. The wall is thin in the sense of section 22.3: the ratio \(h/(2R) = 0{,}02\) bounds the neglected factor \(1 + z/R\), and the outer and inner arcs of the wall are in the ratio \(51 : 49\) (outer and inner arc in figure 22.30). By section 22.5 the membrane stress is therefore wrong by less than \(4\) % in the cylinder and \(6\) % in the hemisphere, and in a thick tube with \(h/R = 0{,}4\) by \(36\) %.

Figure 22.70 builds the answer in three rows. In each row we draw the upper half of the axial section, so each shell is a single line, its middle surface.

We start with the axis of revolution, dashed in every row. Then we draw the position before loading: the straight line of the cylinder and the quarter circle of the hemisphere, meeting at a point at height \(R\) above the axis. The first row shows the pressure acting on each shell alone. The cylinder widens under it by \(w_\mathrm{c}\), because the oil presses on the wall from all sides and pushes it outward. The hemisphere widens less, by \(w_\mathrm{s}\).

Why less? The wall of each shell is held together by the hoop force \(N_\theta\), the force in the wall along the circumference. The cylinder has \(N_\theta = pR\) and the hemisphere \(N_\theta = pR/2\) (lemma 22.36), which we see on two free bodies. We cut the cylinder along its axis (pressure and hoop forces in the right figure of 22.52): the pressure pushes the upper half up with the force \(p \cdot 2R\) per unit length, since the half seen from the side is \(2R\) wide, and two walls hold it, so \(N_\theta = pR\). We cut the hemisphere off along the junction circle (the cap in figure 22.69): the pressure pushes it with the force \(p\pi R^2\), and the wall holds it along the whole circumference \(2\pi R\), so with \(pR/2\) per unit length. A sphere is the same in all directions, so every cut through its centre is like this one, also the cut through the axis, on which the hoop force acts. So the hoop force is \(pR/2\), half that of the cylinder.

A ring that widens by \(w\) stretches its circumference \(2\pi R\) to \(2\pi(R + w)\), that is by \(2\pi w\) or by the fraction \(w/R\). By Hooke's law for shells (theorem 22.28) this fraction equals \((N_\theta - \nu N_{\mathrm{x}})/(Eh)\), where \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the force in the wall along the meridian. It is \(pR/2\) in both shells, as the same cap shows, so the difference of the displacements comes only from the difference of the hoop forces, \(pR - pR/2 = pR/2\), and the smaller hoop force means the smaller displacement. By lemma 22.35

\[w_\mathrm{c} = \frac{pR^2}{Eh}\Big(1 - \frac{\nu}{2}\Big) = 16{,}263\ \mu\text{m} , \qquad w_\mathrm{s} = \frac{pR^2}{2Eh}(1 - \nu) = 6{,}696\ \mu\text{m} , \tag{22.49}\]

and the difference, which we write as the gap \(\Delta\), is

\[\Delta = w_\mathrm{c} - w_\mathrm{s} = \frac{pR^2}{Eh}\Big(1 - \frac{\nu}{2} - \frac{1 - \nu}{2}\Big) = \frac{pR^2}{2Eh} = 9{,}566\ \mu\text{m} . \tag{22.50}\]

The two shells have to be joined somehow, there is no gap in the wall. What happens in the axial direction is shown by the cap cut off along the junction circle (figure 22.69 bottom left). The pressure \(p\) presses on the inner side of the cap. How large its axial force is, the oil in the cap tells. The oil is at rest, and the oil of the cylinder presses on it over the flat cut, which is a disc of area \(\pi R^2\), with the force \(p\pi R^2\). So the wall of the cap pushes it back with the same force, and the oil pushes the wall of the cap with the equal force \(p\pi R^2\) to the left (Newton's third law). The cylinder holds the cap with the force \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) per unit length along the whole circumference \(2\pi R\), so \(2\pi R\,N_{\mathrm{x}} = p\pi R^2\) and \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = pR/2 = 75\) N/mm (theorem 22.32 on the equilibrium of a shell of revolution). With the force with which the cylinder pulls the cap, the cap pulls the cylinder back, so at the junction both shells carry the same axial force \(pR/2\) and the two axial forces balance each other.

Radially, however, the ends do not match: the end of the cylinder would widen by \(\Delta\) more than the end of the hemisphere. Since the wall must not tear, the junction has to push the ends together with radial forces. In the middle row we therefore cut the junction and move the shells apart, as with a free body in statics. The end of the cylinder stays higher than the end of the hemisphere. The junction that holds them together pushes the end of the cylinder inward and the end of the hemisphere outward, each toward the position of the other. The two forces \(Q_0\) are equally large, because they are a pair of action and reaction between the shells (Newton's third law), and we measure them in N/mm of length of the junction circle. The two axial forces point from each shell toward the junction, each pulls its own end toward the other shell. We do not know the moment at the junction yet. We draw it as a pair \(M_0\) that turns the two ends in opposite directions, since the two moments are also a pair of action and reaction. How large it is, also whether it is zero, the calculation tells.

The last row shows the result we shall compute: the wall is a single line that joins the two parts, and at the junction the displacement is the same for both sides. The end of the cylinder has come down from its membrane position by \(\Delta/2\), the end of the hemisphere has gone up by \(\Delta/2\). Grey is again the position before loading. The departure from the membrane displacements is visible only near the junction, far from it the wall behaves as a membrane. Whether this is really so, and how wide the band at the junction is, the calculation will show.

From history

In many problems of thin shells a solution without bending is enough, which assumes stresses uniformly distributed through the thickness, and this was investigated for surfaces of revolution, especially for the sphere and the cylinder (TIMO, PDF p. 350). The general theory of bending of shells was given by Aron and Love, and its first engineering application was Stodola's analysis of stresses in conical shells of constant thickness (TIMO, PDF p. 351). The symmetrically loaded spherical shell of constant thickness was investigated by Reissner. He showed that bending stresses are produced mainly by reactive forces along the fixed edge, and derived equations for calculating these forces (TIMO, PDF p. 351). At our junction this role is played by the force \(Q_0\) and the moment \(M_0\), forced by the difference of the membrane displacements. Meissner and his pupils obtained exact solutions of several practical problems with Reissner's equations. Their usefulness depends on the speed of convergence of the series, and this is poorer for thinner shells (TIMO, PDF p. 351). The source does not give the reason, we see it from our numbers: at \(h = 2\) mm we have \(\beta R = 6{,}43\) and the edge effect dies out within \(\pi/\beta = 24{,}4\) mm, that is \(28{,}0^\circ\) of the meridian, while at \(R/h = 400\) we have \(\beta R = 25{,}7\) and this part is only \(7{,}0^\circ\). A series that has to follow such a narrow layer needs more terms. The difficulty was bypassed by the approximate methods of Blumenthal and Geckeler (TIMO, PDF p. 351). The edge effect, first introduced by Love, was applied by Geckeler to symmetrically loaded spherical shells, and he reduced two coupled differential equations to two independent ones, assuming that for very thin shells the derivatives of the functions are larger than the functions themselves (VK, PDF p. 303).

Let us return to the vessel with the cylinder and the hemisphere and to the gap \(\Delta\) between their membrane displacements. This section does not treat the full equation of an axisymmetric shell, so we take Geckeler's approximation: near its edge the hemisphere is treated as the cylinder that would continue it.

Definition 22.47 Geckeler's approximation (Geckelerjev približek)

Let a spherical shell of radius \(R\) and thickness \(h\) carry an axisymmetric load and let its edge lie at the angle \(\varphi_\mathrm{e}\) between the axis and the normal (for a hemisphere, whose edge is the junction circle, \(\varphi_\mathrm{e} = 90^\circ\)). Let \(s \ge 0\) be the distance from the edge along the meridian. In Geckeler's approximation (a) in the edge-effect equations we neglect the functions and their first derivatives against the higher derivatives and (b) we take the radii of curvature \(R_1 = R_2 = R\) as constant near the edge. The displacement \(w_\mathrm{e}(s)\) of the edge effect (robni učinek), that is the departure from the membrane displacement caused by the forces and the moment at the edge, then solves the same equation as the displacement of a cylinder of radius \(R\) and thickness \(h\) by theorem 22.42, without the right-hand side,

\[D\,w_\mathrm{e}'''' + \frac{Eh}{R^2}\,w_\mathrm{e} = 0 , \tag{22.51}\]

where \(D = Eh^3/(12(1 - \nu^2))\) and \(\beta\) is the same as for the cylinder (theorem 22.43).

Source: The approximation is after VK section 16.4 (PDF pp. 465-466): conditions (a) and (b) are on PDF pp. 465 and 466, the edge-effect equation (16.41) and its analogy with equation (15.44) for the cylinder on PDF p. 466. VK writes it for another unknown, with the parameter (16.42), which for a sphere equals \(\beta R\). VK attributes the approximation to H. Reissner and Geckeler, and Meissner extended it to shells of revolution with an arbitrary meridian (PDF p. 466). The error of the formulas is according to VK of the order \(\sqrt{h\cot^2\varphi_\mathrm{e}/R}\), and they are usable for \(\varphi_\mathrm{e} > 35^\circ\) (PDF p. 469). The approximation is not proved, see the remark below.

What the approximation neglects and how well, the numbers of the vessel tell us. The edge part \(e^{-\beta s}\cos\beta s\) changes over a length of order \(1/\beta = 7{,}78\) mm, so each of its derivatives brings a factor of order \(\beta = 0{,}12854\) 1/mm. The terms the approximation neglects have, in place of a derivative, the factor \(1/R = 0{,}02\) 1/mm, because the geometry of the sphere changes over the length of the radius \(R\). In the figure we see this ratio as a turn of the meridian: over the band of the edge effect of length \(\pi/\beta\) the meridian of the hemisphere turns by \(\pi/(\beta R) = 0{,}489\) rad \(= 28{,}0^\circ\), while the cylinder that would continue it stays straight. The first derivative \(w_\mathrm{e}'\) is therefore of order \(\beta w_\mathrm{e}\), which is \(\beta R = 6{,}43\) times more than \(w_\mathrm{e}/R\), and the second derivative \((\beta R)^2 = 41\) times more than \(w_\mathrm{e}/R^2\). This is not very large, and so the approximation is only an approximation. A comparison is in VK (example 16.1, PDF p. 472): for a hemisphere with the edge at \(\varphi_\mathrm{e} = 90^\circ\) the result of the approximation agrees with the results of the exact equations (16.30) from another source, which VK attributes to \(\varphi_\mathrm{e} = 90^\circ\) and the constant radii of curvature. We have not proved it, and in this section we use it as a given rule.

Now we have everything for the calculation at the junction.

Theorem 22.48 Junction of a cylinder and a hemisphere of equal thickness (spoj valja in polkrogle iste debeline)

Let the cylinder and the hemisphere be of the same material (\(E\), \(\nu\)), both with mid radius \(R\) and thickness \(h\), joined without a notch and without a ring, and let them carry the internal pressure \(p\) with the vessel closed. Let \(x\) be the coordinate along the meridian with its origin at the junction, \(x > 0\) in the cylinder and \(x < 0\) in the hemisphere, so that \(|x|\) is the distance from the junction, \(w(x)\) the radial displacement outward and \(\Delta = pR^2/(2Eh)\) the difference of the membrane displacements from equation (22.50). By Geckeler's approximation (definition 22.47):

  1. The edge part of the displacement is \(w_\mathrm{e}(x) = -\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\,\mathrm{sgn}(x)\,e^{-\beta|x|}\cos\beta x\), and the whole displacement is \(w = w_\mathrm{m} + w_\mathrm{e}\) with \(w_\mathrm{m} = w_\mathrm{c}\) for \(x > 0\) and \(w_\mathrm{m} = w_\mathrm{s}\) for \(x < 0\).
  2. The moment at the junction is \(M_0 = 0\), and the radial force per unit length of the ring is \(Q_0 = D\beta^3\Delta = p/(8\beta)\). The end of the cylinder is pushed inward, the end of the hemisphere outward.
  3. The displacement at the junction is the mean of the membrane displacements, \(w(0) = \tfrac12(w_\mathrm{c} + w_\mathrm{s})\).
  4. The moment along the meridian, \(M = D\,w''\) as in theorem 22.42, is \(M(x) = -(Q_0/\beta)\,e^{-\beta|x|}\sin\beta x\), it has opposite signs in the cylinder and the hemisphere and is largest in size at \(\beta|x| = \pi/4\), where \(|M| = M_{\max} = \dfrac{Q_0}{\beta}\,\dfrac{e^{-\pi/4}}{\sqrt2}\).
  5. The hoop force at the junction is \(N_\theta(0) = \tfrac34\,pR\).
Proof

We must show that the four conditions at the junction determine exactly the four constants of the two edge solutions. We build the solutions from the edge solution of the cylinder, place them at the junction, apply the junction conditions and compute.

  1. On each side the displacement is the sum of the membrane part, which is constant (equation (22.49)), and the edge part, which by definition 22.47 solves equation (22.51). This is the equation of the cylinder without the right-hand side, and its general solution that does not grow with the distance from the junction is given by theorem 22.43: \(w_\mathrm{e} = e^{-\beta x}(A_1\cos\beta x + A_2\sin\beta x)\) for \(x > 0\) and \(w_\mathrm{e} = e^{\beta x}(B_1\cos\beta x + B_2\sin\beta x)\) for \(x < 0\) (in the second case \(|x|\) is the distance from the junction, the same form as for the cylinder).
  2. At \(x = 0\) the product rule (lemma 1.82) and the derivatives of sine and cosine (8.13) give \(w_\mathrm{e}\) and its derivatives of order one to three: \(A_1\), \(\beta(A_2 - A_1)\), \(-2\beta^2A_2\), \(2\beta^3(A_1 + A_2)\) for \(x > 0\), and \(B_1\), \(\beta(B_1 + B_2)\), \(2\beta^2B_2\), \(2\beta^3(B_2 - B_1)\) for \(x < 0\) (SymPy).
  3. There are no external loads at the junction: the pressure acts on the two shells over their area, which on a ring without width gives no force per unit length, and the axial forces \(pR/2\) are equal and so give no radial force. The wall neither tears nor kinks at the junction, so the displacement and the slope are continuous. A ring without width, however, is in equilibrium only if one side acts on it with the same force and the same moment as the other, in the opposite direction, so the moment \(M = D\,w''\) and the transverse force \(Q = -D\,w'''\) are continuous too (theorem 22.42, item 3, for the hemisphere by Geckeler's approximation). The membrane part is constant and contributes nothing to the slope, the moment or the transverse force.
  4. The slope condition gives \(\beta(A_2 - A_1) = \beta(B_1 + B_2)\), the moment condition \(-2\beta^2A_2 = 2\beta^2B_2\), the transverse force condition \(2\beta^3(A_1 + A_2) = 2\beta^3(B_2 - B_1)\). From the moment, \(B_2 = -A_2\). From the transverse force, \(B_1 = -A_1 - 2A_2\). We insert this into the slope: \(A_2 - A_1 = -A_1 - 2A_2 - A_2\), so \(A_2 = -3A_2\) and \(A_2 = 0\). Hence \(B_2 = 0\) and \(B_1 = -A_1\).
  5. The displacement condition \(w_\mathrm{c} + A_1 = w_\mathrm{s} + B_1\) gives \(B_1 - A_1 = \Delta\), so \(-2A_1 = \Delta\), \(A_1 = -\Delta/2\) and \(B_1 = \Delta/2\). So the end of the cylinder moves from its membrane position inward by \(\Delta/2\), the end of the hemisphere outward by \(\Delta/2\). This is item 1 of the theorem, since \(e^{\beta x}\cos\beta x\) for \(x < 0\) equals \(e^{-\beta|x|}\cos\beta x\).
  6. The moment \(M_0\), which we drew as an unknown, is \(M_0 = D\,w_\mathrm{e}''(0) = -2D\beta^2A_2 = 0\). The transverse force is \(-D\,w_\mathrm{e}'''(0) = -2D\beta^3(A_1 + A_2) = D\beta^3\Delta\). Since \(4D\beta^4 = Eh/R^2\) (the definition of \(\beta\) in theorem 22.43), we have \(D\beta^3 = Eh/(4R^2\beta)\) and \(Q_0 = \dfrac{Eh}{4R^2\beta}\cdot\dfrac{pR^2}{2Eh} = \dfrac{p}{8\beta}\). The edge part on the cylinder is negative at \(x = 0\) (\(A_1 < 0\)), so the junction pushes the end of the cylinder inward, and on the hemisphere (\(B_1 > 0\)) outward. This is item 2.
  7. The displacement at the junction is \(w(0) = w_\mathrm{c} + A_1 = w_\mathrm{c} - \Delta/2 = \tfrac12(w_\mathrm{c} + w_\mathrm{s})\), since \(\Delta = w_\mathrm{c} - w_\mathrm{s}\). This is item 3.
  8. For \(x > 0\) we have \(w_\mathrm{e} = -\tfrac\Delta2e^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x\) and \(w_\mathrm{e}'' = -\Delta\beta^2e^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\), so \(M = D\,w_\mathrm{e}'' = -D\beta^2\Delta\,e^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x = -(Q_0/\beta)\,e^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\). For \(x < 0\) we have \(w_\mathrm{e}'' = -\Delta\beta^2e^{\beta x}\sin\beta x\) in the same notation, where \(\sin\beta x < 0\), and so \(M(x) = -(Q_0/\beta)e^{-\beta|x|}\sin\beta x\), in the hemisphere with the opposite sign to the cylinder. The derivative of \(e^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\) is \(\beta e^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x - \sin\beta x)\) and is zero at \(\tan\beta x = 1\), that is \(\beta x = \pi/4\) (the first zero, here \(|M|\) is largest, since \(M(0) = 0\) and \(M < 0\) up to \(\beta x = \pi\), and at the next zeros \(\beta x = \pi/4 + k\pi\) the value \(|e^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x|\) is smaller by the factor \(e^{-k\pi}\)). There \(\sin(\pi/4) = 1/\sqrt2\), hence \(M_{\max}\). This is item 4.
  9. The axial force stays \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = pR/2\), since the equilibrium of the cap above the junction circle (theorem 22.32) does not depend on the displacement. By Hooke's law for shells (theorem 22.28) \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = C(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,w/R)\) and \(N_\theta = C(w/R + \nu\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}})\) with \(C = Eh/(1 - \nu^2)\), since the hoop strain equals \(w/R\). From the first, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} = N_{\mathrm{x}}/C - \nu w/R\), which we insert into the second: \(N_\theta = C(1 - \nu^2)\,w/R + \nu N_{\mathrm{x}} = Eh\,w/R + \nu N_{\mathrm{x}}\). At \(x = 0\) we have \(w(0) = w_\mathrm{c} - \Delta/2\) and \(Eh\,w_\mathrm{c}/R = pR(1 - \nu/2)\) and \(Eh\,\Delta/(2R) = pR/4\), so \(N_\theta(0) = pR(1 - \nu/2) - pR/4 + \nu pR/2 = \tfrac34\,pR\). This is item 5.

Source: The result \(M_0 = 0\) and \(Q_0 = pR^2D\beta^3/(2Eh) = p\sqrt{Rh}\,/\big(8\sqrt[4]{3(1 - \nu^2)}\big)\) is in VK, example 16.2 (PDF pp. 472 to 474), there from the conditions of continuity of displacement and slope with unit loads. The value \(\tfrac34pR\) for the hoop force is also there ("\(1{,}125\,p\)" at \(R = 1{,}5\) m, PDF p. 474), and \(M_{\max}\) with the same formula. The proof by symmetry of the edge solutions is not from the source.

What have we shown? With equal thickness and equal radius the junction carries only the radial force \(Q_0\) and no moment. The reason is the equality of the two edge solutions: both have the same \(\beta\), the same stiffness \(D\) and the same radius, so each end moves by half the gap, each in its own direction. The curve of the displacement is therefore point-symmetric about the junction: if we turn the curve \(w\) by \(180^\circ\) about the dot at the junction, it covers itself. So the slope to the left and to the right of the dot is the same already without a moment (step 4). With another thickness or another radius of the hemisphere the two solutions would have different \(\beta\) and \(D\) and \(M_0 \ne 0\), which we do not compute here.

Example 22.49 Stresses at the junction of the vessel (napetosti na spoju posode)

For the vessel from the start of the section we have, by SymPy and NumPy, \(D = 143\,590\) N mm, \(\beta = 0{,}12854\) 1/mm and \(1/\beta = 7{,}780\) mm. The radial force at the junction is \(Q_0 = p/(8\beta) = 2{,}917\) N/mm. The displacement at the junction is \(11{,}480\) μm, the mean of \(16{,}263\) and \(6{,}696\) μm. The moment is largest in size, \(M_{\max} = 7{,}317\) N mm/mm, at \(\beta|x| = \pi/4\), that is \(6{,}11\) mm from the junction, and belongs to the bending stress \(6M_{\max}/h^2 = 10{,}98\) MPa. In the cylinder this stress stretches the outer face in the axial direction (axial stress \(37{,}50\) \(+ 10{,}98 = 48{,}48\) MPa) and reduces the inner one (\(37{,}50 - 10{,}98 = 26{,}52\) MPa), in the hemisphere it is the other way round. The hoop stress at the junction is \(\tfrac34\cdot 75{,}00 = 56{,}25\) MPa, less than the membrane \(75{,}00\) MPa in the cylinder. The moment dies out within the length \(\pi/\beta = 24{,}44\) mm, that is \(28{,}0^\circ\) of the meridian of the hemisphere, and at \(20\) mm we have \(e^{-\beta x} = 0{,}0765\). The hoop stress on the middle surface of the cylinder, \((Eh\,w/R + \nu N_{\mathrm{x}})/h\) by step 9 of the proof, is largest where the displacement \(w\) is largest. This is at \(\beta x = 3\pi/4\), \(18{,}33\) mm from the junction, where \(w\) exceeds \(w_\mathrm{c}\) by a little, and the hoop stress there is \(76{,}26\) MPa, only \(1{,}7\) % above the \(75{,}00\) MPa far from the junction.

Let us look at the course (figure 22.71), to see how what we computed is distributed along the meridian.

Far from the junction the displacement \(w\) lies on the membrane values \(w_\mathrm{s}\) and \(w_\mathrm{c}\). At the junction it is exactly halfway between them and bridges the gap \(\Delta\) over a length of order \(1/\beta\). The moment is zero at the junction and far from it, and in between it reaches its largest absolute value \(M_{\max}\) near the junction, positive in the hemisphere and negative in the cylinder. The moment is odd about the junction, because the edge part of the displacement is odd (item 1 of the theorem): the end of the cylinder gives way inward by \(\Delta/2\), the end of the hemisphere outward by \(\Delta/2\). So in the cylinder the outer face is stretched more in the axial direction, and in the hemisphere the inner one. Below the graph of the moment is the section of the cylinder wall at \(x = 6{,}11\) mm with the outer face on top: the membrane part \(37{,}50\) MPa is the same across the thickness, the bending part raises it to \(48{,}48\) MPa outside and lowers it to \(26{,}52\) MPa inside. On the \(x\) axis two points \(\pm\pi/\beta\) are marked, where the moment first crosses zero again.

The theorem requires the shells to be equal. Let us look at two cases that violate this by a little, to see what the theorem really needs.

A near miss: a rigid end. If the cylinder is closed by a flat end whose stiffness is much larger than the stiffness of the wall, the junction behaves as a rigid clamp: displacement and slope at the edge are zero (lemma 22.45 in section 22.6). The end of the cylinder must now not move, so the edge part has to return all of \(w_\mathrm{c}\) and not only half of the gap. The flat end, being a thin plate, is not perfectly rigid, its true stiffness is treated by chapter 18, so we do not compute stresses of a flat end here. The clamp is a limiting case that shows how far the junction with a hemisphere is from this extreme.

hemisphere (theorem 22.48) rigid clamp (lemma 22.45)
displacement at the junction \(11{,}480\) μm \(0\)
\(M_0\) \(0\) \(77{,}167\) N mm/mm
\(Q_0\) \(2{,}917\) N/mm \(19{,}838\) N/mm
largest bending stress \(10{,}98\) MPa \(115{,}75\) MPa
axial stress on the face \(48{,}48\) MPa \(153{,}25\) MPa

The reason for the difference is the cause that forces the wall to bend: with a hemisphere the edge part of the cylinder has to reduce the displacement by only \(\Delta/2 = 4{,}78\) μm (step 5 of the proof), with a rigid end by the whole \(w_\mathrm{c} = 16{,}263\) μm, that is \(3{,}4\) times more. The transverse force is \(6{,}8\) times larger (\(19{,}838/2{,}917\)): \(3{,}4\) times because of the larger displacement, and \(2\) times more because the clamp also has to return the slope. At the clamp \(Q(0) = p(1 - \nu/2)/\beta = 4D\beta^3w_\mathrm{c}\) (lemma 22.45), with the hemisphere \(Q_0 = D\beta^3\Delta = 2D\beta^3\cdot\Delta/2\) (step 6 of the proof). The largest bending stress is \(10{,}5\) times larger. The largest axial stress at the rigid end, \(153{,}25\) MPa, is \(2{,}04\) times the hoop stress \(75{,}00\) MPa far from the end, while with the hemisphere it stays below it at \(48{,}48\) MPa. How an end really answers is the task of the plate (chapter 18).

A near miss: a cone. We close the cylinder with a cone instead of a hemisphere. The theorem does not hold here: in step 3 of its proof we claimed that there is no radial force at the junction, but the membrane force of the cone has a radial component. The thickness \(h\), the radius \(R\) at the junction, the material and the pressure stay the same, only the direction of the head at the junction differs.

First we draw the axis of revolution and the wall of the cylinder with the head on the right, which meets the cylinder at the junction \(K\). In the left figure the head is a hemisphere: its tangent at \(K\) is parallel to the axis, so the head pulls the ring to the right with \(pR/2\), the cylinder to the left with the same \(pR/2\), and the forces balance, \(H = 0\). In the right figure the head is a cone that runs from \(K\) downward toward the axis along a generatrix. The meridian force of the cone \(N_{\mathrm{s}}\) is now inclined and has two components: an axial one that balances the force of the cylinder, and a radial one, \(H\), inward, which has nothing to balance it. How large the two are is told by the equilibrium of the cap.

Lemma 22.50 Radial force at the cone-to-cylinder junction (radialna sila na spoju stožca in valja)

Let a cylinder of mid radius \(R\) be closed by a cone of half-angle \(\alpha\) between the axis and the generatrix (\(0 \le \alpha < 90^\circ\)), loaded by the internal pressure \(p\) with the vessel closed. By membrane theory (section 22.4) the meridian force of the cone at the junction is \(N_{\mathrm{s}} = pR/(2\cos\alpha)\), its axial component is \(pR/2\) and equals the axial force of the cylinder, and the radial component, which has no opposing force, is

\[H = N_{\mathrm{s}}\sin\alpha = \frac{pR\tan\alpha}{2} \tag{22.52}\]

per unit length of the junction circle, directed toward the axis. For a hemisphere \(H = 0\).

Proof

We must show the axial equilibrium of the cap above the junction and then split the force \(N_{\mathrm{s}}\) into components.

  1. We cut off the cap of the cone above the junction circle, as the cap in theorem 22.32. The pressure \(p\) on its inner side has the axial resultant \(p\pi R^2\), since the projection of the inner surface onto the plane of the junction circle is a disc of radius \(R\). The reason is the same as for the cap of the hemisphere: the oil in the cap is at rest, so the axial force of the wall on it equals the force of the pressure on the flat cut, whatever the shape of the cap.
  2. The force \(N_{\mathrm{s}}\) per unit length of the circle points along the generatrix, which makes the angle \(\alpha\) with the axis, and over the whole circumference of length \(2\pi R\) its axial component is \(2\pi R\,N_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\alpha\).
  3. Axial equilibrium of the cap: \(2\pi R\,N_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\alpha = p\pi R^2\), so \(N_{\mathrm{s}} = pR/(2\cos\alpha)\) and the axial component \(N_{\mathrm{s}}\cos\alpha = pR/2\), equal to the axial force of the cylinder.
  4. The radial component is \(N_{\mathrm{s}}\sin\alpha = pR\tan\alpha/2\). For a hemisphere the tangent of the meridian at the junction is parallel to the axis, so \(\alpha = 0\) and \(H = 0\).

Source: The proof is not from the source. That the horizontal component of the meridian force at the edge of a shell requires a supporting ring is in VK (PDF p. 380) for a dome, and in example 16.3 (PDF pp. 475 to 476) the horizontal component \(T_0\) of the membrane force at the edge of the head is completed by an equal and opposite thrust among the forces of the edge effect.

At \(p = 3\) MPa and \(R = 50\) mm equation (22.52) gives for the force \(H\) (SymPy and NumPy):

\(\alpha\) \(30^\circ\) \(45^\circ\) \(60^\circ\)
\(H\) (N/mm) \(43{,}30\) \(75{,}00\) \(129{,}90\)

The axial component is always \(75{,}00\) N/mm. In the right figure of 22.72 the force \(H\) at \(45^\circ\) is as long as the axial component, \(1{,}5\) cm, because \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\). For the hemisphere the whole radial force that the junction has to carry is \(Q_0 = 2{,}917\) N/mm. For the cone of \(45^\circ\) the force \(H\) is already \(75{,}00/2{,}917 = 25{,}7\) times larger before any response of the junction. The transverse force condition in step 3 of the proof of theorem 22.48 turns for the cone from continuity into a jump: the radial force of the edge effect on the end of the head differs from the one on the end of the cylinder by \(H\) (this is how VK divides the forces in example 16.3 for a head shaped as a spherical segment, PDF p. 476). We do not compute the solution, because it requires a separate calculation of the edge effect of the cone.

A remark on what stays open. Geckeler's approximation is quoted and not proved, so the proof of the theorem is conditional on it. A proof would need the full edge equation of an axisymmetric shell of revolution (VK, sections 16.2 to 16.3, PDF pp. 454 to 465) and an estimate of the error, which VK gives only as the order \(\sqrt{h\cot^2\varphi_\mathrm{e}/R}\) (PDF p. 469). A different thickness or radius, and a spherical segment instead of a hemisphere, are treated by VK in example 16.3 (PDF pp. 475 to 477). A flat end would require plates (chapter 18), and the same equation is also the equation of a beam on an elastic foundation, which chapter 25 treats.

The next section shows how we compute this edge effect in a finite element program.

22.8 The axisymmetric cylinder element (osnosimetrični element valja)

In the section on bending of the cylinder we worked out the edge of a tube by hand: the equation \(D\,w'''' + (Eh/R^2)\,w = q\) has a closed solution because the radius and the thickness are constant and the load is simple (theorem 22.42, theorem 22.43). A vessel in practice is not like that. The thickness changes at a junction, the shell turns into a cone or a bottom, the pressure changes with height. Programs do not solve such vessels with a closed formula, they divide them into elements, as we divided the beam in chapter 12. This section shows that the element for a cylinder is almost in the book already: it is the beam element of chapter 12 with one more matrix. We then test it on the same tube as before, at the edge where the solution is not smooth, and see how long an element may be so that the moment at the clamp is not wrong. At the end we say what the conical element changes and how the results of an element give the stresses that a program prints.

The tube is the same as in the previous sections: mid-surface radius \(R = 50\) mm, thickness \(h = 2\) mm, steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), internal pressure \(p = 3\) MPa, closed ends. Data: \(D = Eh^3/(12(1 - \nu^2)) = 143\,590\) N mm, \(k = Eh/R^2 = 156{,}80\) N/mm\(^3\), \(\beta = (k/4D)^{1/4} = 0{,}12854\) mm\(^{-1}\), so \(1/\beta = 7{,}780\) mm. Notation: \(h\) is the wall thickness here (as in the whole chapter), so for the element length we write \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) where chapter 12 wrote \(h\). The letter \(K\) is the structure stiffness matrix as in chapter 12, not the Gaussian curvature. The number \(\beta\) is the decay constant of the edge, not \(\beta_{\mathrm{h}}\) of chapter 12, and \(D\) is the bending stiffness of the shell, not the dynamic factor of definition 9.64.

22.8.1 Energy of a cylinder strip (energija traku valja)

First we say what we compute. Figure 22.73 shows the body in a section through the axis: a thin cylindrical shell (definition 22.1) with mid-surface radius \(R\), constant thickness \(h\) and length \(L\). There are three idealizations. The first is Kirchhoff-Love (definition 22.24): the normal of the middle surface stays straight and normal to the deformed surface, the transverse stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is neglected, displacements are small. The second is that the pressure acts on the middle surface, not on the inner wall. The error is at most \(h/(2R) = 0{,}02\) relative to the radius, as in dropping the factor \(1 + z/R\) in the section on the kinematics of the shell (theorem 22.26). The third is axial symmetry: load, supports and material are the same on every circle around the axis (parallel circle), so the radial displacement \(w\) (positive outward) and the axial displacement \(u\) are functions of \(x\) only, where \(x\) is the distance along the axis. The solution is thus one-dimensional, which is the reason that the element can be a beam.

We count the energy per unit circumference: for the part of the shell over an arc of the middle circle of length 1 mm. The unit is N mm/mm. In this way \(R\) does not enter as a factor and the comparison with the beam is direct. The axial force per unit circumference \(N_0\) is known from equilibrium: in a closed cylinder the pressure on the end plate of area \(\pi R^2\) (the plate counted up to the mid-surface radius) is balanced by the force \(N_0\) per unit circumference of the wall, \(N_0\cdot 2\pi R\) in all (Newton's law for the free body of the cut cylinder, lemma 22.36), so \(N_0 = pR/2 = 75\) N/mm.

Lemma 22.51 Energy of a cylinder strip (energija traku valja)

Let the cylinder be as above, loaded axisymmetrically by the internal pressure \(p\) and the axial force \(N_0\) per unit circumference, and let at least one end be free in the axial direction. Let \(C = Eh/(1 - \nu^2)\), \(D = Eh^3/(12(1 - \nu^2))\), \(k = Eh/R^2\). Then:

  1. The potential energy per unit circumference (stretch, widening of the ring, bending, work of the pressure and of the force) is
    \[\Pi[u, w] = \int_0^L \Big[ \tfrac12 C\Big(u'^2 + 2\nu\,u'\,\frac{w}{R} + \frac{w^2}{R^2}\Big) + \tfrac12 D\,w''^2 - p\,w - N_0\,u' \Big]\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{22.53}\]
  2. The axial force \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) equals \(N_0\) everywhere. When \(u\) is eliminated from the energy, what remains, up to a constant, is
    \[\tilde\Pi[w] = \int_0^L \Big[ \tfrac12 D\,w''^2 + \tfrac12 k\,w^2 - q\,w \Big]\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad q = p - \frac{\nu N_0}{R} . \tag{22.54}\]
  3. A field \(w\) for which \(\tilde\Pi\) is stationary satisfies \(D\,w'''' + k\,w = q\) with the natural conditions \(w'' = 0\) and \(w''' = 0\) at an end where \(w\) and \(w'\) are not prescribed. This is the equation of theorem 22.42, derived from the energy.
Proof

We must show three claims: the expression for the energy from the strains, the elimination of \(u\), and stationarity.

  1. Kinematics (theorem 22.26, for a cylinder with axis \(x\) and hoop direction \(\theta\)): the axial strain of the middle surface is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} = u'\). A ring of radius \(R\) becomes a ring of radius \(R + w\) after the displacement \(w\), its length \(2\pi R\) becomes \(2\pi(R + w)\), so \(\varepsilon_\theta = w/R\). The normal turns in the plane of the meridian by \(w'\), so the change of curvature in the direction \(x\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = -w''\) (positive when the outer face is stretched, because \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon^0 + z\kappa\) with \(z\) outward). A parallel circle stays a circle, so \(\kappa_\theta = 0\). There are no shear terms because of the axial symmetry.
  2. By theorem 22.28, for the forces and the moment on an element of the wall, \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = C(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\varepsilon_\theta)\), \(N_\theta = C(\varepsilon_\theta + \nu\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}})\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\kappa_\theta) = -D\,w''\). By theorem 22.29 the energy per unit area is \(\tfrac12(N_{\mathrm{x}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} + N_\theta\varepsilon_\theta + M_{\mathrm{x}}\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + M_\theta\kappa_\theta)\). With \(\kappa_\theta = 0\) this is \(\tfrac12 C(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 2\nu\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}}\varepsilon_\theta + \varepsilon_\theta^2) + \tfrac12 D\,w''^2\).
  3. The pressure \(p\) per unit area does the work \(p\,w\). The force \(N_0\) on the free end does the work \(N_0[u]_0^L = \int_0^L N_0\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(N_0\) is constant. The potential energy is the strain energy minus the work. Steps 1 and 2 give equation (22.53). This proves point 1.
  4. Variation in \(u\): the integrand depends on \(u\) only through \(u'\), and \(\partial(\cdot)/\partial u' = C(u' + \nu w/R) - N_0 = N_{\mathrm{x}} - N_0\). Stationarity requires \((N_{\mathrm{x}} - N_0)' = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{x}} - N_0\) is constant. At the free end \(u\) is not prescribed, so the natural condition there is \(N_{\mathrm{x}} - N_0 = 0\). Hence the axial force \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = N_0\) everywhere.
  5. For a given \(\varepsilon_\theta\), \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = N_0\) is the condition of stationarity of the integrand in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}}\). The value of the integrand at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{x}} = N_0/C - \nu\varepsilon_\theta\) is \(\tfrac12 C(1 - \nu^2)\varepsilon_\theta^2 + \nu N_0\varepsilon_\theta - N_0^2/(2C)\) (checked with SymPy). With \(C(1 - \nu^2) = Eh\) and \(\varepsilon_\theta = w/R\) this is \(\tfrac12 k\,w^2 + \nu N_0 w/R\) up to a constant.
  6. Together with \(\tfrac12 D\,w''^2 - p\,w\) we get \(\tfrac12 D\,w''^2 + \tfrac12 k\,w^2 - (p - \nu N_0/R)\,w\). This is equation (22.54). This proves point 2.
  7. For a variation \(\delta w\), \(\delta\tilde\Pi = \int_0^L (D\,w''\,\delta w'' + k\,w\,\delta w - q\,\delta w)\,\mathrm{d}x\). Integration by parts twice (with \([D\,w''\,\delta w' - D\,w'''\,\delta w]_0^L\)) gives \(\int_0^L (D\,w'''' + k\,w - q)\,\delta w\,\mathrm{d}x + [D\,w''\,\delta w' - D\,w'''\,\delta w]_0^L\). Since \(\delta w\) is arbitrary inside, the integrand is zero. At an end where \(\delta w\) and \(\delta w'\) are not prescribed, \(D\,w'' = 0\) and \(D\,w''' = 0\). This proves point 3.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. Strains and energy are COOK (16.3-3) and (16.3-5) (PDF p. 586) at meridian angle \(0\) to the axis, where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{m}\theta} = w/r\). The cylinder equation is from theorem 22.42.

The proof showed that the energy of the cylinder is the energy of a beam with bending stiffness \(D\) on an elastic foundation of stiffness \(k\). The foundation here is the hoop: whoever wants to widen it must stretch it. The axial force is not an unknown, because equilibrium fixes it, and so \(u\) drops out. For the given tube, \(N_0 = 75\) N/mm, \(q = p - \nu N_0/R = 2{,}55\) MPa, and this is \(p(1 - \nu/2)\), as it must be. Without edges the solution is \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = q/k = 16{,}263\) \(\mu\)m (the ring widens uniformly), as in the equation of theorem 22.42.

The lemma has the condition that at least one end is axially free. What if none is? Let both ends be axially fixed. Then \(\int_0^L u'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) and \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) is constant by step 4, but no longer equal to \(N_0\). In a tube much longer than \(1/\beta\) the edges affect only a small part of the length. If we neglect that part, the axial strain is zero everywhere, so \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = \nu N_\theta = \nu pR = 45\) N/mm instead of 75 N/mm. Then \(q = p(1 - \nu^2) = 2{,}73\) MPa and \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = 17{,}411\) \(\mu\)m instead of \(16{,}263\) \(\mu\)m, a difference of 7 %. The lemma is therefore not self-evident: the elimination of \(u\) at known \(N_0\) works because the axial direction is free.

22.8.2 The cylinder element and its stiffness matrix (element valja in njegova togostna matrika)

Since the energy equals that of a beam on a foundation, we use the Hermite functions (definition 12.1) as in chapter 12. First we say what the element is, then we draw, then we compute.

Definition 22.52 Axisymmetric cylinder element (osnosimetrični element valja)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an interval of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = x_{\mathrm{b}} - x_{\mathrm{a}}\) on the axis \(x\) of the cylinder of lemma 22.51. The axisymmetric cylinder element (osnosimetrični element valja) is the ring of width \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) bounded at both ends by a parallel circle, over \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\). A node (vozlišče) is a whole parallel circle, a circle. The unknowns at each node are the radial displacement \(w\) and the rotation of the normal \(\varphi = w'\), so four in the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (w_1, \varphi_1, w_2, \varphi_2)^\T\). The field of the element is \(w_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the functions \(H_1, \dots, H_4\) of equation (12.1). \(R\), \(h\), \(E\), \(\nu\) and \(q\) are known, all constant on the element.

Explanation

Figure 22.76 shows the element on a meridian. The axis of the cylinder is the dash-dotted line. The middle line is at distance \(R\) from the axis, which the distance \(R\) on the left shows. The element is the part of this line bounded by nodes \(1\) and \(2\), each a parallel circle that we see from the side as a point. After loading, the middle line of the element bends into a cubic curve made of Hermite functions, drawn with a strongly enlarged displacement. The displacement of a node is the distance \(w_1\) or \(w_2\) between the position before loading and after it, since it is radial. The slope of the curve at a node is the rotation \(\varphi_1\) or \(\varphi_2\), the tangent to the curve. The length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the distance between the nodes along the axis. On the right is the section by a plane normal to the axis: a circle of radius \(R\) and, after the displacement \(w\), a circle of radius \(R + w\). That is why the hoop strain is \(w/R\) and why the foundation is elastic.

Figure 22.76 shows that a node is not a point but a ring: the displacement \(w_1\) moves the whole parallel circle by the same distance, so the ring widens uniformly and the hoop forces are the same everywhere. Everything else stays as in chapter 12, except that every radial displacement is now also a stretching of the ring.

Lemma 22.53 Stiffness matrix of a cylinder element (togostna matrika elementa valja)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an axisymmetric cylinder element (definition 22.52). Then:

  1. The energy of the element is \(\Pi_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T(\mat k_{\mathrm{b}} + \mat k_{\mathrm{f}})\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\mat k_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the stiffness matrix of the beam element of lemma 12.4 with \(EI\) replaced by \(D\), \(\mat k_{\mathrm{f}}\) is the mass matrix of lemma 12.43 with \(\rho A\) replaced by \(k\), and
    \[\mat k_{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{k\,h_{\mathrm{e}}}{420}\begin{pmatrix} 156 & 22h_{\mathrm{e}} & 54 & -13h_{\mathrm{e}} \\ 22h_{\mathrm{e}} & 4h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 & 13h_{\mathrm{e}} & -3h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \\ 54 & 13h_{\mathrm{e}} & 156 & -22h_{\mathrm{e}} \\ -13h_{\mathrm{e}} & -3h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 & -22h_{\mathrm{e}} & 4h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = q\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\begin{pmatrix} 1/2 \\ h_{\mathrm{e}}/12 \\ 1/2 \\ -h_{\mathrm{e}}/12 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{22.55}\]
  2. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat k_{\mathrm{b}} + \mat k_{\mathrm{f}}\) is symmetric and positive definite. Unlike the beam element, the cylinder needs no support against radial displacement as a rigid body.
  3. The uniform widening \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}} = q/k\), that is \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (w_{\mathrm{p}}, 0, w_{\mathrm{p}}, 0)^\T\), satisfies \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\).
Proof

We must show that the energy of the element has this form, that the matrix is positive definite and that the uniform widening is a solution.

  1. By lemma 22.51, equation (22.54), the energy of the element is \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}[\tfrac12 D\,w_{\mathrm{h}}''^2 + \tfrac12 k\,w_{\mathrm{h}}^2 - q\,w_{\mathrm{h}}]\,\mathrm{d}x\).
